Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Friday said that the U.S. economy has “broadly” moved in the direction that the central bank expected during its last meeting in September, when it raised rates for the first time since 2023.

In the weeks since, inflation as measured by the consumer price index jumped to 3.7%. For businesses, inflation has hit even harder. That turned investors focus to Warsh’s appearance at the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank for a signal about whether the Fed would hike rates in October or December.

“We made very clear we’d deliver price stability,” Warsh said Friday morning in Bangkok (Thursday night ET), a signal of his focus on inflation and that another interest rate hike is likely on the horizon.
But Warsh stuck to a familiar tone and refused to give any clear hint about how soon that might come. “We’re not in that business anymore,” he said.
However, Warsh, the head of the world’s most important central bank, spoke at length about one major economic force that is causing prices to rise across the economy.
“In the United States, we’re having a massive investment surge,” he said, referencing the seemingly ever-expanding AI boom.
“It’s probably the most important thing that’s happening in the global economy on the upside,” Warsh said. “I think it’s going to fundamentally change the conduct of monetary policy.”
A central feature of the AI boom is an expansive buildout of data centers around the country.

To fund all that building, trillion-dollar companies are spending, and borrowing, big sums for servers, memory and other components. Companies including Apple and Nintendo have raised prices for consumers as a result. “We have never seen a component price increase this much, this quickly,” Apple told NBC News in June.

Companies are also tapping the public debt markets in an unprecedented way. Data center companies and associated utility firms, chipmakers and cloud providers are expected to raise between $300 billion and $570 billion from the debt market this year, according to Vanguard. Those firms are also offering highly attractive interest rates, sometimes better than U.S. Treasury bonds.
Warsh said AI could also “change the real economy,” though he acknowledged not knowing how deeply it would impact employment.

But he projected optimism about the technology’s prospects, predicting that “it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive.” He said it should also generate “more wealth.”
“But the path from where we are to there is likely to be a very bumpy one,” he warned.
Warsh said a Fed task force of outside experts studying the impact of AI on the labor market would hold a public hearing on the topic in November.

“So I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose to the day jobs that you and I have,” Warsh remarked. “I think it’s an exciting development and it’s an innovation that I think a decade from now they’ll look back on and they’ll say this was hugely consequential.”

His comments will be closely scrutinized because they are the last from any Fed official before policymakers enter a “blackout” period on Saturday that lasts through their next interest rate meeting, which is scheduled for Oct. 27 and 28.
Already hammered by soaring interest rates, rising energy prices and stagnant wage growth, American consumers could get an extra dose of financial strain if the Fed raises rates again this month.

Voters are already dissatisfied with President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, polls show, so another rate hike could add to Republicans’ headaches as they face potentially losing their congressional majorities in the midterms.

In recent weeks, Trump has tried to pull multiple policy levers to lower gas and diesel prices, which have pushed inflation higher in recent months. But none of them have yet slowed prices meaningfully.

“Starting on day one, we will end inflation and make America affordable again,” Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024. Inflation as measured by the consumer price index declined to as low as 2.3% four months into Trump’s term.
But that same month, Trump unleashed a wave of tariffs across the globe, dramatically changing the economic story.

By September, inflation breached the 3% threshold again. In February, Trump launched the war against Iran, causing one of the worst energy supply shocks in history. Inflation jumped as high as 4.1% in May, and looks to be headed back in that direction again.

Another Fed rate hike would also further undermine Trump’s yearslong pressure campaign to push the central bank to cut rates. Since Warsh took his post in May, the central bank has either held rates steady or increased them.
Trump hasn’t attacked Warsh after years of hammering former Chair Jerome Powell. But the president has started saying that the other members of the Fed’s board are “very hostile.”

“I’m relying on Kevin,” Trump told reporters in September, “but he’s got, you know, a very tough board. He’s got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high.”
“They’re very political,” Trump said. Four of the Fed’s seven board members were appointed by Trump.

Economists and investors are paying close attention to so-called core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. Both reports this week showed that even this adjusted measure of price growth is running hotter than hoped for.
“Core CPI was the more significant surprise,” wrote analysts at Bank of America.

The core readings showed that skyrocketing fuel prices, particularly diesel, are trickling down. Farmers, truckers and others who keep commerce humming in the United States have to raise their prices in order to digest higher diesel costs. That, in turn, leads to price increases for consumer goods.

“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk told NBC News in an August interview. “Everything from … running a farm … cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped gets that extra fee tacked onto it.” At the time, she described the surge in diesel fuel prices as likely “an inflationary problem for the next several months.”
Despite the challenges facing the U.S. economy, Warsh concluded on an optimistic note, saying that those should strengthen it in the long run.

“What is striking to me are two things: almost everywhere in the global economy showing resilience that I’m not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago, given what’s happening in geopolitics and hot spots around the world.”

Warsh added, “I believe, optimistically, you might think naively, at least in the U.S. we’re going to come out of this stronger, with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.”

New Zealand's Haka explained - meaning and origin of All Blacks' rugby war dance plus Cibi, Siva Tau, Sipi Tau rituals

We look at history of New Zealand's haka in rugby union; the most memorable haka responses over the decades; and at Fiji's Cibi, Samoa's Siva Tau, Tonga's Sipi Tau; Watch All Blacks face Australia in Sydney on Saturday October 17 (6am) live on Sky Sports Main Event
One of the most intriguing and anticipated moments in the sport of rugby union: the sight of New Zealand's All Blacks performing their world-famous haka as the opposition stands before them.
But how much do you know about the haka? And also of the three other ceremonial war dances which take place in rugby: the Cibi, Siva Tau and Sipi Tau.
Find out everything you need to know below...
History of the haka in sport - When did it start? What does it mean?

An ancient traditional Māori practice, there is no single recorded date for the haka's first-ever performance owing to this very reason. It has been practised by indigenous Māori communities for centuries.
The earliest point at which Europeans witnessed the haka was the 18th century: Joseph Banks and James Cook on their first voyage to New Zealand in 1769 recorded the haka as "vigorous and ferocious".

In terms of its introduction into sport, New Zealand's first rugby union side visited Australia in Sydney in 1884 and performed the haka. During 1888/89, a 'New Zealand native team' toured the UK for the first time, performing the haka on October 3 1888 against Surrey in a tour match.
The year 1905 saw the birth of the 'All Blacks' as they toured Britain with a team which came to be known as 'The Originals.'
The All Blacks performed their famous "Ka Mate" haka before Tests against Scotland and Wales, with it having been composed in 1820 by Māori chief Te Rauparaha.
Yet, the tradition of the All Blacks performing the haka on home soil and before every Test they played did not become custom until 1986.
Ahead of rugby's first World Cup in 1987, All Black Buck Shelford set about reforming the haka in order for pre-match performances to be organised, in sync and executed properly.

"If we're going to do it, we're going to do it right. Either perform the haka properly or not at all. Vote on it and decide which way you want to go," Shelford is said to have told team-mates at the time.
Shelford and team-mate Hika Reid subsequently taught and trained the All Blacks squad correct pronunciation of words and actions, and of the haka's importance.
At the 1987 World Cup in New Zealand, with Shelford now captain, the All Blacks performed the haka in New Zealand for the very first time, en route to the All Blacks clinching the trophy.
In terms of what the haka means, "Ka Mate" is the recitation of a traditional Māori poem about life, death and resilience.
The more common haka performed by the All Blacks today is the 'Kapa o Pango', first performed in August 2005 before a Tri-Nations Test against South Africa in Dunedin.
The haka featured an extended and aggressive introduction by team captain Tana Umaga, highlighted by a drawing of the thumb down the throat.
Famous haka responses - how should teams respond?
There have been a number of famous haka responses from opposition sides over the years.

In 1996, Australia famously (or infamously?) decided to totally ignore the haka altogether in Wellington, turning their backs on the All Blacks, following on from Wallabies great David Campese choosing to ignore the haka and do kicking drills ahead of the 1991 Rugby World Cup semi-final between the sides, which Australia won.

In 2019, England adopted a V-shaped formation in Yokohama ahead of their World Cup semi-final against the All Blacks. Once the haka started, English players progressed beyond the halfway line and held their ground as officials tried to move them.

England were later fined £2000 by World Rugby for breaching World Cup 2019 rules relating to cultural challenges, which stated no players from the team receiving the challenge may advance beyond the halfway line. England won the match 19-7 after a sensational performance.

At the 2007 World Cup, France faced the All Blacks in a World Cup quarter-final in Cardiff, and memorably walked up in a line of opposition to the All Blacks, coming within a metre of the haka. France won the match 20-18.
France also marched forward in an arrow-formation facing the haka ahead of the 2011 Rugby World Cup final in New Zealand, before controversially losing 8-7 at Eden Park.

In 2005, the All Blacks agreed to a request from the Welsh Rugby Union to repeat the sequence of events from the original match a century before in 1905, which involved the haka taking place after the New Zealand national anthem but before the Welsh one.

A year later in 2006, Wales demanded a repeat of the sequence, which the All Blacks refused, ultimately performing the haka in the dressing rooms and not in front of the watching fans. Then All Blacks captain Richie McCaw defended the decision by stating the haka was "integral to New Zealand culture and the All Blacks' heritage" and "if the other team wants to mess around, we'll just do the haka in the shed."

Two years later in 2008, another memorable Wales vs New Zealand haka situation unfolded, as following the conclusion of the haka in Cardiff, Wales refused to break and move until the All Blacks did. Neither side did for nearly a minute-and-a-half despite urging from referee Jonathan Kaplan, until McCaw instructed the All Blacks to break off. Wales led 9-6 at half-time but were eventually well beaten 29-9.

In 2016, Ireland faced the All Blacks in Chicago seeking a first-ever win over New Zealand in 111 years. Just weeks prior, Munster coach Anthony Foley had died in his sleep in Paris at the age of 42 ahead of a European Cup contest against Racing 92.

Facing the haka, Ireland lined up in a figure of eight in memory of Foley, a former Ireland and Munster No 8 in his playing days. Ireland went on to clinch a stunning 40-29 maiden win over the All Blacks.
Before their 2023 Rugby World Cup quarter-final, Ireland repeated the same haka response, but lost to the All Blacks in Paris 28-24.

In 2008, a uniquely stirring haka response took place at Thomond Park in Limerick as Munster quartet Doug Howlett, Rua Tipoki, Lifeimi Mafi and Jeremy Manning stepped forward to perform a haka facing the All Blacks with the rest of their Munster team-mates stood behind them.

A similar event took place recently in 2026 when All Blacks great Ma'a Nonu performed a solo haka facing the All Blacks while a player for South African club side the Sharks, ahead of New Zealand's tour match in Durban.
Are New Zealand only nation that perform the haka?
While the haka is rugby's best-known and most famous traditional pre-match ceremonial war dance, the island nations of Fiji, Samoa and Tonga all also perform their own versions.

Fiji perform the Cibi, which sees the team stand in formation and led by a vocal soloist, before dropping into a synchronised low crouch or knee-bend while making aggressive arm and hand gestures, concluding with an explosive jump or step-up.

Samoa perform the Siva Tau, with the ritual led by a designated chanter and players starting in a lowered or kneeling stance before rising into synchronised movements that include chest-slapping, foot-stomping, aggressive gestures, and intense vocal chanting.

Tonga perform the Sipi Tau, which begins with the team huddled or kneeling in a circle led by a central caller, before breaking into a structured formation on the field featuring deep squats, chest-pounding, rhythmic foot-stomping, and aggressive synchronised gestures.
WHO scales up Ebola readiness in 22 countries across three continents

The UN agency’s eastern Mediterranean region comprises 22 countries and territories. Intensified support is being given to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan, which have been identified as priority countries.
This follows deadly outbreaks of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in both the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda and confirmation of a case in Kenya linked to the DRC.
Hostilities and overstretched health systems

Although there have not been any Ebola cases in the region so far, conflict, displacement and overstretched health systems in several countries are making it difficult to prepare and respond should the situation change.
In a speech earlier this week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Gebreyesus described the region as “the epicentre of global humanitarian need”.
More than 117 million people in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Sudan, Syria, Yemen and beyond, require humanitarian assistance to survive.
Assessing readiness, identifying challenges

Between July and September, WHO deployed missions to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan to assess national readiness and identify challenges in Ebola surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, case management and emergency coordination.
The UN agency is helping authorities to address gaps through training, technical support, medical supplies and simulation exercises.

It has developed regional readiness checklists, contingency planning tools and technical guidance, in addition to strengthening coordination with countries in both Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean.
WHO has also provided laboratory supplies, traveller guidance and community engagement resources.
Despite progress, gaps remain in early detection, laboratory confirmation and availability of protective equipment and resources for emergency response.
“Conflict, insecurity and restricted access present additional challenges, particularly in countries already facing major humanitarian emergencies,” WHO said.
Meanwhile, work continues to ensure that national authorities and partners can rapidly detect, investigate and manage suspected Ebola cases.

Gaza: 340 children killed despite ceasefire agreement - UNICEF

A little over one year since a ceasefire agreement was announced between Hamas fighters and Israel, more than 340 children have been reported killed and hundreds more injured, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Friday.
For families “mourning the loss of their children, those terrible statistics do not equate with a ceasefire”, stressed spokesperson Ricardo Pires.

He added that in the last two weeks in Gaza alone, five boys and two girls have been reported killed and at least 33 children seriously injured in airstrikes, drone strikes and gunfire across the Strip. Another two boys died of injuries sustained previously, Mr. Pires told journalists in Geneva.
The consequences of the Hamas-Israel war are everywhere for children: “where they sleep, what they eat, whether they can learn”, he continued, citing the case of

16-year-old Norhan whose mother was shot while eight months pregnant. “She delivered her baby and then died the following day,” Mr. Pires explained. “Norhan’s father is living with a disability, so she now cares for her one-year-old sister Narjis and takes full responsibility. Her days are spent tidying the home, cooking, and playing with Narjis. Her three other siblings attend a UNICEF-supported learning centre and Norhan helps them with their studies after class, which as she says means, ‘They might just have a future.’”

Asked about reports that private traders in Gaza had halted cooperation with the Israeli authorities on allowing commercial trucks carrying food to enter the occupied enclave, the UNICEF spokesperson stressed that the uninterrupted flow of “humanitarian and commercial goods” remained essential, “so children can continue their recovery”.
He recalled being in Gaza City last year before the ceasefire began, when supplies “were not getting in” and famine was declared by UN-backed food insecurity experts.

“We can’t go back to a situation where children and families are not getting all the supplies, goods and services that they require,” he insisted, “where children are not receiving what they need to survive and to continue to have hope for their future”.

The UNICEF alert comes as temperatures drop and displaced families in Gaza fill empty flour bags with sand to keep rainwater out of their tents. Aid agencies continue to repeat warnings that the situation in Gaza remains dire, after three years of war, sparked by Hamas-led terror attacks in Israel.
The ongoing sanitation crisis is a particular concern in the war-torn enclave, where Israeli bombardment has severely damaged the drainage network.

“There are vast pools of wastewater, such as the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin that is half-full,” Mr. Pires warned. “With the winter rains fast approaching, we’re running out of time to pump this out. Just as we warned a year ago, contaminated water could overflow and inundate downstream residential areas with potentially life-threatening impacts for children and their families. Children have drowned in sewage-contaminated water before.”

According to UNICEF, 800,000 children remain displaced in Gaza “and most live in tents or dangerous bombed-out buildings”. An estimated 60,000 children have seen either one or both parents killed during the war, or since the ceasefire, while nearly every child needs some form of mental health support to recover.
As part of UN assistance to Palestinians in Gaza, UNICEF has helped more than 560,000 children return to learning since the ceasefire, including at over 200 UNICEF-supported learning centres.
The agency has also provided digital cash assistance – “a lifeline”, Mr. Pires stressed – to more than 380,000 people, along with safe water to 1.2 million people.

The eighth episode of Apple TV's "Dark Matter" season 2 has just dropped, and we're all on the edge of our seats trying to guess how the strange saga of Jason (Joel Edgerton) and Daniela (Jennifer Connelly) Dessen is going to finish up. Not even fans of the books know, as this superb adaptation of NYT bestselling author Blake Crouch's 2016 novel broke out of its source material for season 2.

For Edgerton and Connelly, "Dark Matter" has been a whirlwind project as their characters search for a safe alternate universe while being pursued by a multiplicity of Jasons. The physical rigors and emotional toll of shooting the show and presenting its nuanced storytelling often proved difficult.

"There's two exhaustions that I’ve found in movie work," Edgerton tells Space. "It's either mental exhaustion from going to dark emotional places in your brain or complex dialogue stuff. Then there's the physical challenges, like for doing a fight scene. One of the weirdest ones on 'Dark Matter' was doing a gravity scene where we’re dangling on wires inside The Box. There's something deeply exhausting about it and a bit humiliating. You feel like a human teabag."
Connelly was also a part of that tough sequence and reflects on Edgerton’s tireless fortitude.

"Joel's schedule on this show is really brutal," she notes. "He's in almost all of it. This season is better, but season 1 was crazy for him. It’s surprising; sometimes the things that are most difficult are the ones you don’t anticipate. That's more exhausting at the end of the day after trying to get something to work that you didn’t think would be tricky. I like the days that are tiring because you feel drained because you’ve explored a lot in a scene. That's a nice feeling."
For Edgerton, the simplest thing to remember is that when practicing your craft, always make sure that you go home each day feeling satisfied with what you shot.

"There's nothing worse than going home and thinking that you didn’t get the best out of yourself," he reveals. "As they say, as actors we're not digging trenches. It's not hard physical labor; it's a different kind of thing. Until actually I shot a movie where I had to dig a trench."
Working with Blake Crouch on the series and its unnerving portrait of a marriage strewn across the infinite multiverse has produced new insights into their own lives.
"I find there’s something to be learned from each experience as an actor," notes Edgerton. "Each story takes you through something, whether you like to think it or not.

"You either learn a skill or meet an actor that you admire, and they teach you something inspired by their presence. We were tasked with helping Blake build the disintegration of a marriage, and it's the opposite of what you’re hoping for in real life. That each day you hope you're turning up contributing in a positive way to your relationship rather than engineering its demise. It makes you think about how you can be a better person in life. And there's always room for improvement."
Likewise, Connelly sees a sort of emotional mirroring effect to be absorbed that extends beyond "Dark Matter's" detailed sets, dizzying locations, and sound stages.

"I think Daniela, at a point when Jason is going down paths, and they're struggling, recognizes that sometimes it's hard to distinguish what is really the other person and what we’re bringing to our perception of them," she adds.

"She has things in her history that bias her vision, and she takes herself off on a journey to reconcile those things and try to take responsibility for healing. And that's a good lesson to remember in relationships in general. Being on top of one's own part of the dynamic. Sometimes things we see in each other are really things within ourselves."
"Dark Matter" season 2 airs each Friday exclusively on Apple TV, with the season finale (and perhaps the series end if not renewed) arriving on Oct. 30, 2026.

Your invitation to revisit the Space Age has arrived.
Whether you miss the days when people got dressed up to fly or you wish your "other" ride was a rocket, Mission: 60s has a *space* reserved for you.

"This is a three-day celebration of Apollo, aviation, space exploration and 1960s culture," reads a promo for the Oct. 23 to 25 event in New York. "You will be fully immersed in the sights, sounds and spirit of the 1960s Space Age."

"The weekend features astronauts, Apollo flight directors, Mission Control engineers, Star Trek legends, space artists, a Saturday Spacefarer Soiree with live music (1960s attire encouraged!), and a Sunday NASA Artemis keynote."

Organized by Luna Replicas, a company specializing in vintage space gear, and Space for Humanity, a nonprofit that underwrites spaceflight experiences, Mission: 60s is aimed at being the bridge between the last time humanity reached for the moon and today's "second space race" to do it again — this time to stay.
Your journey back to the 60s begins when you check into the TWA Hotel at the John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York.
Once a functioning terminal for Trans World Airlines (as featured in the 2002 movie "Catch Me If You Can"), the TWA Flight Center has been reimagined as a hotel like no other.

"At the center of the hotel is Eero Saarinen's iconic TWA Flight Center, where restaurants, bars and retail outlets have taken flight. Two hotel wings, designed to reflect and defer to the landmark TWA Flight Center, sit behind the historic building and contain 512 guest rooms with views of JFK's runways and the TWA Flight Center," reads the hotel's website.

The TWA Hotel is only the first sight straight out of the past that guests will encounter. On Friday (Oct. 23), Mission: 60s begins with a guided tour of the 1964 World's Fair site in Flushing Meadows. Today the home to the New York Hall of Science, the outdoor exhibits includes the Rocket Park, where Gemini-Titan II and Mercury-Atlas D rockets and a Saturn V F-1 engine still stand.

"The space age was less than 10 years old when rockets like these powered incredible missions to outer space," reads the description on the museum's website. "Visitors will learn about the history of these vehicles as well as the United States' mission to reach the moon."

Also on view at the World's Fair site is the Unisphere, a spherical stainless steel representation of Earth, and the Astro-View Observation Towers (later reimagined as actual flying saucers in the 1997 movie "Men in Black").
The first day concludes with Space For Humanity's (separately-ticketed) "Celestial Soiree" and a Mission: 60's pool party on the hotel's rooftop.

Saturday and Sunday at Mission: 60s will bring together members of Mission Control (MCC), spaceflight experts (including ILC Dover, makers of the Apollo spacesuit) and representatives from the Hollywood community who brought about the 60s-era visions of space exploration (including Industrial Light & Magic [ILM]) for a series of engaging panel discussions.
Among the various topics scheduled for the two days of talks are:
- Apollo Mission Control & Flight Operations
- Apollo Communications: The Sights & Sounds From the Moon
- Making Space Real: Art & Visual Effects That Sold Humanity on Space

Featured speakers and moderators include Apollo flight director Gerry Griffin, TIME Magazine science editor Jeffrey Kluger, former NASA astronauts Nicole Stott and Ron Garan, "Star Trek" actor Bob Picardo and researcher Frank White.

On Saturday evening, there will be a second gala, "The Spacefarer Soiree," featuring a limited meet and greet aboard a Lockheed Constellation airliner and music by Bonnie Gordon. Set in 1969, attendees are encouraged to come wearing their finest period clothing.
Then, on Sunday afternoon, Uplift Aerospace will host a shared "Overview" VR experience for up to 50 people participating together.

Both days will include a vendor and artists' hall, with guests signing autographs and their books, as well as companies such as NASA's official patch provider A-B Emblem, selling Apollo-themed souvenirs and memorabilia.

I know perfectly well that the moon comes out during the day. I have known this for decades. Yet whenever I spot it in a blue afternoon sky, some primitive part of my brain still thinks it has turned up early.

I'm certainly not the only one. Many people don't understand how it could be visible in daylight. In their eyes, the moon is a nighttime object. Why? Because that's when they notice it — it appears brighter.

We tend to think of the sun as belonging to the day and the moon to the night because that's how they're usually presented to us as children. Astronomically, it makes little sense. The moon spends plenty of time above our horizon while the sun is also up — it spends half its time in the daytime sky, in fact.

If the moon, pale but unmistakable, looks slightly out of place against a blue sky, it's not — you are. This week is a great time to get used to seeing it there. Just past first quarter, the moon will spend each afternoon hanging in the daytime sky, becoming easier to spot as the sun sinks towards the horizon.

The moon reached first quarter on Sunday, Oct. 18, and is now waxing toward full moon, which occurs early on Monday, Oct. 26 (Oct. 25 in some time zones). That puts it in the right part of its orbit to be conspicuous during the late afternoon this weekend.

Here's the useful bit to remember. Around first quarter, the moon rises roughly around midday. As it waxes towards full, it rises progressively later in the afternoon. By full moon, it rises around sunset.

That makes the days immediately after first quarter an excellent time to get into the habit of finding the moon before sunset. On Monday, Oct. 19, look southeast in the afternoon for a moon just over half-lit. Each afternoon this week, it will become a little more illuminated, move farther east against the background stars, and appear progressively later in the day.

You don't need to wait until dusk. In fact, that's the point. Start looking during the afternoon, when the sun is still well above the horizon. Once you find the moon, it can be surprisingly conspicuous against the blue sky.

I'll start looking in the mid-to-late afternoon this week, when the waxing moon should already be high enough to find easily. You can check the exact moonrise time where you are, but there's no need to catch it as it rises. Look towards the east or southeast and scan the blue sky.

Once you've found the moon in daylight, keep checking on it as sunset approaches. The moon doesn't suddenly become brighter, of course. Instead, the surrounding sky darkens, increasing the contrast until the pale daytime moon seems to switch on at dusk and grow increasingly brilliant.

Binoculars will give you a superb view at dusk, particularly along the terminator — the boundary between lunar day and night. That's where low-angle sunlight throws mountains and crater rims into sharp relief. As the moon waxes this week, the terminator will move steadily across its surface, revealing a different landscape each afternoon.

That's another reason not to wait for the full moon. The full moon gets most of the attention, but the week beforehand is arguably a much better time to get to know our nearest celestial neighbor — and you don't even have to wait until dark.

This is a bright-moon week. Full moon arrives early on Monday, Oct. 26, so moonlight will wash out faint stars and make galaxies and nebulas much harder to see. So go for Saturn instead. It reached opposition earlier this month and remains very well placed in the evening sky. Better still, the nearly full moon passes near Saturn around Oct. 23-24, giving beginners a convenient landmark for locating the planet. The moon's glare will hide faint nearby stars, but Saturn itself is easily bright enough to cope. A good example will be Oct. 27, when the Pleiades is passed closely by a bright moon. The Seven Sisters therefore won't be at their best, so you'll need to use binoculars — if you do, you'll see them easily enough.

Auriga, "the Charioteer," is climbing in the northeastern and eastern sky during late October evenings. It's easiest to find if you start at Capella, one of the brightest stars in the entire night sky. It's just 43 light-years from the sun. From there, I look for the other stars that form Auriga's rough pentagon, including Menkalinan, Mahasim and Almaaz. The fifth corner is Elnath, although it officially belongs to neighboring Taurus.

Auriga gets even better with binoculars. The Milky Way runs straight through it, bringing with it three bright open star clusters — M36, M37 and M38. All three show up in binoculars under a reasonably dark sky, while a small telescope starts to resolve them into individual stars. There's always another layer to find in the night sky.

There's something special about stargazing during the blue hour — that brief transition when daylight drains from the sky and night's window begins to open. It's particularly beautiful a few days before full moon, when the near-full orb is already rising in the east as the sun sets in the west. Look below it, and you may also see the Belt of Venus, a pinkish band above the eastern horizon caused by reddened sunlight shining through Earth's atmosphere, with our planet's dark blue-gray shadow beneath. As the sky fades through ever-deeper shades of blue, the moon brightens, and the first stars emerge around it.

USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
Scientists have created a potentially renewable source of engineered immune cells that fight cancer, offering a promising path toward longer-lasting, ready-made immunotherapies.

- USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.

Scientists at the University of Southern California (USC) have discovered a way to produce a potentially renewable supply of cancer-fighting immune cells, opening a promising new direction for cancer treatment. By working with immature cells that can develop into powerful immune defenders, the researchers have created a system capable of generating large numbers of genetically engineered cells that recognize tumors and help activate the body's natural defenses.

The breakthrough, described in a study published in Cell, could help overcome some of the biggest obstacles facing cancer immunotherapy, including the difficulty of manufacturing enough immune cells and keeping them active in the body. In experiments involving mice, the engineered cells established themselves in bone marrow, produced new immune cells, and slowed the progression of both blood cancers and solid tumors.

The USC Stem Cell-led team focused on a type of immature immune cell called granulocyte-monocyte progenitors (GMPs). These cells normally develop into macrophages and other immune cells that protect the body from infections and participate in immune responses. The researchers found that GMPs could be grown extensively in the laboratory while retaining their ability to develop into functioning immune cells. They could also be genetically modified to recognize specific cancer markers and strengthen broader immune responses.

"The study establishes a scalable and engineerable GMP platform for cellular immunotherapy and introduces concepts that we believe could have broad implications for both cancer immunotherapy and stem cell biology," said the paper's corresponding author Qi-Long Ying, MD, PhD, professor of stem cell biology and regenerative medicine at the Keck School of Medicine of USC.
Scientists Discover a Surprising Ability in Immune Cell Precursors
Beyond its potential applications in cancer treatment, the discovery challenges a long-standing understanding of how blood and immune cells develop.

Stem cells are known for their ability to self-renew, meaning they can repeatedly divide while maintaining their original properties. In the blood-forming system, this ability has traditionally been associated primarily with hematopoietic stem cells, which can produce all the major types of blood and immune cells.

Progenitor cells, by contrast, are further along in development and are already committed to producing a more limited range of cells. They are generally thought to have less capacity for long-term self-renewal.

The USC researchers demonstrated that GMPs can retain this ability under carefully controlled laboratory conditions. Rather than quickly maturing into other cell types, the progenitors continued multiplying while preserving their identity and their capacity to generate functional immune cells.

"The prevailing view has been that long-term self-renewal in the blood system is primarily a property of the hematopoietic stem cells that can generate any type of blood or immune cell," said Ying. "We found that, under the right conditions, GMPs can also self-renew, dividing extensively while keeping their identity and ability to produce functional immune cells. That gives us a scalable starting point for engineering cell therapies for cancer, infectious disease and potentially many other conditions."
This finding could be especially important for developing treatments that require large, reliable supplies of genetically engineered immune cells.
Why Macrophages Could Be Powerful Weapons Against Cancer

Macrophages are among the immune system's most versatile defenders. Their name comes from Greek words meaning "big eaters," reflecting their ability to surround and engulf bacteria, damaged cells, and other unwanted material.

They also help coordinate immune responses by sending signals that influence the behavior of other immune cells. Some macrophages can enter tumors and attack cancer cells, making them attractive candidates for cancer immunotherapy.

One particularly promising application involves solid tumors, which include cancers that form masses in organs and tissues. Existing therapies based on engineered T cells have achieved their greatest successes against certain blood cancers, but treating solid tumors has proven more difficult.
Macrophages offer a potentially different approach because they naturally migrate into tissues and can penetrate tumors. However, turning them into practical treatments presents several challenges.

Once macrophages have fully matured, they are difficult to multiply in large quantities outside the body. They are also challenging to modify genetically and can be damaged during freezing and storage, complicating the production and distribution of cell therapies.

Another problem occurs after administration. Mature macrophages often collect in organs such as the lungs and liver instead of spreading widely throughout the body. Their relatively rapid disappearance can also limit how long a treatment remains effective.
To work around these limitations, the scientists decided to begin at an earlier stage of immune cell development.
Creating a Renewable Supply of Cancer-Fighting Immune Cells

Rather than trying to manufacture large numbers of mature macrophages, first author Shi Yue, MD, of Ying's laboratory and his colleagues concentrated on GMPs, the progenitor cells that can produce macrophages.

The researchers developed a precisely defined mixture of chemicals that allowed GMPs to survive and multiply for extended periods in the laboratory. The mixture prevented the cells from prematurely developing into mature immune cells, preserving a renewable population of progenitors.

Even after extensive laboratory expansion, the GMPs maintained the molecular characteristics that defined them. Importantly, they also retained the ability to develop into functional macrophages and other related immune cells when needed.

This approach could make it possible to manufacture large numbers of engineered immune cells from a starting population that can be continually expanded, instead of repeatedly collecting and preparing mature cells.

To confirm that the method could be reproduced, collaborators in the laboratory of Ravi Majeti, MD, PhD, at Stanford University independently demonstrated that GMPs could be maintained for extended periods and genetically engineered. Their results provided additional support for the reliability of the technique and its potential use in future cell therapies.

Majeti, Director of the Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine at Stanford University, noted: "This method for the expansion and engineering of GMPs opens the door to numerous translational applications, much like T cell expansion and engineering. We have already demonstrated engineering of these cells to drive multiple potent functions, and there is a lot more to be explored."
Engineering Immune Cells to Recognize and Attack Tumors
The team next investigated whether these expandable progenitor cells could be programmed to fight cancer.

They genetically engineered GMPs to carry a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This engineered receptor allows immune cells to identify a particular molecular marker on the surface of cancer cells, helping direct their activity toward tumors.

CAR technology is already an important part of cancer immunotherapy, particularly in treatments that modify a patient's T cells to recognize and attack cancer. The USC researchers explored whether a similar strategy could be applied to GMPs, allowing them to generate engineered macrophages and other immune cells.

The scientists also equipped some of the progenitor cells with an additional immune-activating signal. This modification was designed to recruit and stimulate nearby immune cells, including T cells, which can help mount a stronger attack against cancer.
The added signal offered another potentially important advantage. It remained effective even when the immune characteristics of donor cells did not match those of the recipient.

That finding raises the possibility of developing off-the-shelf treatments using cells manufactured in advance from donors. Unlike personalized cell therapies, which must be prepared separately using each patient's own cells, such products could potentially be produced in larger batches and made available to multiple patients.
Engineered Cells Slow Cancer Progression in Mice
After successfully expanding and engineering GMPs from both mice and humans, the researchers investigated their therapeutic potential in mouse experiments.

When administered to mice, the progenitor cells established themselves in the bone marrow and other locations responsible for blood cell production. These environments provided places where the GMPs could generate additional engineered macrophages and related immune cells.

This was an important difference from treatments using mature macrophages. Instead of relying solely on immune cells that may disappear relatively quickly, the progenitors could provide a continuing source of replacement cells from within the body.
The strategy may therefore help overcome the rapid clearance that has limited macrophage therapies, including approaches evaluated in recent clinical trials.
The researchers tested the engineered cells in mice with blood cancers and solid tumors. GMPs carrying CAR receptors slowed disease progression in both types of cancer.

The effects were even stronger when the progenitors carried both CAR receptors and the additional signal designed to activate other immune cells. This combination improved the treatment's ability to stimulate a broader antitumor response.

Although these findings are encouraging, the cancer-treatment results remain preclinical. Further research will be needed to establish whether engineered GMPs can be used safely and effectively in people, particularly if they are intended to persist and produce immune cells over extended periods.
Potential Applications Beyond Cancer Treatment
The scientists also explored whether their approach could help treat conditions involving defective immune defenses.

In a separate mouse experiment, they studied chronic granulomatous disease, an inherited disorder that interferes with the ability of certain immune cells to kill harmful microbes. People with this condition are particularly vulnerable to recurrent bacterial and fungal infections because their immune cells cannot eliminate some pathogens effectively.
When the researchers administered GMPs to mice with the disorder, the cells restored the animals' ability to fight bacterial infection.

This result suggests that renewable, genetically engineered immune cell progenitors might eventually have applications beyond cancer, including treatments for inherited immune deficiencies and potentially infectious diseases.
The broader lesson, according to the researchers, is that the developmental stage of an immune cell may be just as important as the genetic modifications used to turn it into a treatment.

By engineering cells before they fully mature, scientists may be able to create therapies that are easier to manufacture, more adaptable, and capable of maintaining a continuing supply of specialized immune defenders.
"Our study suggests that the future of immunotherapy may depend not only on designing better CAR receptors, but also on choosing the right developmental stage of the cell," said Ying.
The study, published in Cell, is titled "Expansion and CAR engineering of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors for cellular immunotherapy."

The uranium cubes that exposed Nazi Germanyâs nuclear failure

- Scientists investigating Nazi Germany's secret nuclear program have uncovered evidence that its final experimental reactor was nowhere near as close to working as previously claimed. Analysis of surviving uranium cubes and wartime documents reveals that Germany lacked the enormous quantities of uranium and heavy water needed to make its reactor operational.

During World War II, the United States raced to develop the atomic bomb partly out of fear that Nazi Germany might build one first. But how close did Germany actually come to achieving that goal? A new scientific investigation suggests the Nazi nuclear program was much further from success than its leading physicist claimed.

By examining surviving uranium cubes and previously documented historical evidence, researchers have uncovered major limitations in Germany's final experimental nuclear reactor. Their findings indicate that the project was not simply missing a few materials. The reactor would have required far more uranium and heavy water than Germany had available during the war.

The Manhattan Project, the secret American effort to develop nuclear weapons during World War II, was driven partly by the possibility that Nazi Germany might achieve a similar breakthrough first. Scientists knew that whoever succeeded could gain an unprecedented military advantage.

One possible route to an atomic bomb involved building a nuclear reactor capable of producing plutonium, a radioactive element that can be used in nuclear weapons. Inside a reactor, uranium atoms undergo nuclear fission, a process in which their nuclei split apart and release energy along with additional particles called neutrons. Under the right conditions, those neutrons trigger further fission reactions, creating a sustained chain reaction.
Although Nazi Germany pursued nuclear research through a program known as the Uranprojekt, historians have long debated how close its scientists came to developing a functioning reactor.

Germany's final attempt was an experimental reactor known as the B8 pile, constructed in 1945 under the direction of physicist Werner Heisenberg. The device used cubes of natural uranium suspended in heavy water, a specialized substance that played an essential role in controlling the nuclear reaction.
Why Heavy Water Was Essential to Nazi Germany's Reactor
Heavy water looks much like ordinary water, but its hydrogen atoms contain an additional neutron. This subtle difference makes it particularly useful in certain nuclear reactors.

In a reactor, heavy water serves as a neutron moderator, meaning it slows down the neutrons released during fission. Slower neutrons are more likely to trigger additional fission reactions in uranium, helping sustain the chain reaction needed for a working reactor.
For Germany, however, obtaining enough heavy water was a major obstacle.

During the war, the only European facility capable of supplying the heavy water needed by the German program was the Norsk Hydro plant in Vemork, Norway. Germany gained control of the facility after occupying Norway in April 1940.

Recognizing its importance to Germany's nuclear ambitions, Allied forces targeted the plant through sabotage and bombing operations. A major American bombing raid struck Vemork on November 16, 1943, contributing to the eventual end of heavy water production there.
Scientists Reexamine Hitler's Final Nuclear Reactor

When American forces discovered and dismantled the B8 reactor in 1945, it had never achieved criticality. In nuclear physics, criticality refers to the point at which a chain reaction becomes self-sustaining, with each generation of fission reactions producing enough neutrons to maintain the next.

Reaching this threshold is a fundamental requirement for operating a conventional nuclear reactor. Despite its name, criticality does not mean that a reactor is about to explode. It simply means the nuclear chain reaction can continue without relying on an external neutron source.

Heisenberg, who led the German reactor effort, maintained that the B8 experiment had come close to reaching this milestone. He argued that the device needed only a relatively modest increase in its uranium supply to become operational.
But a new study led by Timothy Koeth and his colleagues challenges that assessment.

The researchers examined two surviving cubes of natural uranium that had been used in the German nuclear project. They also studied historical records, technical reports, correspondence, and other archival documents to reconstruct the reactor's capabilities and determine what would have been required for it to work.
Their findings paint a very different picture of Germany's nuclear progress.
A Massive Uranium and Heavy Water Shortage

According to the researchers' calculations, the B8 reactor would have needed approximately twice as much uranium and more than twice as much heavy water as it actually contained to achieve a sustained nuclear chain reaction.

The required quantities exceeded the materials available to Germany during the war. In particular, the heavy water needed for a functioning reactor was far beyond the amount the German program could obtain from its Norwegian supply.
The researchers also examined whether German scientists could have avoided the heavy water shortage by using graphite, a form of carbon that can also slow neutrons in nuclear reactors.
This approach had worked for American scientists, who achieved the world's first controlled, sustained nuclear chain reaction using a graphite-moderated reactor in 1942.

However, the graphite available in German-controlled territory contained impurities that made it unsuitable for the same purpose. In particular, traces of boron could absorb neutrons that would otherwise help sustain the reaction, preventing the reactor from reaching criticality.
That meant Germany could not simply substitute graphite for heavy water to overcome its supply problems.
Why Nazi Germany's Nuclear Program Was Doomed
The findings suggest that Heisenberg significantly underestimated how much additional material his reactor would have required.
Rather than standing on the verge of a functioning nuclear reactor, the German scientists faced shortages they could not overcome with the resources available to them.

The research also provides a clearer explanation for why Germany's nuclear program failed to make the transition from experimental reactor designs to a working reactor capable of producing material for an atomic bomb.

Based on the designs and materials available during World War II, the researchers conclude that Nazi Germany lacked the resources necessary to make either its heavy water reactor or a graphite-based alternative operational.

More than eight decades after the war, the surviving uranium cubes have helped resolve a longstanding historical question, revealing just how far Nazi Germany remained from achieving a critical step toward building an atomic bomb.

Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger

- Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

Stress does more than influence how we feel. It can also change what we remember, particularly when an experience is emotionally intense or personally meaningful. Scientists have long known that cortisol, a hormone released during stressful situations, can strengthen emotional memories. What has been less clear is exactly how this happens inside the brain.

Researchers at Yale University have now uncovered important clues. Their study reveals that cortisol strengthens emotional memories by changing how brain networks involved in emotion and memory function and communicate with one another. The findings offer a deeper understanding of why certain experiences leave such powerful impressions while others quickly fade.

"We all experience stress, and my lab is interested in understanding how stress can be helpful," said corresponding author Elizabeth Goldfarb, an assistant professor of psychiatry at Yale School of Medicine and of psychology in the Faculty of Arts and Sciences.
The findings were published in the journal Science Advances.

Previous research involving both humans and rodents has shown that stress and cortisol can improve memory for emotional events. Scientists also know that certain brain regions, including the amygdala, play an essential role in this process. The amygdala is particularly important for processing emotions and identifying experiences that may be significant.

However, understanding precisely how cortisol strengthens memories has been challenging. Many brain regions participate in several mental functions, making it difficult to determine whether the hormone is influencing emotional responses, memory formation, or both.

"Forming memories for emotional experiences involves different processes in the brain: first, perceiving an experience as emotional or intense, and second, encoding that experience into long-term memory," said Goldfarb, who is also a member of Yale's Wu Tsai Institute, an interdisciplinary research initiative that explores cognition.
The researchers wanted to examine these processes separately to determine how cortisol affects the brain's ability to recognize emotional significance and preserve an experience as a lasting memory.
Watching the Brain Form Emotional Memories

To investigate, the Yale team conducted an experiment in which participants took a pill containing either hydrocortisone, a form of cortisol, or an inactive placebo. They then viewed a series of pictures while undergoing functional MRI (fMRI) scanning.

This imaging technique measures changes in blood flow and oxygen levels associated with brain activity, allowing researchers to identify which areas of the brain are more active during different tasks.
As participants examined the pictures, they reported their emotional reactions to each image. The following day, researchers tested how well they remembered what they had seen.

Each person completed the experiment twice, once after receiving hydrocortisone and once after receiving the placebo. The study used a double blind design, meaning neither the participants nor the experimenter knew which substance had been administered during a particular session.
This approach allowed the scientists to compare how the same person's brain responded with and without the additional cortisol.
A Five-Second Look at Brain Network Activity
One of the study's most important advances came from the way researchers analyzed the brain scans.

Scientists often study a measurement called functional connectivity, which describes how closely activity in different parts of the brain fluctuates together. When two regions show synchronized patterns of activity, it can indicate that they are participating in related processes.

Traditionally, examining these relationships requires several minutes of brain imaging data. The Yale team instead analyzed functional connectivity during individual trials lasting only around five seconds.

Using these brief snapshots, the researchers tested whether patterns of brain activity could predict two different outcomes: how emotionally intense participants found a picture and whether they would remember that picture the following day.

The approach worked for both. By identifying patterns associated with emotional intensity and memory formation separately, the scientists were able to examine how cortisol influenced each network and the interactions between them.
This gave the researchers a more detailed picture of the changing brain activity associated with emotional memory formation.
Cortisol Changes How Brain Networks Work Together
First, cortisol improved participants' ability to remember emotionally significant experiences, confirming what earlier research had suggested.
Second, and more importantly, the hormone strengthened emotional memory through distinct changes in the brain networks responsible for processing emotion and forming memories.

In networks associated with emotion, cortisol produced more consistent patterns of activity and increased their engagement. This suggests that the hormone helped the brain respond more strongly and reliably to the emotional significance of an experience.

In memory networks, cortisol had a different effect. It made their activity patterns more specialized for emotional information, suggesting that the brain was adjusting how it encoded emotionally meaningful experiences.

The hormone also increased coordination between the networks involved in emotion and memory. In other words, cortisol appeared to help these different brain systems work together more effectively when processing experiences that carried emotional weight.
Together, these findings suggest that stress strengthens emotional memories through several interacting brain mechanisms rather than through a single region or process.
Why Emotional Experiences Can Be So Memorable

The results help explain why stress does not necessarily improve memory for everything. Instead, its benefits appear to be selective, making experiences that feel particularly intense or meaningful more likely to be remembered.
The researchers believe this reflects the brain's ability to adapt to stressful situations by prioritizing information that may be important.

"Stress responses are fundamentally adaptive and can help you form strong memories -- but this is specific to experiences that you find to be emotionally intense or meaningful," Goldfarb said. "This is in part related to your brain increasing engagement of networks that track emotional intensity. So, if you are stressed out and trying to learn something new, it might help to think about exciting elements or strong feelings connected to what you are learning."

The findings also point to a potentially useful insight about learning. Connecting information to something exciting, personally important, or emotionally engaging could make it easier to remember, particularly during stressful situations.
Rather than simply disrupting memory, stress can sometimes help the brain identify which experiences deserve special attention and strengthen the networks involved in preserving them.

Other Yale researchers involved in the study include Rajita Sinha, the Foundations Fund Endowed Professor in Psychiatry and professor in the Child Study Center and of neuroscience at Yale School of Medicine (YSM), and Todd Constable, the Elizabeth Mears and House Jameson Professor of Radiology and Biomedical Imaging and professor of neurosurgery at YSM.
