For those with celiac disease, even a little bit of gluten can cause damage to the intestine.
The only available solution is a strict gluten-free diet.
Yet even when foods are carefully scrutinized, accidents can be made, and symptoms can persist in up to 40 percent of patients.
Several new pharmaceuticals are being investigated by drug companies, and one just passed a phase 2 clinical trial.
The medicine is called FB102, which admittedly doesn't sound very glamorous, but don't judge a book by its cover.
This intravenous medicine has the potential to protect the gut against accidental gluten exposure, a feat that no approved drug can currently achieve.
The company that owns the pharmaceutical, argenx SE, has now announced positive topline results from its phase 2 clinical trial.

The results are not yet peer-reviewed, but patients with celiac disease who were treated with FB102 demonstrated better preservation of the intestinal lining during gluten exposure compared to a placebo.

"These positive Phase 2 results strengthen our conviction in the potential of FB102 to address a significant unmet need for people living with celiac disease, where there are currently no approved therapies," says Luc Truyen, the chief medical officer at argenx.
The recent clinical trial enrolled 126 patients with confirmed celiac disease, who were symptom-free and who had been on a strict gluten-free diet for at least the past year.
Participants underwent a controlled, eight-week oral gluten challenge. Some were randomized to receive a placebo during this time, while others received intravenous infusions of FB102.
Neither participants nor researchers knew who was receiving what.
At day 78, researchers analyzed how much gluten-induced damage had occurred in the mucosal lining compared to at the start of the trial.
When people with celiac eat gluten, it tends to shorten the tiny projections that stick out from their intestinal walls while also deepening the grooves between them.
But FB102 seems to protect against this.
Participants in the trial who received this novel drug showed fewer signs of injury from eating gluten. They also showed a smaller inflammatory immune response in the mucosal lining.
This does not mean that FB102 will one day allow patients with celiac disease to eat gluten without care.
This drug was given under controlled conditions, and it's unclear if its protective effects work in a real-world setting.
Still, it's worth investigating further, especially as there is currently no way to protect the gut against accidental gluten exposure.

"Combined with the consistent safety profile observed across studies," says Truyen, "these findings support advancing FB102 into Phase 3 development and further exploring its broader potential across immune-mediated diseases."
The FB102 drug has been in clinical trials for several years now. It was specifically designed to target a receptor on immune cells called CD122.
This receptor responds to inflammatory messengers, and in 2009, researchers showed that if this receptor was blocked in mice with gut autoimmune issues, it led to a reversal of intestinal damage.
That led to the hypothesis that CD122 and its interaction with inflammatory signals are critical in the development and maintenance of celiac disease.
To that end, drug researchers at Forte Biosciences Inc (later acquired by argenx) developed FB102.
This drug is designed to block CD122 receptors on only some disruptive T cells, while preserving the receptor on other ones.
It shows promise in treating not just celiac disease, but other autoimmune diseases, too, like vitiligo.
This is a rare chronic autoimmune condition that causes skin to lose its pigment in patches.
Researchers suspect the drug could also work for alopecia areata.

According to the United States Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) draft guidance, a chronically administered compound like FB102 would need to show efficacy in clinical trials for at least 52 weeks, and it would need to demonstrate efficacy without a gluten challenge.
Researchers at argenx are still working up to that.

"The study builds on the Phase 1b trial, providing consistent clinical evidence that CD122 blockade can protect against gluten-induced intestinal damage and prevent emergence of patient symptoms, even under a more intense gluten challenge, validating CD122 as a promising therapeutic target in celiac disease," says Truyen.
Plenty of people like to start their day with a cup of tea or coffee, but the temperature of your preferred beverage could matter a lot more than you realize.
A decade ago, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) made headlines when it classified very hot beverages at temperatures above 65 °C (149 °F) as "probably carcinogenic to humans".
That 2016 finding followed evidence that mate, a herbal drink popular in South America and often drunk at very hot temperatures, was associated with an increased risk of esophageal cancer.
Mate is typically consumed at temperatures as high as 70 °C (158 °F), but until now, the evidence for hot beverages consumed at cooler temperatures was inconclusive.

"International research has shown for some time that drinking beverages like mate at very high temperatures, as is typical in South America, is linked to increased risk of certain esophageal cancers," says nutritional epidemiologist Keren Papier from the University of Oxford.
"What was less clear was whether this also applied to the temperatures at which hot drinks are usually consumed in Western populations."
To examine the issue, Papier and fellow researchers analyzed data from two large UK cohorts, the Million Women Study and UK Biobank.
In total, the researchers incorporated data from 977,282 participants, in what they claim is the largest study to date examining the associations between hot drinks and esophageal cancer.

In both studies, participants were asked similar questions about hot drink consumption, including how hot they liked their beverages to be ('very hot', 'hot', 'warm', etc.), and how many cups of tea and coffee they consumed each day.

The researchers found that participants who preferred 'very hot' drinks had a 3.17-fold higher relative risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) during the study period compared to people who took their drinks 'warm', after accounting for drinking frequency.
People who indicated they preferred 'hot' drinks had a 69 percent higher SCC risk than those who drank 'warm' beverages, the researchers found.

Further, the data showed that the amount of hot drinks participants consumed was also associated with cancer risk, with those consuming six or more hot drinks a day having a 71 percent increase in SCC risk compared to people who drank fewer than six hot beverages daily, after accounting for drink temperature.

The association was similar regardless of whether participants primarily drank tea or coffee, and adding milk (which was recorded in the Million Women Study) didn't appear to significantly alter the temperature-associated risks identified.

While the observational findings don't establish that hot drinks cause cancer, the researchers suggest that reducing the temperature of hot beverages even slightly could potentially prevent a substantial number of SCC cases.

"Assuming a causal association between preferred drink temperature and the risk of esophageal SCC, the estimated proportion of esophageal SCC cancers that would be prevented if individuals who consumed drinks at a very hot temperature instead consumed their drinks at a hot temperature is 14 percent," the study authors write.
"Based on national incidence rates for SCC esophageal cancers in the United Kingdom, these attributable risks translate into absolute numbers of cancers that could be prevented each year of 440."

A significant limitation with the study, however, is that the researchers didn't collect absolute temperature measurements of the beverages the participants were drinking – only their self-reported preferences of 'very hot', 'hot', 'warm', etc.

The researchers say future studies might be able to clear that up, but for now, they suggest their findings could indicate that temperature ranges below those cited in the IARC report (above 65°C) may increase cancer risk.

While their own study did not examine the biological mechanisms involved, the researchers say their findings – with similar risks seen across tea and coffee, and with milk or without – suggest that beverage temperature is the key risk factor, rather than what's in the drink.
"Animal studies support this, showing that very hot water (70° C) promotes premalignant lesions and esophageal necrosis, whereas lower-temperature beverages do not," the researchers write.
"The most likely mechanism is thermal injury, which may impair mucosal integrity and promote carcinogenic processes."
The findings are reported in the International Journal of Cancer.
Tiny fragments of plastic are making their way deep inside our bodies in concerning quantities, particularly through our food and drink.
But research suggests there is something you can actually do about it.
Scientists in China found a simple and effective means of removing them from water – and it starts with something already sitting on your stove.

Back in 2024, the team ran tests on both soft water and hard tap water (which is richer in minerals). They added nanoplastics and microplastics to the water before boiling the liquid and then filtering out any precipitates.
The tests showed that boiling and then filtering the water can make a significant difference to the plastic contaminants you might otherwise ingest.

"Tap water nano/microplastics (NMPs) escaping from centralized water treatment systems are of increasing global concern, because they pose potential health risks to humans via water consumption," the researchers explained in their published paper.
Watch the video below for a summary of the findings:
In some cases, up to 90 percent of the NMPs were removed by the boiling and filtering process, though the effectiveness varied based on the type of water.
Of course, the huge benefit is that most people can do it with what they already have in their kitchen.

"This simple boiling water strategy can 'decontaminate' NMPs from household tap water and has the potential for harmlessly alleviating human intake of NMPs through water consumption," biomedical engineer Zimin Yu from Guangzhou Medical University and colleagues explained.
A greater concentration of NMPs was removed from samples of hard tap water, which naturally forms a buildup of limescale (or calcium carbonate) as it is heated.

Commonly seen inside kitchen kettles, the chalky substance forms on the plastic's surface as changes in temperature force the calcium carbonate out of solution, effectively trapping the plastic fragments in a crust.
"Our results showed that nanoplastic precipitation efficiency increased with increasing water hardness upon boiling," the team wrote.
"For example, from 34 percent at 80 mg L−1 to 84 percent and 90 percent at 180 and 300 mg L−1 of calcium carbonate, respectively."
Even in soft water, where less calcium carbonate is dissolved, roughly a quarter of the NMPs were snagged from the water.
Any bits of lime-encrusted plastic could then be removed through a simple filter like the stainless steel mesh used to strain tea, the researchers say.
Past studies have measured fragments of polystyrene, polyethylene, polypropylene, and polyethylene terephthalate in potable tap water, which we're consuming daily in varying quantities.
To put the strategy to the ultimate test, the researchers added even more nanoplastic particles, which were effectively reduced in number.
"Drinking boiled water apparently is a viable long-term strategy for reducing global exposure to NMPs," wrote Yu and team.
"Drinking boiled water, however, is often regarded as a local tradition and prevails only in a few regions."
The scientists hope it might become a more widespread practice as plastics continue to take over the world.
Tiny pieces of plastic are an increasingly big problem. Microplastics originate from clothing, kitchen utensils, personal care products, and countless other everyday objects.
Their durability makes them persistent in the environment – including in human bodies.
Not only are many people on Earth already contaminated by microplastics, but we're also still being exposed every day, as there is minimal regulation of these insidious specks.

According to a 2025 literature review from The University of Texas at Arlington, a significant portion of our microplastic exposure may come from drinking water, as wastewater treatment plants are still not effectively removing microplastics.

Roughly 9 billion metric tons of plastic have been produced globally since plastic production began, much of which has progressively degraded into ever-smaller fragments without truly breaking down, forming a fine plastic dust that now pervades the planet.
Wastewater treatment plants actually do remove a lot of these small particles, the new review indicates, but not enough.
Related: Glass Bottles Actually Contain More Microplastics, Scientists Find
While it's still not certain exactly how damaging this plastic is to our bodies, it's clearly not the healthiest of snacks.
Plastics have already been linked to changes in the gut microbiome and the body's antibiotic resistance.

The team behind this study wants to see more research into how boiled water could keep artificial materials out of our bodies – and perhaps counter some of the alarming effects of microplastics that are emerging.

"Our results have ratified a highly feasible strategy to reduce human NMP exposure and established the foundation for further investigations with a much larger number of samples," Yu and colleagues conclude.
The research was published in Environmental Science & Technology Letters.

Triceratops’ massive skulls were built for horn-to-horn grappling. The rhino-like Centrosaurus could withstand stabbing its nose horn up and down. And the parrot-faced Psittacosaurus would have been wise to avoid a fight: Its head was ill-suited to handle blows.

New simulations using 3-D models of the heads of five different horned dinosaurs reveal what forces the skulls could withstand in battle. The results provide insight into how these dinosaurs evolved to use their face-based armory in combat, researchers report September 24 in PeerJ.
Ceratopsians — horned dinosaurs like Triceratops — have been hypothesized to use their imposing headgear as armaments for battling with other members of the species.

Fossilized facial injuries consistent with head-to-head violence have provided physical clues. “We know from many fossils that ceratopsian skulls tended to get banged up a little bit … in very particular spots on the frill or on the cheek,” says Andrew Farke, a paleontologist at Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California. But little else was known about how ceratopsians actually used their horns in battle.

Studying the biomechanics of the animals’ weaponized skulls could provide information on what movements and forces the dinosaurs evolved to tolerate. Such biomechanics research had previously been done on the bite stresses of theropod dinosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and on the forces felt by the club tails of armored dinosaurs, says vertebrate paleontologist Eric Austin Ames Jr.

Ames and his colleagues at the University of Bristol in England developed digital 3-D models of six skulls across five ceratopsian species spread across the group’s evolutionary tree. They simulated the combat stress experienced across the skull, varying the direction of attack and how the weaponry was used. Higher stresses in the skull meant a greater risk of mechanical failure, Ames says. The dinosaurs are more likely to have evolved to fight in a way that was well-tolerated by the skull’s mechanics.

The team found that early members of the group from about 125 million years ago — like the hornless, husky-sized Psittacosaurus — didn’t have skulls well-suited for combat of any type. The pig-sized Protoceratops had a skull that tolerated ramming fairly well. Larger, later-diverging species like Centrosaurus and the three-horned Triceratops and Spiclypeus appeared adapted to a wider range of combat styles.

Centrosaurus may have been a specialized stabber, lunging its head to jab at opponents. “When we tested [the skull] with vertical forces, it actually handled the stresses really well,” Ames says. “But when we tried side-to-side, it did not perform very well.”In contrast, Triceratops and Spiclypeus had skulls that tolerate the forces generated by interlocking horns and wrestling.

Ames thinks ceratopsians’ horns and frills probably first evolved for social and sexual display, but were soon used for full contact purposes. “Throughout their evolutionary history, their [horns’ traits] started to really explode in diversity and that coincided with different intraspecific combat styles,” he says. “This is something we see in modern herbivores.”

Much like with the antlers and horns of modern deer, buffalo or antelope, these weapons could have easily been turned on predators as well. “These adaptations are kind of like a Swiss Army knife,” Ames says. “They can be used for multiple things.”

The team created its 3-D models from surface scans of fossilized skulls. More detailed models that better simulate the complicated internal structure of these dinosaurs’ immense, bizarre skulls could provide even more insight to this prehistoric fight club, Farke says.

Six months after the Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon, the value of their closeup view is coming into focus. The first science results, released on October 7, reveal details of the moon’s array of colors, how often it gets hit by tiny rocks and lessons for squeezing as much science as possible out of future human lunar missions.

“We worked extremely hard to make sure we were able to maximize lunar science return from wherever we could in this mission,” said Artemis II flight science operations lead Kelsey Young at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting on October 7. “This is creating yet another tool in our toolbox as planetary scientists to understand our moon, our solar system, even our own planet.”

NASA’s Artemis II mission sent four astronauts on a 10-day journey around the moon in April — the first time humans had been anywhere near our natural satellite in more than 50 years. Astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen spent about seven hours in close proximity to the moon taking scientific observations, describing the moon’s surprising colors and textures and witnessing a solar eclipse from space.

Almost all of that event was livestreamed. But the astronauts took thousands of photos, notes and audio recordings that weren’t immediately made public. Part of the science team’s job was to digest those observations and release the data to anyone who wants to study them within six months of splashdown on April 10.

With three days to spare, the team released three reports and a massive data archive on October 7, the 67th anniversary of when the Soviet Luna 3 spacecraft took the first photograph of the farside of the moon. The results offer a rare test of what trained human observers can add to lunar research and what NASA can learn for future missions to the lunar surface.

“We’re really excited to release all of this data,” earth scientist Sara Schmidt of NASA Johnson Space flight Cener in Houston said during the meeting. After six months of hard work, “this is enabling science to happen for the next, I don’t know, 60 years, if not more.”
How astronauts learn to observe the moon
Surprisingly, the most valuable data from the mission were not the mind-blowingly gorgeous photos, but the astronauts’ verbal and written descriptions of what they were seeing.

Before launch, the astronauts had extensive training in lunar geology and science observations. They were an extension of the science team, said field geologist Cindy Evans also of NASA Johnson Space Flight Center, one of the astronauts’ instructors.
“You could hear it in their voices. They understood the language of geology,” she said.
That training was meant to help answer a question Young hears often: What can humans add that a camera can’t?

During the flyby, the astronauts worked in pairs. Two of them spoke to mission control on the ground, giving periodic updates to the science team on what they were seeing. The other two recorded themselves describing their observations and reactions and used a stylus to annotate specially made maps of the moon that had been uploaded to their tablets during flight. Those notes, doodles and recordings were not made public until now.
The idea was to give the crew high tech field notebooks, Young says.

“If you have any field experience, you know your field notebook is your best friend,” she said in the meeting. On Earth, geologists capture nuance and context in written and spoken words, as well as sketches, she said. “We wanted to provide the ability to capture that nuanced information from the crew.”
One example of this was when Koch sketched her view of the Orientale basin, detailing differences in texture and layers around the crater.
“Sketches can be so powerful,” Young says. “They’re quick and dirty and that’s exactly the right thing to do. You’re capturing that nuance really quickly before it leaves your brain.”

Some of the most unique observations came during the 54 minutes when the moon eclipsed the sun, giving the astronauts a view of the solar corona, interplanetary dust and other stars and planets. That was a favorite moment for planetary scientist Jennifer Heldmann of NASA’s Ames Research Center in California.

“That audio showed their sheer joy and amazement in what they were seeing and where they were,” Heldmann says. “They were so blown away by what they were seeing, while also taking very relevant science observations.”
But some of the most affecting moments were when words failed. When Glover and Koch saw the Earth emerge from behind the moon, for a while all they could say was “Oh my gosh!”
“I guess I should be trying to describe it, but I mean, good grief,” Glover’s tablet recorded him saying.
“No, I tried, but it’s impossible,” Koch agreed. “You might be able to fly a spaceship and talk, but if you can see that and talk, you just ain’t right.”
Astronauts spotted tiny impacts on the moon
Another thing the astronauts were able to see during the eclipse were impact flashes — tiny blips of light marking where bits of rock hit the moon.
“It’s a pinpoint of light,” Hansen said in his recorded observations. “It’s not like a meteor, you didn’t see anything else, it’s just like a bloop.”

Before launch, the science team identified and prioritized observations they hoped the crew would be able to make during the flyby. Impact flashes were at the top of the list. Seeing the flashes would give scientists a way to estimate how often the moon is struck by incoming rocks, and how large those rocks are. That’s an important thing to know for protecting future missions where astronauts will walk on the surface or build a long-term moon base.

Scientists didn’t know whether the astronauts would see any flashes at all. They saw five. The flashes were “pinpricks of light lasting less than a second, with no color associated with the flash,” Heldmann said at the meeting.

Comparing the number of flashes per minute to theoretical models of how many impacts the moon might experience, scientists determined that the incoming rocks were tiny, about 8.5 grams and just over 4.5 centimeters across — about the size of a golf ball.
“With these observations, we believe that the Artemis II crew set a record for the smallest meteorites ever optically observed to impact the moon,” Heldmann said.
The resulting craters are probably less than a meter wide, too small for cameras on NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to see.

That’s good news for future astronauts. Artemis IV, planned for 2028, is supposed to bring astronauts to the lunar surface for the first time since Apollo. If successful, it will be a two-week mission using landers from spaceflight companies Blue Origin or SpaceX. The probability of dangerous impact during such a mission is less than 1 in 10 million, Heldmann said. For a larger moon base meant to last a decade, the probability is higher, but still low.
“Now we can start to quantify those impact probabilities, which turns out are very very low,” she says. “Crews will be very safe.”

The moon’s muted colors were another high-priority observation for the science team. Lunar hues and brightnesses can change with terrain roughness, surface temperature and mineralogy — and they’re much more discernable with human eyes than with cameras. The crew also saw how colors changed as the viewing angle and light levels changed.
“This is such a cool demonstration of the value of human eyes as scientific sensors,” said planetary scientist Ariel Deutsch, also of NASA Ames.

Combining the crew’s observations with other data going back to the 1970s let scientists connect colors to composition. Blues were associated with titanium-rich volcanic rocks. Browns reflect different iron levels. Greens are from glass formed during volcanic eruptions or asteroid impacts.
Future astronauts could use this information to create terrain maps and to find specific materials on the moon for sample collection or resources.
The crew also was enamored with the terminator, the boundary between light and dark, which revealed lunar topography in a new way.

“Even as rugged as the far side looks … man, when you look at the terminator, it is just, like, impossibly rugged,” Wiseman said during the flight. “And it reminds you that the whole farside is that way. It’s just the terminator is really bringing out the shadows and the hills and the valleys. And it is just — it’s unbelievable.”
The lighting at the terminator is similar to what future astronauts might expect at the moon’s south pole, where the sun will be low on the horizon and may cast dramatic shadows.
“We want to make sure we have a good handle on that for both science and operations and exploration,” Heldmann said.
What Artemis II taught NASA for future moon missions
With the lessons from Artemis II in hand, now it’s the next astronauts’ turn.

Some recommendations coming out of Artemis II focus on improving conditions in the spacecraft and weaving science into mission planning better. For example, due to time constraints, the astronauts’ cameras were not calibrated before flight. The team is now trying to calibrate them back on Earth, but it can’t re-create how the windows affected images because the windows were charred on the way back through Earth’s atmosphere.

Another takeaway from Artemis II is to continue to refine and train astronauts in descriptive notetaking. The audio notes will be even more important for the first landed missions, where astronauts in spacesuits will not be able to write in a notebook.
“We want to train astronauts to be field scientists, regardless of the landing site, regardless of the mission that they’re given,” Young says.
The buddy system of two astronauts at the windows, two talking to the ground, led to better science, the team concluded.

“The crew had scientific discussions and tried to understand what they were viewing,” Heldmann says. For surface missions, where time is limited and choices must be made quickly, that collaboration will be even more important.
The crew also commented on how helpful it was.

“When we actually do go down there to the surface, I know for safety reasons that we would never send someone alone, but I just want to really emphasize how important the discussion time was,” Glover said. “When we started to talk, we not only got better science discussion, we got better human connection.”

Recently, a slender, yellow-striped California whipsnake, small enough to fit in a person’s hand, was brought to the California Wildlife Center in Calabasas. Its lower body was so twisted in fine strands of fake spiderwebs that it was essentially a ball, with twigs and leaves stuck in the mess.

“Had that gone on much longer, it could have started severing into its skin,” says Lauren Michaels, director of animal care at the center. Fortunately, the snake recovered and was eventually released. Not every animal is so lucky, though. Cambria Wells, the center’s education and outreach manager, recalls a hummingbird that was similarly wrapped in webbing and didn’t make it.

Every Halloween season, wildlife rehabilitation centers across the country see cases in which birds, bats, snakes, rodents, deer and other wild animals become injured or entangled in seasonal decorations.

The good news is that you can have a spooky spectacle in front of your house and still protect wildlife. Here are five ways to make your Halloween display friendlier to the creatures that fly, slither and scurry through your yard.

Of all the Halloween decorations people display outdoors, synthetic spiderwebs are the most dangerous, according to many wildlife experts. Made of strong, stretchy plastic, the webbing’s thin, hard-to-see strands can cling to animals and become wrapped around their bodies, posing a serious entanglement hazard. Trapped animals can go hungry, suffer constriction injuries, or even dislocate their limbs as they struggle to free themselves, Wells explains.

To get the spiderweb look without the stretchy strands, the best option is a solid web decoration made from rigid plastic or metal, she advises. Rope-style webs are safer than stretchy spiderwebbing, but they can still pose an entanglement risk.

If you do use stretchy or rope webbing outdoors, Wells recommends pulling it taut against a solid surface, such as your house, rather than across an open space where an animal could fly or travel through it.

The same principle applies to other decorations. Choose solid objects over anything with netting, strings, ropes, ribbons or other materials in which an animal could become entangled. Think tombstones, solid skeletons, signs or other decorations that hold their shape and don’t have loose or dangling parts.
Popular inflatables can be a safer alternative to netting or webbing, but you should make sure their anchoring cords and power cords are secured and check regularly for damage.

In general, look for durable decorations you can reuse year after year rather than items that are designed to be thrown away after a single season to reduce the broader environmental impact of your Halloween display, Wells notes.
Turn Halloween lights off when you go to bed

“Lighting is an underappreciated form of impact on wildlife,” Wells says. Artificial light can interfere with wildlife behavior and disorient migrating birds, many of which travel during the middle of the night and the early morning at this time of year, she explains.

If you want lights as part of your decor, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service recommends opting for ones with warmer colors, such as amber, orange or red, rather than blue, white or other cooler-colored lights, whose shorter wavelengths are more disruptive to biological rhythms.
But regardless of the type of lights you use, the simplest and most effective step, Wells says, is to turn them off when you go to bed, giving wildlife darkness during the overnight hours.

Window decals, creepy figures, glowing jack-o’-lanterns and other decorations displayed on or just inside your windows can still be seen from the street without introducing loose materials into your yard that wildlife could encounter.

Pumpkins are a Halloween staple, but you should remember that they’re also food. If you want to keep wildlife from chowing down on your carefully carved jack-o’-lantern without harming any creatures, Wells says, try bringing it in in the evening or coating it with a bitter apple spray or cayenne pepper diluted with water.

When spooky season is over, you can then compost your pumpkins or dispose of them according to your local food- or yard-waste guidelines. You can also check whether a local wildlife center or animal sanctuary accepts intact, untreated pumpkins for animal feed.

Other natural materials, such as gourds, hay, and cornstalks make for festive decor, but Wells suggests choosing materials from your local area to reduce the risk of introducing invasive plants or seeds.
If you find an entangled animal, call for help
If you discover an animal caught in or injured by Halloween decorations, resist the urge to untangle and release it. Injuries may not be obvious at first, and the animal may need medical care.
Instead contact a local wildlife rehabilitation center for guidance. You can find nearby resources through Animal Help Now.

When I was a kid, I once watched a science-fiction flick called Journey to the Far Side of the Sun. The story’s main conceit was that scientists discover an Earth-like planet directly opposite our own in the same orbit around the sun, always hidden from our vantage point. The plot itself was somewhat silly, but the idea of a counter-Earth really stuck with me.

We know no such planet exists in real life, though; its gravitational effects on other worlds such as Mars and Venus would be obvious. Also, we’ve sent probes all through the solar system, and they’ve never spotted such a planetary arrangement.

But is this possible? Could two planets physically share the same orbit? The circumstances would have to be just right, and such a situation would be incredibly unlikely to occur. But the answer, surprisingly, is yes. In fact, many planets can technically share the same orbit! And when they do, their behavior gets pretty weird.

The basic physics of how one object orbits another—say, a planet revolving around a star—has been known since Isaac Newton’s day. The math for such a simple system is pretty straightforward. And it’s deterministic; once you write down the equations, you can predict what the system will look like as far into the future or past as you like.

Throw in a third massive object, though, and the math gets ridiculously more complicated and difficult to solve. Under some circumstances, however, solutions exist that allow for a stable system even if two such planets interact. One of those solutions is a bit of weirdness called a horseshoe orbit, and it relies on a quirk of orbital mechanics.

Imagine that two planets orbit a star on very similar paths, but one (call it Planet 1) is just barely closer to the star than the other (Planet 2). This inner planet, being closer, will move more rapidly around the star than the outer planet. Eventually it will catch up to Planet 2. What happens next is counterintuitive: instead of smashing into each other, or one of them getting flung away on a high-speed slingshot trajectory, they will start to interact gravitationally while they are still hundreds of thousands of kilometers apart. Looking just at Planet 1 for a moment, it will be pulled ahead by Planet 2’s gravity, giving it more orbital energy.

This is where the oddity of orbital mechanics really factors in: if you give an object more energy (say, by accelerating it), it will naturally move to a higher orbit, one with a larger radius. So as Planet 1 accelerates, it moves slightly outward from the star. But objects in larger orbits move slower. Thus, Planet 1 slows down and begins to lag behind Planet 2, widening the gap between them. As seen from Planet 2, Planet 1 will appear to approach on the inside lane, slow down, move to the outside lane and then fall away once again. It’s as if Planet 2 has repelled its sister world! In reality, both objects orbit the star in the same direction, just at different, changing speeds.

But what about Planet 2? It’s affected by Planet 1’s gravity during the encounter as well. Planet 1 pulls Planet 2 backward, stealing some of the latter’s orbital energy. That drops Planet 2 into a smaller orbit, where it speeds up and moves ahead of Planet 1. So now Planet 1 is on the outside path, and Planet 2 on the inside. They’ve swapped orbits!
Eventually they meet again, and this time the roles are reversed: they swap orbits once more, and we’re back to the original situation.

This is not just theoretical; we see this happening in the solar system. Saturn has a pair of moons called Janus and Epimetheus, which orbit the planet on paths that are only 50 kilometers different in radius, and they undergo exactly this orbit swapping every four years or so. So not only does this occur in real life, but it’s actually a stable configuration.
That means two planets can indeed share (or nearly share) the same orbit. And while they will encounter each other, they can do so safely.
But what about an arrangement with more co-orbital planets, such as, say, three? Does that work?

According to research by a team of international scientists published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS), yes, you can have more than two planets share an orbit. Astonishingly, many more can coexist!

First, the researchers used the mathematics of orbital mechanics to simulate the physics of two Earth-sized planets orbiting a sunlike star at 150 million kilometers (the real life Earth-sun distance) and showed they can persist in such horseshoe orbits for billions of years! Then the team added more and more planets to see what would happen.

When two planets meet up with each other, they swap orbits, as is already understood. But eventually one will then approach the third planet. When it does, they swap orbits and move apart. Eventually one of those two meets up with the first planet, and the whole situation repeats. This happens with every planet-on-planet encounter.

Incredibly, the scientists found this to be true if they had as many as 24 Earth-sized planets packed into a single orbit! Twenty-four! That shocked me. Still, it seems to work in the simulations; any planet can’t get very far along its path without meeting another, and when the two do so, they swap positions and continue on until the next encounter with the next planet down the line, constantly sliding around and jockeying for position.
The scientists even tried this in a simulation of our own solar system, which, they found, could support the addition of an extra couple of Earths or Venuses—or another Mercury or Mars.

Creating a system like this isn’t easy. It’s possible that a very thick ring of dust around a star could form several planets in the same orbit simultaneously, though conditions would have to be rather fine-tuned to allow that to happen. Also, planets can migrate toward and away from their host star on much grander scales as they interact gravitationally. And if enough smaller planets get tossed around by this process, they could also end up in shared orbits.

Detecting such planetary systems from Earth is possible, too. One way we find planets now is through the transit method, in which a planet passing directly in front of its star creates a mini eclipse, as seen from Earth. If several transits occur in sequence when we should only see one for that particular orbit, that would be a sign. Also, the fact that planets in this arrangement slide along their orbit and swap positions means that their positions in that orbit change, which, in turn, changes the timing of the transits. That would be detectable, too, even if all of the planets don’t actually join the transit parade.

Delightfully, the authors of the MNRAS study speculate that there is another way to form these systems: building them on purpose. Having multiple worlds all in one orbit might be handy for interplanetary travel. And while moving them around physically is a daunting task, a sufficiently technologically advanced alien civilization might feel that it’s worth the effort. If we ever were to find such a system, well, that would be interesting, wouldn’t it?
What a way to discover aliens exist! And it would really make me reassess my opinion on Journey to the Far Side of the Sun—possibly
Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.

How much time did you spend on your phone this week? It’s okay; you don’t actually have to tell me. But chances are good, like really good, that the number is higher than you’d like it to be: according to a recent survey by Pew Research Center, more than half of U.S. adults say they spend too much time on their phones. Folks under 50 are especially dissatisfied with their device usage: 64 percent of adults aged 30 to 49 think their screen use is out of hand, and 70 percent of adults aged 18 to 29 say the same.

Setting aside the survey data and just speaking personally, I think that these days, you’re either someone who actively avoids using screened devices, someone who knows they use screened devices too much or someone who’s currently in deep denial.

There are now apps, physical phone accessories and even pared-down smartphones designed to help us curb our reflexive swiping and scrolling. But some people are taking things a step further by treating screen addiction with the same kind of programming traditionally reserved for substance abuse.

Scientific American associate editor Allison Parshall explored the new frontier of screen addiction in a feature for the latest issue of the magazine. She’s here to tell us what she’s learned about our dependence on technology—and what we can do to take back control.
Allison, thanks so much for coming on to chat. It’s always great to have you.
Allison Parshall: Thank you for having me.
Feltman: So I’d love to start by asking how you, you know, first got interested in writing this piece.

Parshall: I don’t know if you saw there were a lot of court cases to do with social media addiction earlier this year. They’re still ongoing, but, like, some of the biggest headlines were hitting. Basically Meta and Google were on trial from plaintiffs who said that their products were addictive and that they’d addicted kids, and the jury actually held them liable for that, which was a big first. So that got me interested in understanding, kind of, what’s behind these social media addiction claims because the companies claim it’s not an official addiction because there’s no diagnosis, and then, on the other side, you know, clinicians are like, “No, we’re seeing a problem.” So I kinda wanted to understand and get to the bottom of that tension.

But there was also a more personal motivation, which was that I just kept getting those, like, Sunday weekly screen time recaps, and they were always, like, way higher than I could possibly ever have fathomed. Like, I think I pushed up to seven hours a day, and that’s outside of work. So I’m doing the math, going like, “Am I on my phone literally every waking moment? That doesn’t seem possible.”
Feltman: Eight hours for work, eight hours for sleep, eight hours for what you will—is all we will phone. [Laughs.]

Parshall: All I will is phone. And then I, like, run through justifications, right? It was the winter. I was actually talking with friends most of the time; I’ve got a lot of really close long-distance friendships. A lot of it was, like, engaging creatively in things that I was very passionate about.

And then a lot of it was frankly just TikTok scrolling. So, I basically have just been kind of at war with myself and noticing a lot of my friends at war with themselves over these screen times and, like, wondering, “At what point do I say this is actually a problem? At what point does this helplessness and ambiguity I feel, like, resemble something closer to the experience of people who experience addiction to substances or to gambling and other behaviors?”
So that’s kind of where I started, with a little bit of a personal mission to figure out if I thought this was a problem or not. I can’t say I landed on a really satisfying place.

Feltman: [Laughs.] Well, it is, as you know, like, such a complex question. You know, even just speaking personally and, you know, based on the experiences of other people I know personally, because so much of it is very contextual, like you said. Like, there isn’t a distinction between online life and real life anymore. We live a lot of our lives through the channeling of these devices, so it’s like, there are many, like, good, prosocial, beneficial things one can and maybe even should do that involve staring at a screen. And then there’s the stuff that we know is just scrolling through TikTok.

I’m curious, you know, I have some familiarity with the whole, you know, “Is it an addiction?” question, not just for screens and social media specifically but really anything that’s behavioral. And I think it feels especially complicated when it’s behavioral and involves a relatively new technology. So I’d love to hear, sort of, you know, what you’ve learned and, and what your takeaways are in terms of that whole “Is it an addiction?” question.

Parshall: I think, [the] “Is it an addiction?” question is one that I am just going to have to say: I think we’re just gonna have to live in the nuance of this forever. I don’t think we’re ever gonna have a super satisfying answer because the more you look into the history of our concept of addiction, the muddier it gets.

I think a lot of people have an understanding of, like, okay, drugs are straightforwardly addictive because they can hook your brain in a chemical way. Then when we start getting into behaviors, things get a little more squishy. Gambling, we’re like, “That’s really an addiction because it does something very specific to your brain, almost like a drug.” So, you know, that—you could put it there. Well, then you get into love and sex addiction, food addiction, and it all gets quite complicated.

But I think the thing that I realized in talking to researchers was, like, even when you go back into the history of drug addiction, we’ve had to push this line to get cocaine accepted as an addictive drug. So there’s, like, all of [these] questions of: “At what point are we going to broaden it enough?” And there’s a lot of concern among various pockets of addiction researchers and clinicians that if we make it too broad, the word loses meaning. It’s, like, a serious concern, but at the same time, you do have to let it be broad enough to encompass the problems that people are experiencing, and people are experiencing this problem of tech addiction.

Feltman: Yeah. There is so much nuance, and the focus on whether screen addiction is a real addiction or not can kind of miss the point. I mean, what do we know about why screens are so compelling to us and, so often, you know, leave us feeling worse or to make worse choices in our lives?

Parshall: Well, I mean, I think it would be helpful to start with, kind of, threading the needle on where we do want to demarcate the line of addiction, not around specific behaviors and what can and can’t be addictive but around, like, what we actually see with people that we say, “Okay, that’s where it becomes an addiction. That’s where it’s not. Hanging out with your friend for eight hours on video games, that’s where it actually becomes a problem.”

One of the researchers I talked to is Mark Griffiths, and he’s one of the people who helped develop this framework. And he was saying, you know, video game addiction, you can have someone who plays video games for seven or eight hours a day, and they are not addicted to video games. Excessive use and the length of time you spend doing something is not the marker of it. It can really dovetail with it, but it’s not the marker.

So there’s six characteristics of addiction, according to this framework, that a lot of researchers use. It needs to involve a salient behavior or a drug, so something that, kind of, is grabby to you, that causes mood modification effects, which you develop tolerance to over time, which leads to this cycle of increasing use and then withdrawal when you can’t use enough. Then those withdrawals induce craving, which induces a relapse, and that can cause conflict in your life. So those six factors are salience, mood modification, tolerance, withdrawal, relapse and conflict.

And it’s not like every single researcher agrees that you need all of these in order for things to be addictive. There’s a lot of questions specifically around withdrawals and their importance because that, kind of, comes from the drug framework and not necessarily the behavioral one. But it’s really, like, this cycle of amplification where things are getting worse and your life is deteriorating that I think is what leads people to seek help in the first place from doctors or from 12-step programs, and that leads doctors to point to that and say, “Okay, we can count that as addiction.”

And for tech addiction, specifically, or social media addiction or Internet addiction or whatever grab bag of technologies you wanna use, there’s not really any great data showing the prevalence of it. Like, it seems like it’s in the low single digits, but it really depends on how wide of a net you wanna cast. People will overestimate their own addiction to technology if you give them the opportunity. People are more ready to say, “I’m addicted to this technology” and then you give them little screening tools, and they’re actually not really that addicted. Part of that is because we use this word very casually, colloquially.

Just to, like, set the groundwork here, there’s a lot of people probably who are clinically addicted to social media and technology. Whether you want to call what I’m experiencing, which is, like, periodic loss of my ability to stop scrolling TikTok even though I know it’s not good for me, and maybe, like, I’m not taking full advantage of the in-person opportunities of my life because of it, that’s a very different thing.

Feltman: So moving from this idea of “Is it addicting?” “Are people addicted?” You know, we know that the reality is, like you said, separate from people who do have clinically significant addictions to this behavior. Many of us, myself included, again, feel this compulsion to be using screens, be on social media, be on the Internet more than we know actually makes us feel good. And I feel like it’s important to stop and reflect on the fact that that is what they are designed to do. So can we talk a little bit about tech culpability here?

Parshall: Yeah. I mean, I talked to, like, 30 people for this story. Everyone I talked to would stop in the middle of saying—whether or not they were saying, “Social media addiction’s overblown. What are their habits? What is their, I don’t know, family genetic history of addiction and predisposition to find this really hooking?

There’s a concern that you’re, kind of, looking in the wrong place for the problem. And I’m very sympathetic to that. Like, I think part of the reason I can’t put this down, even though I wouldn’t say I have a lot of tendencies toward addictive things, is because it’s, like, kind of uniquely designed to hook me, and I will scroll forever. You know, you know that thing where you go back to see a video you just saw, and you scroll back up to it, and it’s, like, actually 10 videos ago? That’s what these cases are kind of resting around. These cases are really more about showing what social media companies knew based off of internal documents about the potential of their products to hook people, especially kids, and how they proceeded, kind of, regardless of those concerns.

So there’s a lot of papers that came out both in the Facebook files—I know that The Social Reckoning movie will be out by the time listeners hear this—and through these court cases with discovery, there are cases of people internal at Meta saying explicitly, “Instagram is a drug. We’re basically pushers.” What the plaintiffs argue is a company that knew what its product could do and could have harms and didn’t do anything about it. So the company argues that, like, you know, social media addiction is not an official diagnosis, which means that it’s not something we should be resting these court cases on.

It was interesting how hard it was to find legal experts to analyze these cases on the terms of social media addiction. It’s kind of like the word we use to talk about it, but it’s actually not the main character of these trials. The main [characters] of these trials are, like, the kids who are bringing these personal liability cases and the state’s [attorneys] general that are saying, you know, “You defrauded our consumers,” or, um, “You’ve [misled] our consumers.”

Feltman: Well, so getting back to individual action, in this idea of addiction or at least, you know, excessive, unhappy social media use. You talk to folks who are really treating this in themselves as an addiction, including with 12-step programs. Could you tell us a little bit about how this seems to be similar to, you know, treating drug or alcohol addiction and how it seems to be different?

Parshall: I talked to one woman who I met through this Internet and Technology Addicts Anonymous. And she had her own struggles with alcoholism, and she has been clean and sober for 30 years now, and from alcohol specifically.

And then, you know, when Facebook came out, she kind of realized that she was getting sucked in. And sometime in the last, I believe it was five years, she managed to start attending these basically AA meetings but for technology and get sober from that. She says that it feels like the same thing to her. Like, internally, this, like, loss of control, this [is] doing things that she doesn’t want to do and looking around at the people in her life that she feels like she’s constantly letting down and are increasingly learning to expect very little of her as, like, kind of the same kind of heartbreak.

It seems from talking to these people who go to these 12-step programs that, for certain people, they can be really beneficial in the same way that they’re really beneficial for people who are struggling with other addictions. I mean, just from the outside looking in, it seems like a lot of that is down to community support and dedication. You get involved in these programs, and you can just go to meetings. There’s, like, a saying, “Meeting makers make it.” But also a lot of the people I talked to said, like, getting involved, volunteering, helping run the meetings, everything like that really helped pull them out.

And I think some of that is, like, it’s something to fill your life with purpose, becoming a sponsor for other people. You know, some of the addiction researchers I talked to pointed out that there’s a reason that you’re smoking all the time, or there’s a reason that you are filling all your time with TikTok. I mean, I feel that way, like, at times of life when I feel that TikTok is hardest to resist is when everything else feels like a monumental effort, and scrolling is the only thing that can, kind of, turn my brain off. The things that 12-step programs and then other forms of treatment that are more clinically evidence-based, like, you know, seeing psychologists or therapists, many of which do use 12 steps but—can help you, kind of, fill that gap or fill that hole or however you wanna think about what it is that the vice is coming into your life to replace or to fill.

And so, yeah, I think that could be done through 12-step programs. For some people, those don’t work very well ’cause they have such a heavy focus on sobriety. You can get trapped in a cycle of shame of, like, getting sober and then breaking it and then hating yourself and coming back crawling, and for some people, that just doesn’t work well. Addiction treatment in general is kind of trying to move away from the sobriety approach to a more evidence-based harm reduction. Like, okay, we’re not going to say you have to be 100 percent sober from this thing. You see this with sex and porn addiction a lot where, like, that can be a really harmful cycle.

And so the point of therapy might not necessarily be: we’re gonna cut out social media entirely. It might be: we’re going to build these guardrails around it, or we’re gonna make sure that you find a way to only stick to just a little bit. For some people, that’s also not possible, and that’s why they go for the whole sobriety thing. The researchers and clinicians and people who have been through these 12-step programs, they all kind of stress that, like, you need to have compassion with yourself and find something that works for you.

Feltman: Yeah, I know that, for me personally, relative to how much I was on social media until this point, for the last couple of years, I’ve been, like, functionally not on social media. And it’s really interesting because, every once in a while, I start to feel, you know, disconnected enough that I really want to, like, be spending some time on Instagram on my phone, and I redownload it. And the first couple times this happened, it was a real shame cycle because I was like, “Wow, I can’t do it in moderation.”

And now I’ve really, I think, successfully reframed it as less of trying to be sober from social media and more like detoxing, where it’s like, you know, I know what it feels like when it doesn’t feel good anymore. And, like, when I really miss it in a way that feels kind of holistic and healthy and that, like, I just sort of want to be enjoying the Internet again, I redownload it. And then when I get to the point where I’m like, “Oh, no, now, now it’s poisoned my brain again,” then I get rid of it for a while.

And I think it does, for me at least, seem to work in terms of, like, recalibrating me to stop, the decreased sensitivity to it where you’re just, like, totally desensitized and spending more and more time on there and not actually using it for the things that, like, again, are prosocial and actually feel good, like reaching out to friends and seeing cool art they’re making and stuff. But, yeah, I feel like it—what that looks like is [so] personal and context dependent that it feels really tough and unfair that, like, everybody has to figure out what that looks like for them.

Parshall: And it’s constantly changing, too. That’s the thing that gets me. Like, I feel like I’ve navigated, I’ve, like, negotiated a good relationship, and then it changes. It’s kind of like the slippery slope doesn’t stop.
Feltman: Yeah, the algorithm changes; what’s going on in your life changes.

Parshall: I think part of that is, like, the way they’re designed to, like, kind of keep it as a slow slope. So, like, even if you start it with a good relationship, it is pretty easy to stop, and then you look up and you go, “Where am I?” And then you delete the app because you’re like, “I don’t like that I’m here.” I think your point about reframing is a really good one and one that I wanna stress that, like, if the addiction framing to you feels like it is unhelpful, it is really not necessary that you think of it as addiction.

There’s a lot of other ways to think about it. Some researchers really like just thinking about it as a habit. And the differences between those things are a little bit hard to literally pin down. You know, a habit is like biting your nails. We don’t really say people are addicted to biting their nails, but it’s like there’s a particular cue: “I’m bored; I’m anxious.” With your phone it might be “It’s bedtime,” and you develop these habits.

And, like, you know the thing where, like, you literally can open Instagram through muscle memory or any other app that you use and start scrolling and realize you didn’t even realize that you’d chosen to do it? So, like, the researchers I talk to stress that, like, we do know how to get people to change their habits. I mean, we have more research than we do maybe on, like, tech addiction. You can shuffle around the way the apps are on the home screen. You can delete them entirely. Something I do with TikTok is: on the iPhone, it lets you remove it from your home screen but not from your phone entirely, so every time I want it, I have to search for TikTok. That doesn’t always work. Um, but it stops, it stops me from having a literal rote muscle memory on it. I might need to do that with Instagram soon, honestly. So yeah, there’s little tweaks that you can do to try to resist this thing that is probably, profit-motive-wise, going to continue to exist to want to pull you in.

And you don’t have to think of it like addiction if you don’t want to. That can be a really stigmatizing framework, and it can be one that, you know, I mean, especially with alcoholism, like, the, kind of, the way that people who are alcoholics talk about it often is like, “I am an alcoholic,” and for the rest of your life, you frame yourself as an alcoholic. You’re just, like, in recovery. People I talk to in 12-step programs, some of them did have that framing for tech addiction. But I would say their experience is, like, more extreme than a lot of the people that I know who use technology—in, subjectively, in their experience—too much.
Feltman: We’ve brushed against this, but I would love to hear where you actually have landed in terms of managing your own screen use and social media use?

Parshall: Yeah, I would love to say that I cut down my screen time drastically. When I first started this story, I was like, “How great of an arc would it be if, at the end, I can say that I managed to cut it down to three hours a day, and here’s what I did?” I did not do that. My screen time last week was higher than ever, but I was sick, in my defense.

And I think what I’ve noticed through observing these Sunday screen time notifications every week is: it really depends on the type of week I had. And there isn’t some terrible trend line for me where it’s getting worse and worse and worse and worse. It looks like this more than anything. And I think taking the advice of the researchers I talked to who said to give yourself grace ’cause you’re in kind of a screwed-up system, I’ve been trying to do that.

I’ve also been trying to listen to myself when I have that little voice in my head that’s saying, like, “You’re doing this to numb yourself,” and the things that are worth living about life in the physical world are things that take time to build. Like, you’re gonna have to go through going to, like, a deeply unpleasant social situation for a little while in order to meet the friends, to meet the friends, to meet the friends, instead of just focusing on the vicious cycle of screen time, thinking of the virtuous cycle of doing things that you’re passionate about and that can be on a screen. Trying to not have this bifurcation in my head of, like, screen time—bad. Like, noticing when I have had seven hours of screen time, being like, “Oh, actually four of those was ’cause I was reading a book I really liked, and that’s okay.” So yeah, I, I haven’t fixed myself. But I do think I’ve started to pay more attention in a way that is healthier. I would say I hope other people can, too, but I know that I’m not leading the charge on this. I’m in the muck with every single person in my life, trying to figure out what works for them. So I hope you’re able to, to make it work better for you, too.
Feltman: Thank you so much for that. And, thank you for coming on to talk about your story with us.

Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. You can check out Allison’s feature article online or in the latest issue of Scientific American, on newsstands now. We’ll be back on Monday with our weekly science news roundup.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great weekend!
Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes.

On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events.

Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria, who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy. Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget.

She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady."

Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways."

The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce.
In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype.
Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to."
Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead.
"The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote.
Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%.

YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention.

"If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again."

Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun."
He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup.
Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms.
Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed.
In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade.

With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring."

Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October.
Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast.

"[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem."
