A billion-dollar war chest was meant to be Republicans' great equalizer heading into a bleak midterm election environment defined by economic frustration, President Donald Trump's unpopularity and fallout from the war in Iran.

From Labor Day through Oct. 14, GOP groups injected more than $740 million into congressional races that will determine control of Congress, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. That includes at least $220 million in spending from Trump-linked groups. Elon Musk has separately given another $276 million to Republican groups since July and helped boost the GOP's Senate Leadership Fund super PAC to a record quarter.

Yet with less than three weeks until the Nov. 3 Election Day, the spending blitz has barely moved the map. Democrats lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling averages across nine of the Senate's most competitive races – Alaska, Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas – little changed from before the Republican spending spree. Minnesota was expected to be solidly blue, making its tight race a concern for Democrats.
And Republican political operatives and independent election observers CNBC spoke with say the money hasn't had the effects its magnitude would be expected to in voter sentiment.

Meanwhile, the broader battlefield continues to deteriorate for Republicans. Democrats are favored to flip the House and remain competitive in the Senate, according to the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter, forcing the GOP to burn millions protecting once-safe seats while abandoning former pickup targets.

"Money is an amplifier, not a magic wand," said Neil Newhouse, partner at Republican polling firm Public Opinion Strategies. "You can buy all the airtime in the world, but if the political climate is blowing 30 miles an hour in your face, ad volume alone isn't going to turn the weather around."
Republicans entered the final stretch of the midterm election with unusually deep pockets.

MAGA Inc. had nearly $416 million on hand at the end of August, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Across the broader ecosystem, major Republican organizations had roughly $1 billion available, eclipsing the $579 million available for comparable Democratic groups, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings.

Then came Musk — after saying he'd be less involved in this year's election. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO has given more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund Republican-boosting super PAC and more than $76 million to his own America PAC, according to figures confirmed to CNBC by an America PAC spokesperson. Musk's known federal political giving this election cycle now totals roughly $366 million, making him the largest known donor of the midterms.

And Musk is far from alone. Nine of the 10 largest individual and family donor groups this cycle are Republican-aligned, accounting for 86 cents of every dollar contributed by the top 10, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC records.

"We are watching an unprecedented concentration and scale of political influence and wealth this election cycle," said Hilary Braseth, executive director of OpenSecrets, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group that tracks campaign spending.
AdImpact projects $11.6 billion in political advertising this 2025-2026 cycle, surpassing both the 2022 midterms and the 2024 presidential election.
However, the size of Republicans’ financial advantage may overstate how much advertising that money can actually buy.

That's because much of the GOP's money, particularly spending by Trump-aligned groups, has arrived late and via super PACs, which can pay far more for airtime than candidates. Federal law entitles candidates to broadcasters' lowest unit rate during the final 60 days before a general election; outside groups get no such protection.
It's an edge for Democrats whose candidates have generally outraised their Republican counterparts.

In Dallas, for example, Democrat James Talarico's campaign spent about $2.4 million on local broadcast ads from Oct. 1 through Oct. 14, enough for the average viewer to see his ads about 48 times, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. The pro-Ken Paxton Texas PAC spent about $7.8 million for roughly 81 views per viewer – more than three times as much money for only about 70% more exposure, according to the analysis.

Airtime has become so expensive that Paxton's allies have begun buying ads during national sporting events, calculating that reaching enough Texans through a national broadcast can cost less than buying across the state's local television markets, according to the Associated Press.
"R money advantage not what it appears to be on [the] surface," Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who lost to Paxton in the primary, posted on X on Oct. 5.

Across the nine key Senate battlegrounds identified by the Cook Political Report as of Oct. 1, Republicans led broadcast TV spending in seven and outspent Democrats by 26% overall through Sept. 30, yet generated only 7% more airings.

To be sure, super PACs don't face the same pricing disadvantage on digital ads, where campaigns and outside groups compete on more equal footing. But broadcast TV still dominates political spending, with AdImpact projecting it will account for 48% of the 2026 cycle total.
But the payoff from all that spending has been harder to see in political polls.

Despite more than $113 million spent on negative advertising targeting Talarico since the Texas primary, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, a Siena College poll released Tuesday showed Talarico leading Paxton 48% to 44%, down only slightly from his six-point lead in September.

In Michigan, after more than $87 million in attacks targeting Democrat Abdul El-Sayed this year, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, Fox News polling from late September found El-Sayed's favorable rating among registered voters up five points from its early August survey, while Republican Mike Rogers' fell four points.

Part of the challenge is diminishing returns on ads as Election Day nears. Political advertising experts tell CNBC that as campaigns repeatedly target the same small pool of persuadable voters, each additional dollar is less likely to reach someone who has not already heard the message.

"When an undecided voter has already seen 20 negative ads today, the 21st ad doesn't persuade them. It just gets tuned out," said Michael Beckel, money in politics reform director at Issue One. "Their eyes glaze over." Issue One works to reduce the influence of money in politics and has a board that includes former Democratic and Republican elected officials.

Still, some Republicans counter that topline poll movement is the wrong barometer. They say the September cash influx helped keep vulnerable candidates competitive as the political environment deteriorated.

In Texas, Republicans spent $121.5 million on the Senate race in September, up from just $5.5 million over the previous three months, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, while Musk's America PAC added direct mail and canvassing. Republicans involved in the race said the picture could have been far worse without that support.

"The spending hasn't put Paxton ahead, but it kept a messy race and flawed candidate from becoming an unwinnable one," said a Republican operative involved in the Texas Senate race, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the state of the contest.

Maine offers another test. Republicans have poured more than $50 million into the state to support incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, nearly twice Democratic spending, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. Since early September, FiftyPlusOne's polling average has tightened modestly, from about a three-point advantage for Democrat Troy Jackson in early September to roughly two points now.
The clearest sign that the GOP's cash advantage has stalled, however, is where the money is migrating.

In April, the Senate Leadership Fund announced a record $342 million advertising program across eight states designed to protect the GOP majority and expand the map. Texas, Kansas and Nebraska were not among the states.

Since Sept. 1, the SLF and affiliated groups — according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data — have spent or committed roughly $180 million across those three states, all of which Trump carried by double digits in 2024.
"Outside groups are diverting millions into deep-red territory to build defensive moats, leaving pickup opportunities starved for cash in the final stretch," Beckel told CNBC.
But those emergency defenses have come at a cost, diverting money from races Republicans once hoped to win and forcing national groups to narrow the map elsewhere.

In North Carolina, the Senate Leadership Fund initially pledged $71 million to back Republican Michael Whatley. On Oct. 2, however, the group pulled most of its remaining ad reservations after spending about $32.8 million, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data, as Democrat Roy Cooper continued to hold a double-digit lead in FiftyPlusOne's polling average.
It's a striking retreat in a perennial battleground where Republicans have won every presidential and Senate election since 2008.
The same triage is unfolding in the House.

The Congressional Leadership Fund cut off spending this week for vulnerable GOP Reps. Thomas Kean Jr. of New Jersey and Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa following grim internal polling. The group also shelved efforts to flip Democratic-held seats represented by Reps. Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan and Greg Landsman of Ohio. The spending shifts were first reported by the New York Times.

Those four races had already absorbed about $13.7 million in Congressional Leadership Fund spending through Oct. 14, according to a CNBC analysis of AdImpact data. CLF is redirecting roughly $10 million from those races across 16 other districts, according to the Times.
The new spending includes the South Texas seat held by Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, a district Trump carried by 18 points in 2024. De La Cruz herself won reelection by about 14 points in 2024.

There was no indication LaRoyce Hawkins, better known to fans as Kevin Atwater, would be leaving Chicago P.D. when the 13th season concluded back in May. Then, over the Fourth of July holiday weekend came the news that he would be departing the series he has starred on since it launched, and now, that final episode has aired.

A fan-favorite and original series star ever since the show premiered with “Stepping Stone” on Jan. 8, 2014, news of Hawkins’ departure quickly became social media chatter. With no official explanation from Hawkins or NBC, speculation turned to money and cost-cutting measures across the industry. Not even until the preview of the episode that aired last week were fans made aware that the Oct. 14 episode (“Don’t Blink”) would be Atwater’s last.

The idea of Atwater leaving Chicago was floated and shot down when Karen Obilom’s Tasha Fox, a fellow officer who attended the police academy with Atwater, announced her intention to leave Chicago and join the police force in Miami in the episode of the same name last October. Fox and Atwater shared a night of passion that resulted in a pregnancy reveal in January episode “On the Way,” and an agreement that they would work on making their relationship real in “The Wicked River,” a few episodes before that season finale. At the start of season 14, the only thing that was clear in the premiere (“Demolition”) was that the baby was coming.

“Don’t Blink” starts in the hospital with the baby, a son, and Atwater and Tasha. As Atwater goes back to work dealing with a robbery, he is an attentive father, calling in during breaks and rushing to the hospital when the baby becomes sick. But he becomes deeply affected by a suspect, a father who had been absent from his son’s life. That gets Atwater thinking about what he wants not just for himself, but for his own son. His stance against the Blue Wall and systemic racism within the police force back in season eight blocked his options for promotion and a raise. In the end, he decides to relocate with Tasha and the baby from Chicago to Atlanta. And the finale in the bar, with colleagues and friends singing “He’s A Jolly Good Fellow” ends Atwater’s Chicago P.D. reign.
It was a bittersweet moment with many agreeing that the final episode was handled well.

Last year, the Chicago-area native from Harvey spoke with The Hollywood Reporter about Atwater’s evolution and expressed his gratitude, as well as discussing the pressure of representing his hometown. He also shared the honor and privilege he felt being part of the Dick Wolf universe.

Speaking with THR now, a day before his last episode aired, he said he planned to watch the hour in real time for the first time surrounded by family. Hawkins pondered Atwater’s significance and impact.

“Because I grew up watching reruns from shows that were over way before I was born, I wasn’t unaware of the impact that you can still have for generations that you’re not necessarily a part of,” he said. “So now I’m very interested in how we will rediscover and explore Atwater.”

How Chicago P.D. tackled the pandemic is of particular significance. “By the time we remind ourselves about the pandemic period and we unpack how Atwater had to be on the front line as a cop for television, and the way that the Black man and his life seem not to matter as much [then], and to play a character that had to hold the weight of both of those, at the time, I was just ready,” he shared. “I was locked in, and I don’t think I even understood then that this is going to be a capsule of a time period that is going to [represent] a significant shift in TV. It was a significant shift in the nation.

“I’ll never forget how intentional the Dick Wolf team and the powers that be in that universe were about how we told stories after the pandemic, and I was grateful to be instrumental in how we were able to tell those stories,” he added.

Then, after watching his final episode as Atwater, Hawkins took time again to speak with THR about the episode, sharing behind the scenes gems, dishing on everything from the babies who played Atwater’s son to sharing the screen with Jason Beghe one last time, the fan reaction to his exit and stacking the show’s final scene with friends and family to say goodbye.
I was struck by the tenderness and thoughtfulness in the final episode. I don’t think we see cops presented in this light. And I really don’t think we’ve ever seen a Black cop presented like this.
I think that is something that is good to see, especially in today’s world. And when you consider all the characters that have left this show at a high level, nobody really goes out like that.
People on social media were upset when they thought Atwater got shot and might be killed off.
They had to throw that in there just to throw people off. That was crazy. Yeah, my mama was tweaking. My big sister was mad. I was like, Nah, everything is going to work out.

While the episode was really strong in showing how fatherhood can change a man, how parenthood changes a person, it also showed how this other man’s regrets as a father inspires even more responsibility and care in Atwater.

That was the part that got me. I remember when I made notes for the episode before we really got into it. After I read [the script] a few times, one of the things I said was that what I see is this father was absent in his son’s life, and how that affected his son. I see how it’s affecting him. I said, “We don’t really need the bullet. I understand the bullet because you want to be dramatic, but I don’t want it to be the bullet that [connects the dots for Atwater]. I want the case to have a handle [or impact] on me, and for my opinion to reflect, Oh I can have it all. I think I trust Tasha Fox. I think I feel like my son’s going to be amazing.” Could you tell that wasn’t a boy?
Speaking of babies, we don’t often see fathers showing up at the hospital when the baby is sick. It was tiny things we don’t see represented, that we almost never see represented for a Black father.
That wasn’t a bad way to go. I was proud of it.
What did you feel when you were filming it?

To be honest, there were moments, especially at the beginning of filming, where I had to isolate myself because everybody knew it was my last episode. Imagine the crew and the cast, like everybody, trying to throw in their last conversations or create that last impression. That was throwing me off, because I’m trying to cook on what we got going. I learned that after the first day of shooting. When I noticed people were going to try to take those windows, I was off to the side. I’m pretty social on set, because there’s an energy I like to try to maintain. I like to hop around and engage with people, and I couldn’t really do that because I couldn’t afford to.

It was the second episode back after a strong hiatus, and it really takes four or five episodes to get warmed up for a season like Chicago P.D. When you’re doing 20 something episodes, you don’t really get warm until episode six. So for us to still just be on [episode] two, I was trying to get my bearings back. I had to isolate myself from distractions.

But I was confident because Jesse [Lee Soffer who played Halstead until exiting in season 10] directed it, and Jesse gave me one of the best notes I’ve probably had since I’ve been on the show. He was like, “Bro, are you hyper aware of yourself? I was like, “Yeah, low key, I am.” And he was like, “You got to stop that. You can’t be so aware of yourself because sometimes I can see you editing your performance within the performance. You have to block out LaRoyce Hawkins’ thoughts and focus on the Atwater’s thoughts.”

You can’t tell me to trust myself. Directors, sometimes [are] like, “Yo, just trust yourself.” But I can trust myself too much, and I can forget there’s a world to get lost in. So it felt great shooting with Jesse directing, because every day was like a masterclass on being specific in the character thoughts. Sometimes the LaRoyce Hawkins thoughts and the character’s thoughts aren’t always aligned. So I was confident that the episode was going to be okay because I remember working hard on set on that.

Shooting it was dope, but it was also bittersweet because certain scenesm, I knew it was going to be my last scene in the bullpen. The last scene that I shot was this scene with me and Sarge [Jason Beghe who plays Sargeant Hank Voight] in his office.
How was that experience character to character with Atwater and Voight, but also actor to actor with you and Jason Beghe?

It was emotional sometimes, to be honest with you. I didn’t even realize until I looked at [the episode] that it looks like I might cry. But that’s how I felt in the moment. To be honest, it was like, Damn, dude. It was my last scene with Sarge. I love Sarge. So the conversation paralleled what was going on with the character and with myself, which was cool. Sarge saying that I can do anything, that I deserve it all, all of those moments felt like it really reflected our real relationship sometimes, and I could tell he was getting emotional sometimes, too. But we just made sure it was fun. That scene was less on paper. I’m not going to say we put humor in it, but we did find moments where it felt real. Like when [Atwater] was like, “Why didn’t you give them my name?” [And Sarge was] like, “Well, I ain’t wanna lose you.”

So there were more smiles on that day we discovered that weren’t on the page at first. [The original scene] almost felt too dramatic. It felt like a scene where I was being dismissed, and we didn’t want it to feel like that. We were able to make some adjustments. Then on the actual [last] day, I had my family and a bunch of close friends pull up. As soon as I was done shooting, a whole bunch of [folks] swarmed the set. It was like I heard trumpets and chants. Everybody marched out. It was pretty dope.

You said that scene with Sarge was the last one you shot. How did it feel when you filmed the finale in the bar and everyone is telling Atwater, including his boy Ruzek (Patrick John Flueger), one-half of Ruzwater, how much he and you have meant?

That was a dope day. I made sure I filled that scene with homies. That’s what helped it feel so real. I had a big homie fly into Chicago from New York just to be in the background for that scene. I had one of my big homies, Raekwon [Neighbors], he owns the best daycare centers [Raekwon’s Scholastic Daycare Academy] in Cook County, back there. I just filled it with friends. I had my niece in the scene because I wanted real energy, camaraderie, togetherness and family to come through. It wasn’t the last scene we shot. I think we might have shot maybe day three or day four. So it didn’t feel like it was hard to try to conjure up that last moment type of energy because it wasn’t the last moment. I filled the space with loved ones. And that was the best part about that scene, seeing my homies behind me. Seventy-five percent of them were actually friends, and not just background extras.
I imagine knowing that that scene was the ultimate destination helped with the other scenes because you knew where you were going.

Yeah. Even when I look at the performance, I could tell I was a little bit more locked in and a lot more specific about where I was going and coming from. The episode itself isn’t the most dynamic, but it felt grounded and I was prepared, which is what I like about my final performance. It was real. It wasn’t over the top. But I don’t think anything underwhelmed you, either. It felt pretty solid across the board.

I also like that it felt logical. It felt like, okay, my life has changed. I’m making different decisions, and what I wanted before is not what I want now, because I’m not thinking about just myself. And because I live in Atlanta and am from Chicago, I was thinking to myself, oh, it’s crazy that he’s coming to Atlanta. Especially when it was potentially Miami before.
It’s crazy because I’m actually in Atlanta right now. It’s so funny, but it’s so real.
What do you think of the ship name “Foxwater” for Tasha Fox and Kevin Atwater?

Yeah. What a lot of people don’t know is I came up with all the names. I was the one who started Burgewater [Atwater’s name merged with partner Kim Burgess, who is now married to Ruzek]. I was the first one to be like, yo, let’s just put our names together, because I felt like Atwater was just dope; you can put anything before “water” and make it sound cool. Burgewater was the first one I came up with. Foxwater was easy. I like Tasha Fox [portrayed by Karen Obilom] a lot. I think she was proud of me. She was my personal favorite love interest. I know everybody had their opinions about them all, but I think she was the best one. I think we got it right when we found her.
I think also that Atwater and Tasha are evenly yoked. They both understand what the job is and where they both come from. Tasha Fox seems like the most compatible woman for Atwater.

Social media reacted very well to the episode itself, with many people agreeing it was beautiful. Some people did share that since Atwater is gone, they are, too; that they would try the show out next week to see what they were doing after Atwater. What are your thoughts?

I’ve been hearing a lot of that, too. And it’s hard because I love the show. I’m a fan of the show minus myself, but it’s because of myself that I’m a part of the show. So there’s a part of me that’s like, yeah, y’all ain’t gotta watch that shit no more. And then there’s a part of me that does want to see the show grow still. Actually it confirms the fact that Atwater is a true vibe [and a] part of the fabric of the show that makes it good. You don’t always know that you’re doing that.
It seems like there is potential in an Atwater show in starting over in Atlanta. Aside from Will Trent, there is no other cop show or procedural based in Atlanta.

Watching the Celeste episodes with Amanda Payton, Atwater seemed kind of dirty to me. Not telling her he was a cop when a case came up involving her and her students didn’t seem right. And then in other episodes, there were so many times when I didn’t always agree with Atwater’s actions, even though it may be part of the job.
You said you haven’t always agreed with Atwater?
Yeah, especially going back through the episodes, I just wasn’t cool with a lot of his actions.

I haven’t been either. And that was a struggle for me too as an actor. Because Atwater is a cop, sometimes the hard part for me was wrapping my mind around how a cop would think and what a cop’s opinions would be. And that didn’t always align with what LaRoyce would do. But that’s why LaRoyce isn’t Atwater. I would infuse and texturize Atwater with what made sense for LaRoyce. Whether it was empathy or some humor here, or I would drop in moments that made sense. But Atwater’s a cop, so you know his opinion would probably disagree with the average Black person based on his intentions to protect and serve.

In the final moments of the episode when Atwater makes his decision, I thought back to when he was with the psychologist Val Soto [Natalee Louise Linez] and she told him he didn’t make time for himself. I think in this final moment with Atwater, we see him finally doing what he needed to do for himself.
He put himself first obviously because of his family. And you gotta understand Atwater lost his family once upon a time because of the job, and he wasn’t willing to do that this time.
Chicago P.D. airs on NBC Wednesday nights at 10pm ET as part of the One Chicago Block that includes Chicago Med and Chicago Fire.

I don’t watch television. I mostly read, go to shows, see some clown. So I had only a vague idea of who Kelly Clarkson was. I knew she was on some talent show with Justin Guarini, whom I know from theater work.

On Oct. 10, Ms. Clarkson entered Art of Play, the Brooklyn curiosity shop where I live. She spent less than five minutes here and caused quite a hullabaloo. She asked a sales associate if she could purchase me, Molly, the mascot of the store and was duly informed that while that was impossible, she could contact artist Bliss Kolb to ask for a $15,000 duplicate. Bliss, of course, makes crank-driven mechanical contraptions that imitate living creatures, much like daytime talk show hosts.

The first clue that I wasn’t for sale might have been that I’m mounted on the wall. Other items not for sale in Art of Play include the light fixtures, the commode and the sign that reads, “The Art of Play,” which a number of people also inquire about, nearly all of them gay men. I’m sure Ms. Clarkson also wants an Oompa Loompa, but we don’t sell them either.

Why would a store have an item that’s not for sale? Perhaps Ms. Clarkson has never been to Brooklyn. None of the things in any of the stores here are for sale. They are like the frozen yogurt shop and doll store underneath Barbra Streisand’s house. We are all funded by our parents, some of whom are Barbra Streisand.

Ms. Clarkson posted on X that she “literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y’all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts’ character in Pretty Woman.”

Although I have not seen Pretty Woman, or any of Garry Marshall’s work other than his excellent performance in Lost in America, I have since viewed the clip she’s referencing and find the comparison perplexing. If 1990 Julia Roberts walked in wearing a cropped white tank top attached to a blue miniskirt with a silver O-ring, I would have jumped into her purse. As the security footage uncovered by podcaster Pablo Torre shows, Ms. Clarkson wore the same dreadful outfit as every other Art of Play customer. Maybe now the owners will listen to my plea for a dress code. Then again, one of them wrote the children’s book Dragons Love Tacos, so I’m not holding my breath. Unless you don’t crank me.

This is not the first Karen to enter Art of Play. One white woman demanded to talk to the manager about how the $1,200 applause machine wouldn’t clap for her. Another complained after asking for help solving the $185 egg-shaped puzzle, and we joshingly suggested that she “Goop it.”

The online kerfuffle had Clarkson supporters doxxing our owners and sending them death threats, causing the Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union to issue a formal statement defending us from celebrity-fueled mobbing. America is sadly divided between people who kneel at the altar of television celebrity, and those who want to enter the secret theater in the back of a curiosity shop and see Jay Gilligan’s “Stories About Gravity” magic show.

Before you decide whose side you’re on, let me remind you of what Voltaire wrote about a little animatronic wooden duck from 1764 made by artist Jacques de Vaucanson that could eat, digest and excrete. He said, “Without … Vaucanson’s duck you would have nothing to remind you of the glory of France.” Replace “France” with “America” and “Vaucanson’s duck” with “Kelly Clarkson” and it’s really funny.

Part of why I write is that once you wind me up, I can’t stop. But also to warn other institutions about Ms. Clarkson. The Louvre might want to post extra guards around the Mona Lisa to prepare for her visit.
We have now posted an ironic price tag of $15 million because, by law, we can only do things in Brooklyn with irony. But also because we think Blake Shelton might really buy it for her.

Ms. Clarkson is now doing a residency at a hotel in Las Vegas, a place I am about as likely to visit as Manhattan. I hope she is comforted by whatever wooden toys she’s been able to acquire there, perhaps a Thomas the Tank Engine. It’s not a city for a bird with a wooden worm gear that operates a star gear and eight cams that each operate a lever that controls either one movement or a leather bellows that blows air through a brass whistle whose pitch is varied by a plunger operated by its own lever and cam.

All of this is a media distraction from what we should really be talking about, which is Palestine. As a wooden toy bird of privilege, I feel a responsibility to use my animatronic voice in allyship with oppressed people, birds, toys, toy birds and bird toys. As another famous wooden toy once said, “There are no strings on me!” Though for $15 million, I’m willing to sing whatever you want.

For Obsession writer-director Curry Barker, rolling out a follow-up to the biggest surprise breakout of the year is a pretty daunting task — especially given Barker cast himself in the film’s lead role.
But Seth Rogen says he’s actually seen Barker’s follow-up, Anything But Ghosts, which is released next year.
And The Studio creator claims the film is not only better than Obsession, but that Barker crushes his major feature film on-camera debut.

Writing for Time magazine’s Time 100 package, Rogen described the experience of watching Obsession for the first time in a theater, then added, “I’ve seen Curry’s next film, Anything But Ghosts—and for those of you who, like me, are uncomfortable with this amount of talent in a person so young, I have bad news … it’s even better, and, to add insult to injury, he’s just as good an actor as he is a director.”

Anything But Ghosts stars Barker and his producing partner and Obsession co-star Cooper Tomlinson as two fake paranormal investigators hired by a couple (Bryce Dallas Howard and Aaron Paul) who have a real haunted house. The film was written by Barker and Tomlinson and shot before Obsession was released. Like his hit debut, Ghosts will be distributed by Focus Features.

During Barker’s interview for The Hollywood Reporter‘s cover story on the director’s wild success in June, he was in the middle of editing Ghosts and expressed concern about comparing the film to the rather high bar set by Obsession. “If I’m worried, it’s comparing it to Obsession that’s hard,” he said.

“It’s a buddy comedy, but it’s still going to be scary and messed up,” he said. “You can’t not have these feelings when your first movie is breaking box office records and you’re in your room editing your next movie thinking, ‘Oh my god, did I take this beat from Obsession?’ Thank God I have people around me to ground me and tell me that Anything But Ghosts is good and different, and that’s OK. Nobody wants the same movie twice. So people can expect it to be very different than Obsession, but my voice will still be very strong in it.”

Ghosts had a production budget of $5 million — which is rather lavish when compared to the famously frugal $750,000 budget of Obsession. Obsession topped $500 million globally, and is in the awards conversation. It stands as the fifth highest-grossing horror movie of all time globally. The film will be released in May, 2027.

It’s been more than sixteen years since My Chemical Romance dropped their fourth album, Danger Days: The True Lives of the Fabulous Killjoys, the 2010 release that, for now, served as their recorded swan song.

Since then, the group has gone radio silent on new music, though they reunited for a 2017 tour and released the one-off new single “The Foundations of Decay” in 2022. They’ve been on a two-year swing of dates around the world celebrating their most beloved album, 2006’s The Black Parade, and on Friday (Oct. 16) they surprised fans with the streaming debut of the blistering, previously unreleased song “Someone Out There Loves You (Live From Hoboken).”

The track appears on the upcoming The Black Parade (20th Anniversary) expanded edition — due out on Oct. 23 — with the accompanying video (see below) capturing the emo rock legends in top form during a show at their 200-capacity hometown Hoboken, N.J. club Maxwell’s in 2007.

The reissue features the entire original album, which spun off the hit title track, “Welcome to the Black Parade,” the highest-charting single from the group to date, which hit No. 9 on the Billboard Hot 100 in September 2006.

It is one of six bonus tracks on the expanded edition, including two more live tracks from that Hoboken show, “Dead!” and “The Sharpest Lives,” which have not been released on LP, CD or streaming to date, as well as three fan-favorite B-sides that have previously been available as B-sides on older releases, “Heaven Help Us,” “Kill All Your Friends” and “My Way Home Is Through You.”

“Twenty years ago, we wrote what would become The Black Parade, our third record and the follow-up to Three Cheers for Sweet Revenge,” the band said in a statement. “At the time, we could never have imagined what the record would mean for the band. All we knew is that we had made something crazy, and something we couldn’t wait to get it out into the world… For the first time, we have included everything we finished during those sessions in a single collection.”

“Someone Out There Loves You” is classic Black Parade-era MCR, featuring that album’s signature blend of punk/emo energy and pop songwriting chops and an urgent, yelping chorus on which singer Gerard Way wails, “And would you stay right here/ Then I’ll tell you/ That someone out there loves you/ If you stay right here/ Then I’ll tell you/ That someone out there loves you after all.”
MCR will mount a grand finale for the U.S. leg of their Black Parade 2026 tour with a five-night run at the Hollywood Bowl beginning on Oct. 21 and culminating on Halloween night (Oct. 31).

Though fans will have to make due with the unearthed bonus single for now, Way hinted that the band may be gearing up to record their first new album in 15 years at the Sept. 12 Black Parade show at San Antonio’s Alamodome. “Just know that, like, we’ve kind of really always wanted to make another record, so we hope that life allows us to do that,” he said. “Cause you guys, honestly, you guys kept us alive so long. You guys deserve another record. I don’t know when it’ll be. But it’ll be awesome.”

The Princess of Pop is paying tribute to another member of pop royalty — although Britney Spears thinks that Janet Jackson is actually on an even higher level among the gods.

In a reverent post on Instagram on Thursday (Oct. 15), Spears shared a photo of Miss Jackson and recalled how, at the age of 13, her “mouth dropped open” any time one of the “That’s The Way Love Goes” singer’s music videos came on TV. “I kept repeating in my head, ‘No, No … Please come back, I wanna see that again … Where the hell did that come from ???'” she wrote.

“It was her ability to be incredibly mysterious, so dark with a vibe that sucked you in immediately, and then this haunting simple angelic tone … The feeling she gives with her voice when she sings is so pure and genuine,” Spears continued. “She’s not trying to be sexy … She just is … She can’t help it … She has always been god to me.”
The superstar went on to say that Jackson isn’t just a singer, but “an entertainer in people’s eyes” who leaves adults “spellbound” just as much as she “captivate[s] the hearts of children.”

“I was so young, and she spoke to my heart and soul like no one else … I have no idea why I’m writing this, but I do believe people like her are here for a reason,” Spears added. “Just her smile alone changed the world forever … She’s my girl crush this month.”
In response, Jackson reshared the post on her Instagram Story and added a red heart emoji and kissy-face emoji.

Spears may be one of the iconic singer-actress’ most famous fans, but her praise echoes what countless others have loved about Jackson for decades. The singer, who is the younger sister of Michael Jackson, dominated the late ’80s and ’90s, scoring 10 No. 1s on the Billboard Hot 100 over the course of her career. (Only the King of Pop, The Beatles, Mariah Carey, Taylor Swift, Drake, Rihanna, Madonna, The Supremes and Whitney Houston have had more.)
Miss Jackson would eventually pass the baton to Spears, whose music was inescapable in the late ’90s and 2000s, earning her the nickname of Princess of Pop, with five No. 1s on the Hot 100 to date.

Something the “Toxic” singer probably didn’t expect back when she was a teenager worshipping Jackson, however, was that they’d someday be linked through their respective connections to Justin Timberlake, who in 2021 apologized to both women at the same time after facing very belated backlash for the way he treated them in the past.

“I am deeply sorry for the times in my life where my actions contributed to the problem, where I spoke out of turn, or did not speak up for what was right,” he wrote at the time in reference to his disrespectful comments about Spears following their 2002 breakup and his lack of support for Jackson after he exposed her breast at the 2004 Super Bowl. “I understand that I fell short in these moments and in many others and benefited from a system that condones misogyny and racism. I specifically want to apologize to Britney Spears and Janet Jackson both individually because I care for and respect these women and I know I failed.”

It doesn’t seem as though Spears harbors any ill will toward JT, however, as the star has had kind things to say about him in the past couple of years. She also surprised fans Oct. 9 by releasing a song they wrote together more than two decades ago titled “She’ll Never Be Me.”

Universal Music Group and Sony Music have filed a new legal case seeking to force DistroKid to disclose how many AI songs it uploads to streaming services each month, arguing it’s crucial evidence in their ongoing battle against Suno.

In a new action filed Wednesday (Oct. 14), the music giants ratcheted up the pressure on DistroKid, calling the huge DIY distributor “one of the primary conduits by which the streaming market is being flooded with AI-generated recordings.”

In technical terms, the new filing aims to compel DistroKid comply with a subpoena, sent last month, seeking internal metrics on how many AI songs it uploads. UMG and Sony want that information to use as evidence in their massive legal fight with Suno, but say DistroKid “refuses to produce a single document.”

“Suno’s industrial-scale theft will lead to a market flooded with machine-generated recordings that compete with human-created works,” UMG and Sony’s attorneys write in their filings, obtained and first reported by Billboard. “DistroKid’s AI-detection results are direct evidence of that flood.”
Reps for DistroKid and Suno did not immediately return requests for comment.

Wednesday’s new case essentially links up a two-front legal war on unauthorized AI music. UMG and Sony have spent years suing Suno for copyright infringement, claiming it stole millions of real songs to train its machines to spit out millions of new ones. Then last month UMG filed a scathing lawsuit against DistroKid, the world’s largest music distributor, that claimed it was enabling bad actors to upload “AI-generated slop” that’s “polluting the listening experience.”

In the new filing, lodged in Manhattan federal court, UMG and Sony argue that they need information from both companies to fully analyze the AI music landscape. Suno “does not track where its outputs are distributed once they leave Suno’s platform,” they say, but DistroKid “sits upstream of the streaming services” and has admitted it tracks AI usage in songs it uploads to them.

“That makes DistroKid a singular source of relevant evidence,” lawyers for the labels write. “The question of how much AI-generated music is reaching digital platforms, and what it is earning there, is not information that is available from Suno.”

According to UMG and Sony, DistroKid has thus far refused to turn over that information on the grounds that it isn’t relevant to how Suno created its models. But the labels say it is obviously relevant to Suno’s crucial defense of fair use, since that all-important legal issue turns on whether a torrent of AI-generated music is crowding out human-created songs.

“DistroKid has admitted that it measures that flow with an AI-detection tool,” UMG and Sony’s attorneys write. “Whether that flow is harming the market for plaintiffs’ recordings is a question at the center of Suno’s fair use defense.”

The new filing against DistroKid comes just days after the company admitted that it had removed some user uploads in response to the recent UMG “slop” lawsuit. The company has denied any wrongdoing in that case, saying it strongly disputes the label’s accusations.

A painting by the Russian artist Wassily Kandinsky that was looted by the Nazis has sold at an auction for more than 31.5 million pounds (nearly $42 million). The work, “The Colorful Life,” spent decades in a German museum before it was returned to the family that owned it until 1940, opening the way for a private sale.

It sold after about six minutes of bidding on Wednesday in London, according to the auction house Christie’s, which had expected it to fetch between $24 million and $33 million. The buyer’s identity was not disclosed.

Experts consider the painting, from 1907, an important marker in Kandinsky’s journey from figurative painter to abstract artist. It depicts a vibrant, dreamlike scene that shows brightly dressed characters in a fantasy landscape. On its website, Christie’s described it as a panoramic landscape pulsing with life.
Before the hammer came down on Wednesday during Christie’s 20th- and 21st-century evening sale, the painting had taken a circuitous route to the auction block.
Before World War II, “The Colorful Life” was part of the collection of a Dutch Jewish industrialist who ran a sewing machine factory, Emanuel Lewenstein, and his wife, Hedwig Lewenstein Weyermann.

The Lewensteins’ art collection was sold at an auction in Amsterdam in October 1940, five months after Nazi-led Germany invaded the Netherlands. By then, the Lewensteins had died and their two surviving children had fled Europe. Historians have not been able to determine the exact circumstances of the 1940 sale.

The German bank Bayern LB bought the work in 1972 and lent it to a museum in Munich. That’s where it hung for about half a century until 2023, when the Lewensteins’ heirs filed a lawsuit to have the painting returned to them.
Bayern LB returned the painting to the heirs in 2023 after the German government’s advisory commission on Nazi-looted art recommended it do so.

The commission said at the time that, whether through sales or confiscation, art losses experienced by people from persecuted groups in the Nazi-occupied Netherlands should be assumed to have been involuntary unless there is clear evidence to the contrary.
“There are numerous indications that this was a case of a seizure as a result of Nazi persecution,” the commission said.
Wednesday’s sale did not exceed the highest price paid at auction for a Kandinsky. In 2023, a painting by the Russian artist sold for roughly $45 million at a Sotheby’s auction.
Oct. 16 (UPI) -- Former Hampton County, S.C., attorney Alex Murdaugh was back in court on Friday for a status hearing ahead of his retrial next year.

South Carolina Judge Debra R. McCaslin heard disputes between the prosecution and defense over evidence to be shared prior to the retrial. Evidence in question included cellphone data from Maggie Murdaught and Paul Murdaugh's phones, information about a law enforcement officer with ties to the Murdaugh family and discussion of possible alternate suspects.
McCaslin said during the hearing "the court shouldn't even be involved in this at all," urging both parties to work out disclosures of evidence with each other.

"To be honest with you, I don't care what happened in the first trial," McCaslin said. "Quit telling me about stuff you all did to each other during the first trial. I don't care. We're not going to do that this go-around."
The retrial is set to be held in Sumter County, S.C.
Alex Murdaugh's attorneys seek to have the prosecution reveal more evidence ahead of the retrial, including a report on local police's handling of the murder weapons.
The defense has requested to move forward with more DNA testing on samples found under Maggie Murdaugh's fingernails and it seeks to obtain ballistic reports from the scene.
Alex Murdaugh was convicted in 2023 for the 2021 murder of his wife, Maggie, and 22-year-old son, Paul, at their home in Colleton County, S.C.

Murdaugh was sentenced to two life sentences for murder. However, the conviction and sentence were vacated by the state supreme court after it found Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill may have influenced the jury in the first trial.
Murdaugh remains held in prison for state and federal financial crimes for stealing millions of dollars from clients and others. Those crimes have been linked as a motive in the killings.

Hill pleaded guilty to obstruction of justice, perjury and misconduct for sharing court-sealed information about the trial with the press. Concerns about her conduct around the trial were raised after she co-authored a book about the trial while it was ongoing.
Oct. 16 (UPI) -- Real Madrid called on Javier Tebas to resign after the La Liga president likened the club's approach to Joseph Goebbels, the Nazi's propaganda chief.

Madrid issued the response to Tebas on Friday to a lengthy post he made earlier in the day on social media. The La Liga club also asked for Tebas' "immediate resignation" as vice president of the Royal Spanish Football Federation, or RFEF.

"Real Madrid C. F. considers it absolutely intolerable and extraordinarily serious that someone holding two positions of utmost responsibility in Spanish football resorts to a comparison with the propaganda methods of the Nazi regime to discredit our club, its management, and its television," Madrid said.
"The clarification that he is not referring to Nazi ideology does not mitigate the deeply offensive, morally repugnant, and institutionally unworthy nature of his statements."
Madrid said the statements "constitute yet another episode in the repeated attacks by Javier Tebas against Real Madrid, its president, and its media outlets."

The club also demanded a "comprehensive overhaul" of the refereeing system and "full clarification" from the Union of European Football Associations about an ongoing probe into alleged payments made by rival Barcelona to a former official on the technical committee of referees of the RFEF.
Tebas' initial social media post criticized Madrid's TV channel for consistently showing reels of errors by referees who are set to work their matches.

"Real Madrid's management directs an orchestra of mouthpieces and Real Madrid TV leads the singing," Tebas wrote. "Their score is always the same: select the plays that suit them, repeat the grievance, feed the suspicion and point fingers at the enemies.

"That method recalls propaganda mechanisms exploited by Goebbels, Nazi Germany's minister of propaganda: systematic repetition, construction of an enemy and subordination of facts to the narrative. The comparison is with those propaganda techniques, not with an ideology or, of course, with the Madridista fanbase."
Madrid (6-2-0) sits in fourth place in the La Liga standings, six points behind first-place Barcelona (8-0-0). They will host Sevilla (4-2-2) at 3 p.m. EDT Saturday in Madrid.
