Last night, with considerable showmanship, Tesla CEO Elon Musk proudly unveiled the Roadster 2 just nine years after first announcing the car, and made it “fly.” While undeniably impressive, you could also describe the spectacle as Tesla making its long-delayed luxury car “do a big hop” and then, as Buzz Lightyear would say, “fall with style.”

During the reveal in McGregor, Texas, at SpaceX’s rocket development and testing facility, the two-seater Roadster 2 launched itself over the automaker’s entire lineup, shot from 0 to 60 mph in less than a second, and then drove upside down off a high ramp to then flip over mid-air and land back down on the ground, cushioning its rapid descent using on-board thrusters.

All this was pure gold for social clips (though at the time of publication, Tesla’s stock price was down after the event), but how did Tesla make its new EV prototype perform these tricks? Tesla vehicle engineering head Lars Moravy went into detail with auto lifestyle and insurance brand Hagerty before yesterday’s event, explaining how the Roadster 2 works.

Franz von Holzhausen, Tesla’s chief designer since 2008, designed the angular exterior. He also helmed the aesthetic of the Cybertruck, Models S, X, 3 and Y, as well as the Semi. Blacked-out windows obscured any view inside the EV, which carried no human driver anyway because, as Musk said, Tesla wanted “to make sure we don’t kill anyone” during the gravity-defying demonstration.

The Roadster 2 will be rear-wheel drive only, a departure from Tesla’s track record of all-wheel drive EVs. Two motors will deliver over a megawatt of power (1,341 horsepower) and over 1,400 Newton-meters (Nm) of torque, meaning this car will have more torque and power than a three-motor Plaid. But all of that power goes through just the rear wheels.
The car will be light, at “just under 1,700 kilos” (under 2 tons), according to Moravy, not significantly heavier than the original 1,300 kg (1.4 tons) Roadster, despite a larger size.

Tesla claims a range of over 300 miles for the Roadster and hopes to mitigate this distinctly average range by also giving the EV the fastest-charging battery the automaker has ever produced, supposedly capable of zipping from 15 to 80 percent in 10 minutes.

At a 2013 auction, Elon Musk bought the iconic "Wet Nellie" Lotus Esprit S1 submarine car from the 1977 James Bond film The Spy Who Loved Me for just shy of $1 million. Musk is so taken with his Bond memorabilia that it apparently inspired one of the Roadster 2's key abilities.

That submarine Bond car has four propellers at its rear, so Tesla decided to ape this with four 20-kilowatt fans on the Roadster 2. Moravy says these fans break the laws of tire physics and dramatically increase the EV's traction by becoming what Tesla calls the car’s “sucker system.” Four independent replaceable skirts drop down on the sides of the car, allowing the Roadster 2 to stick (or suck) to the road at lower speeds where its aerodynamic wings aren't yet contributing to downforce. Moravy claims the system can produce over two Gs in a corner when accelerating, even below 50 mph.

This type of aerodynamic manipulation also appears on the McMurtry Spéirling Pure, which uses two high-speed electric fans spinning at up to 23,000 revolutions per minute to actively suck air from underneath the chassis, generating up to 2,000 kg (around 4,400 pounds) of downforce.
This extreme suction lets the Roadster 2 drive up the vertical ramp at the Texas demonstration and hold onto the surface even when upside down.

So how does the Roadster 2 hover, correct itself, and dampen its fall? That's thanks to what Tesla calls the car’s “SpaceX system,” referring to Musk’s aerospace company, which helped with this part of the car’s development.

Originally, the Roadster was meant to have a 2+2 cabin. Now it’s a two-seater because behind the seats sits a 200-liter carbon-overwrapped pressure vessel (COPV) that holds up to 10,000 PSI to supply the car’s cold gas thrusters, which use expansion of pressurized nitrogen gas to generate thrust, a tech predominantly used for spacecraft stabilization. Cold gas thrusters are the simplest manifestation of a rocket engine.

This combination of suction system and thrusters helps the car hit 0 to 60 mph in supposedly under a second. In this launch mode, Moravy says the rear thrusters produce more than 80 kilonewtons of thrust, which, staggeringly, matches the Dassault Falcon 10X jet. Tesla has seemingly cracked the sub-second race, while the aforementioned McMurtry Spéirling Pure can only manage this feat in a bowel-clenching 1.3 seconds. During this astonishing acceleration, the driver will endure up to 5 Gs.

The Roadster 2's Performance model will feature the sucker system and no thrusters, so 0 to 60 will take a touch longer at 1.6 seconds and a top speed of 210 mph. The Thrust model gets the whole package and a top speed of 230 mph.

Moravy says the “flight system,” as he calls it in Hagerty’s walkthrough, requires yet another 400-liter cold gas COPV, occupying the space where the passenger seat is, making the car a single-seater and bringing total thrust fuel up to 600 liters. This “flight system” also requires six extra thrusters: one in each corner, plus two at the front to yaw.

Unlike in space, where cold gas thrusters provide consistent levels of thrust until the last drop of fuel is used, on Earth the “flight system” will lose thrust as the compressed gas depletes. Moravy likens it to blowing up a balloon then letting the air out: “When I open the end of a balloon, all the gas comes out, and at a certain point, it starts tapering off. That same thing will happen here.”
Apparently, refilling the 600-liter nitrogen tanks takes Tesla six to seven hours, but the company is supposedly working on a system to dramatically reduce this to 30 minutes.

The current Roadster 2 prototypes are being used for further development, and production won’t begin until 2028—but remember that Musk previously said Roadster deliveries would begin in 2020, so take this with a very large pinch of salt. That's without talking about how the Federal Aviation Administration will react to this "flying" car.

Still, for the Tesla faithful, a reservation page is already live where a $5,000 reservation fee secures the Performance variant, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days. The Thrust is available for an initial $5,000 fee, with a whopping $245,000 due within 10 days.
It’s official: Lena Dunham’s millennial magnum opus Girls is coming back, and it’s in large part thanks to Gen Z giving the show its long overdue redemption arc.

Using their native tongue: the internet, Gen Z proselytized the show through memes, clips, and podcasts, and now, as if by collective manifestation, it’s being rebooted for five episodes, which HBO announced Wednesday.

When Girls first aired in 2012, it was cataclysmic. Rave reviews were usurped by the relentless onslaught of sexism and misogyny, which commented on Dunham’s body, the kind of sex depicted onscreen, and the nepo baby allegations against the show’s stars—as well as the series’ lack of diversity. There was endless backlash and backlash to the backlash; it became everyone’s favorite show to both fairly criticize and willfully misunderstand, and creator Dunham was the one stuck grasping onto the lightning rod of so much ire, as she began to stand for everything wrong with millennial white women.

But then something happened. A decade after it aired, everyone started rewatching Girls. It’s not just that people were talking about it online; the series’ viewership doubled between November 2022 and January 2023, compared with the previous three months, The New York Times reported. On Tiktok and Instagram, memes and supercuts started unfurling: Marnie poised with a microphone in the infamous teal dress; Hannah snapping “I am busy, trying to become who I am,” or Shoshanna saying, “Obvi we’re the ladies!” It finally clicked for viewers, spawning a cultural and critical resurgence. While the reviews aged like milk, the show had aged like wine.

It was a phenomenon largely fueled by Gen Z viewers who had missed the show the first time around. (As well as prominent millennial Girls “truthers” like Hunter Harris, Peyton Dix, and Evan Ross Katz.) Among these Gen Z viewers were Amelia Ritthaler and Evan Lazarus, Brooklyn comedians who launched the Girls Rewatch podcast in 2023.

“I think the rest of society caught up to (Dunham),” says Ritthaler, 28. “Everybody was kind of under the impression that they weren’t allowed to be publicly saying that they loved the show and thought it was great. But me and Evan were like, this show is amazing. Why is everybody mad at her?”

Gen Z especially was able to identify with a style that so many millennials had failed to grasp. “So much of what we were raised on was this post-ironic, emotionally removed, ‘world is burning, but let’s dance through it’ kind of social media,’” she says. “I feel like when it was coming out, millennials were just kind of in their earnest era. The millennial optimism of it all. I feel like Gen Z never got that, so we were always watching it from this satirical lens that Lena wrote it in.”

Ritthaler and Lazarus posted Girls memes on TikTok and Instagram, amassing a following that allowed them to have guests like Dunham, as well as cast members Allison Williams (Marnie), Andrew Rannells (Elijah), and Zosia Mamet (Shoshanna) on the show. “I think this was like 70% cuz of you guys,” Jemima Kirke (Jessa) commented on the podcast’s Instagram account the day the revival was announced. “I feel like I loved my favorite show back to my life,” Lazarus said in a teary-eyed video.

The show’s redemption arc coincided with Dunham’s memoir Famesick, published in April, further fueling the Girls nostalgia. “I feel like reading Famesick felt like getting a director’s cut of girls,” says Dix, who hosts the podcast Lemme Say This with Hunter Harris.

The book was an instant New York Times bestseller with a buzzy tour. More importantly, there was a public reckoning around the way culture mistreated Dunham. It felt like a bow tied neatly around the physical and mental toll making Girls. She had moved to London, gotten sober, written extensively about chronic illness, worked on shows like Industry and Too Much. Last month, she announced she’d welcomed a baby via surrogacy.

There were never explicit fan calls for a reboot, particularly after the universally-panned Sex and the City reboot And Just Like That… But the swell in the show’s popularity undoubtedly caught the attention of HBO execs, thanks to the tenacious Gen Zers who spread the good word online. In a Substack post published Wednesday, Dunham credited the fans for helping her be ready to return to the series. “Maybe there was once a part of me that wanted to outrun Hannah and her ladies,” she writes. “Seeing the love you’ve so generously shared for it helped to turn me around.”

“The fans are just tender queers and sensitive girls who journal and heart their eyes,” says Dix. “The people she’s reaching and nurturing aren’t critics anymore, it feels like, or people who want to make weird comments about her body. It’s just young people, she wants to help inform or entertain.”

Part of the reason for the revival is, of course, that everything has come back: Gossip Girl, Pretty Little Liars, iCarly, and countless others have also seen reboots and sequels in recent years. “It’s nostalgia-core for sure,” Ritthaler says. “But it sucks that we don't have any new IP that has topped it. I walk around Brooklyn every day, thinking ‘how did we make Girls in 2012 and then everything went back to being worse?’”

But Gen Z is also ripe for a millennial optimism they never got to experience. Nostalgia for the mid-2010s has been cropping up online, with people posting photos of themselves in 2016, longing for fixed gear bikes, sepia toned photos, and stomp-clap music.

“I think there’s an energy, particularly in New York right now, that really embodies millennial optimism, and I think that Girls is absolutely a part of that cultural conversation,” says Dix. “It falls neatly into this new world we’re building that is kind of based on ‘Obama first-term joy.’ It’s nice to feel joy again when it’s really difficult to find it.”

Elon Musk has quietly financed a major canvassing operation to help Republican candidates in the midterm elections that rivals his effort in the 2024 presidential election, according to federal filings posted Thursday night. To monitor the trillionaire’s overall influence on November’s elections, WIRED created a live-updating tracker that pulls federal filings daily.

The Musk-aligned America PAC has spent $76.7 million in the third quarter of 2026, $35.8 million of which has been spent on a field operation to drive turnout among President Donald Trump's core base across all seven Senate battleground states and a number of House races, the filings show.

That compares with the roughly $45 million America PAC had spent on putting together a field operation at the same point in the 2024 cycle, when the super PAC effectively ran the vast majority of canvassing for Trump's presidential campaign.

In short, Musk has assembled a presidential-level field operation this midterm cycle, underscoring the extent to which he has taken over the get-out-the-vote effort for the party and created something of a shadow Republican National Committee. With three weeks until Election Day, the total contributions are only set to rise even higher.
Canvassing has been America PAC’s largest expense, ahead of the $23.7 million it spent on a combination of digital ads mostly attacking Democrats, campaign literature, and phone bank efforts.

But in an effort to save Republicans' Senate majority, Musk also gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting the GOP's candidates in that chamber. The same amount appears to have been funneled into Texas PAC, which was registered with the FEC in August 2026 and is backing embattled Republican candidate and Texas attorney general Ken Paxton.

Musk has been particularly focused on the Senate race in Texas this midterm cycle, where he has extensive personal and business interests. Musk lives near Austin and his businesses SpaceX and Tesla are based in the state. Musk accounted for nearly 60 percent of the $273 million that the Senate Leadership Fund raised for Texas PAC.

The stunning war chest that Musk has unleashed into all seven battleground Senate races and, to a lesser degree, a number of competitive House races, makes him the largest known donor in the midterms among both Republicans and Democrats.

Since its inception, America PAC has relied primarily on outside firms to conduct paid canvassing, in which people are hired to knock on the doors of likely Trump or Republican voters to remind them to register to vote and vote early.

The super PAC has used mostly the same contractors as in the 2024 cycle, the filings show. The biggest canvassing contract went to Blitz Canvassing, a subsidiary of the political affairs firm GP3 Partners, which helped stand up America PAC.

The other vendors listed in America PAC’s filings were the firms Patriot Grassroots LLC, The Synapse Group, In Field Strategies, Echo Canyon Group, Threshold Strategies, and GEG Strategies LLC. All but the last two also worked for America PAC in 2024.
Going into the final stretch of campaigning, America PAC has more than $12 million remaining, though Musk, the richest man in the world, may contribute more to his PAC as required.

America PAC has spent in 40 races in 17 states since July. The Texas Senate race drew the largest share, in which Musk’s team has spent $15.3 million attacking Democrat James Talarico and $3.5 million supporting Paxton.

The super PAC has also spent about $5.3 million attacking Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio’s Senate race against Republican Jon Husted and $3.5 million attacking Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running against Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan, according to the WIRED tracker.

A Great Dane is lucky to see its 10th birthday, while a Chihuahua might live to celebrate its 20th. But exactly why smaller dogs tend to live longer than their larger counterparts has long been a mystery.

Now, new research suggests the differences may stem, in part, from what’s happening at the molecular level. A study published October 8 in the journal Science suggests big dogs’ cells age faster because of changes that allow potentially harmful “jumping genes” to move around their genomes, or complete sets of genetic instructions.

The work is “fascinating,” Borbála Turcsán, an animal behavior researcher at Eötvös Loránd University in Hungary who was not involved with the study, tells Nature’s Heidi Ledford. “It provides a molecular background for something we also observe at a behavioral level.”

Researchers behind the new study used data from the Dog Aging Project, a citizen science initiative in which participating dog owners and their veterinarians regularly share information about their pup’s health, behavior, environment and physical activity. Founded in 2014, the project has since enrolled roughly 55,000 canine companions of various breeds.

Scientists analyzed the DNA of 894 pet dogs spanning diverse breeds and body sizes. More specifically, they looked at methyl groups, or chemical tags on DNA that scientists often use as biological markers of aging. Methyl groups are part of the epigenome, chemical changes that regulate gene activity—controlling which genes are turned on or off—without affecting the underlying genetic code. Factors like diet, exercise, stress and pollutants can alter the epigenome.

They also looked at detailed demographic and genetic information. Using correlations between DNA methylation patterns and chronological age, they developed a molecular clock that could predict a dog’s age with a median error of less than one year based on its epigenome.

Analyses revealed that larger dogs tend to accumulate epigenetic changes associated with aging more quickly than small dogs, and that male dogs also tend to accrue these modifications faster than female dogs, even if they were neutered at a young age. In other words, both big dogs and male dogs showed signs of accelerated molecular aging. The study also found that dogs whose biological age was older than their chronological age were at greater risk of early death.
Did you know? World’s tallest and shortest dogs
In 2025, the world’s tallest dog, a 3-foot-3 Great Dane named Reggie, and the world’s shortest dog, a 3.6-inch-tall Chihuahua named Pearl, met up for an adorable playdate.

In large dogs, this faster molecular aging trajectory seems to be related to “jumping genes,” also known as transposable elements, or DNA sequences that can move from one location in a genome to another. These rogue sequences can interfere with normal gene function, leading to a variety of health problems, as well as inflammation and aging.

Methyl groups help keep jumping genes in place. The study suggests that large dogs tend to lose these methyl groups more rapidly as they age, which might make it easier for jumping genes to hop around and disrupt gene function.

“Large dogs show a faster-moving DNA methylation aging signature in blood, and that this acceleration is especially strong in parts of the genome that normally help keep ‘jumping genes’ quiet,” study co-author Noah Snyder-Mackler, a genomicist at Arizona State University, tells Reuters’ Marta Serafinko. In such canines, “methylation at those regions appears to erode more quickly with age, as if the genome is losing some of the tape or clamps that keep these mobile elements suppressed.”

Humans may have inadvertently sent big dogs down their accelerated molecular aging path, Snyder-Mackler adds. By breeding dogs to grow and reach their large adult sizes quickly, we may have unknowingly shortened their life spans.

“Their bodies have to make this trade-off between really rapid growth and maintenance of that, versus investment in the immune system and integrity of the organism,” Snyder-Mackler tells Live Science’s R.J. Mackenzie, adding that, for now, this is just a hypothesis.

In male dogs, meanwhile, the study suggests epigenetic changes on the X sex chromosome might be driving their accelerated molecular aging. Male dogs typically have one copy of the X chromosome, while female dogs usually have two—and the researchers think the extra copy might help female dogs stave off some of these aging-related epigenetic changes.

“This was an unexpected result,” study co-author Brianah McCoy, a biologist now at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who conducted the research at Arizona State University, says in a statement. “It challenges some of our assumptions about how the X chromosome is regulated and highlights the complexity of epigenetic aging.”

The molecular aging differences between males and females appear to be distinct from the aging-related differences between big dogs and small dogs, so Snyder-Mackler considers it “a separate biology that needs follow-up, rather than the same mechanism in disguise,” he tells Reuters.

Additionally, while the study finds an association between DNA methylation patterns and longevity in dogs, it doesn’t establish whether or how these patterns contribute to aging. Researchers hope to use this paper as a jumping-off point to learn more about the relationship between DNA methylation and aging in canines.

Moving forward, the findings might one day lead to developments that could help extend the life spans of larger dogs. There “may be processes we can measure, follow over time and potentially modify before disease appears,” Snyder-Mackler tells Reuters. However, even if scientists find a way to slow down molecular aging, it wouldn’t be a cure-all. Large dogs would still face breed-specific risks that might affect their longevity, Snyder-Mackler notes.

Longer term, the research could even have implications for human aging. In the meantime, however, methylation changes are probably more like wrinkles—evidence that someone is getting older, but not an underlying cause of aging.

“Wrinkles are certainly diagnostic of aging,” Trey Ideker, a biologist at the University of Oxford in England who was not involved with the study, tells Nature. “There’s a big business in curing wrinkles. But is that going to cure aging? Probably not.”

Some 165 million years ago, a predator that looked like a strange mishmash of a platypus and river otter roamed what’s now China. And surprisingly, the now-extinct “chimera” already had certain throat features that define today’s living mammals—even though it wasn’t a true mammal.

A well-preserved fossil of the odd creature reveals it could suckle its mother’s milk, researchers report in a study published October 7 in the journal Nature. The specimen represents a previously unknown genus and species, and it’s the earliest known example of a semi-aquatic mammal-like animal.

“It’s a fascinating specimen,” says Jessica Theodor, a paleontologist at the University of Calgary in Canada who wasn’t involved in the study, to NPR’s Ari Daniel. “The whole setup looks more like what we see in modern mammals.”

Scientists discovered the fossil roughly a decade ago in a northern part of China called Inner Mongolia. The animal is estimated to have been around 16 to 20 inches long and weighed roughly 2 to 4.5 pounds. It was a docodont, a member of an extinct group of close relatives to mammals dating back to the Mesozoic Era, some 66 million to 252 million years ago. Researchers named its genus Megacauda in reference to its wide tail and its species sungei in honor of paleontologist Sun Ge.

Digital reconstructions based on CT scans revealed M. sungei had a shockingly modern throat structure. The sharp-toothed creature had small bony projections on the roof of the mouth, which, in modern mammals like humans, support the soft palate. This tissue structure separates the oral cavity from the throat, allowing suckling, swallowing and breathing. What’s more, the researchers found hyoid bones in the throat, which anchor certain muscles and help today’s mammals swallow without the aid of gravity.

The structures suggest M. sungei could chew bits of food and swallow one morsel at a time, rather than shaking its head to jiggle large hunks of food down its throat like a crocodile, according to a statement. Scientists suspect that this evolutionary adaptation allowed mammal species to develop a variety of diets and become carnivores, insectivores, omnivores or herbivores.

The findings also hint that a young animal could suckle its mom’s milk without the liquid entering its nose, a trait that “literally defined our biology,” study co-author Zhe-Xi Luo, a paleontologist at the University of Chicago, tells NPR. “That’s why our group is called mammals. We’re named after the mammary glands,” or milk-producing structures.

“Neonatal suckling behavior was previously thought of as being a hallmark of advanced mammals,” Sue Hand, a vertebrate paleontologist at the University of New South Wales in Australia who didn’t participate in the study, tells Live Science’s Chris Simms. “But it now appears to have evolved well before then, in the common ancestor of docodontans and mammals at least 165 million years ago.”

The animal may have navigated its watery environment by using its front legs to paddle, swishing its tail in a wave-like motion and using its hind legs to steer. The fossil represents the earliest evidence of a mammal conducting a partially aquatic lifestyle, study co-author Thomas Martin, a paleontologist at the University of Bonn in Germany, says in a separate statement. The findings suggest that swimming evolved early in the mammal lineage, Luo tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s Peter de Kruijff.
More broadly, M. sungei sheds light on how early mammal relatives experienced their ecosystems while living alongside dinosaurs.

It’s “cool to see that this sister lineage to today’s mammals had evolved an aquatic lifestyle, which is something we have seen multiple times across the mammalian family tree, including in the platypus,” says Oliver Griffith, an evolutionary biologist at Macquarie University in Australia who wasn’t involved in the study, to New Scientist’s James Woodford.

More than 250 years ago, a young Pacific Islander named Mai made a splash when he arrived in England. He became “a sensation, a star of the press, the darling of the intelligentsia [and] the subject of poems, books, musical plays,” as Hampton Sides wrote in an adapted Smithsonian magazine excerpt of The Exotic: Intrigue and Cultural Ruin in the Age of Imperialism. Joshua Reynolds, a leading portraitist of the day, immortalized Mai’s visit in a massive portrait measuring nearly eight feet tall.

Now, for the first time, the painting has made its way across the Atlantic. It’s on view now at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles, giving art aficionados in America a chance to witness one of Britain’s most significant early portraits of a person of color.

Mai, also known as Ma‘i or Omai, was a Polynesian man from the island of Raiatea in the South Pacific. After a childhood of hardship, Mai decided to join British explorer James Cook’s second Pacific expedition, aboard the HMS Adventure—a companion ship to the HMS Resolution—under Captain Tobias Furneaux.

After the two ships became separated in a storm in October 1773, Furneaux opted to return to England. When the Adventure sailed into Portsmouth on July 14, 1774, Mai became the first Polynesian to visit Britain.

Joseph Banks, a botanist who had accompanied Cook on his first voyage, became Mai’s patron and chaperone. Over the next two years, Mai became a celebrity of sorts, visiting aristocratic estates, attending concerts and dinner parties, riding horses, hunting and exploring the English countryside. Many Britons assumed he was a Polynesian royal—a misconception Mai did little to correct.

Reynolds is believed to have painted Mai sometime around 1776. He “modeled Mai on ancient Roman senators and military leaders, dressing him in robes reminiscent of Tahitian tapa cloth but with a Roman flair,” Saar Shahar, an English scholar at the University of Southern California, writes for the Conversation. Reynolds depicted the young man barefoot, with a white turban atop his head and intricate tattoos covering his hands.
Mai departed England in 1776 aboard the Resolution and settled on the South Pacific island of Huahine, where he is believed to have died of a virus just a few years later.

The artist evidently loved the portrait so much that he kept it in his studio until he died. From there, it passed into the hands of Frederick Howard, 5th Earl of Carlisle, whose family held onto it for roughly 200 years.

In 2001, Irish business magnate and art collector John Magnier reportedly purchased it for $12.4 million. To keep the painting from being sold abroad, the British government imposed an export ban on the portrait in 2022.

The National Portrait Gallery in London tried to raise enough money to buy the painting outright. But, in 2023, the institution ultimately teamed up with the J. Paul Getty Trust to complete the purchase, with each contributing half of the roughly $62 million price tag.

Nicholas Cullinan, then the director of the National Portrait Gallery, told the New York Times’ Alex Marshall at the time that the portrait is a “supreme work of art” that will likely inspire important conversations about European colonialism.

Earlier this year, Davide Gasparotto, senior curator of paintings at the Getty, echoed that sentiment, telling the Los Angeles Times’ Anthony Solorzano that the painting doubles as “an anthropological artifact.”
“It talks about this incredibly important moment of encounter of cultures, sometimes difficult, problematic,” he added.
The unusual joint ownership arrangement for Portrait of Mai means that the painting will travel back and forth between Britain and the United States periodically.

The portrait arrived in California for the first time in July. Conservators from the Getty and the National Portrait Gallery spent weeks studying the painting, ultimately discovering several places where Reynolds had reworked the composition using multiple colors and layers of paint.

“[Reynolds] is notoriously someone that never is satisfied with what he’s done,” Sally Higgs, a conservator for the National Portrait Gallery, told the Los Angeles Times. “And you can really see that in this painting that he just can’t stop—it’s never finished.”

The painting will remain on view at the Getty until March 2027, when the museum is scheduled to close for renovations. It will be transferred to the Getty Villa and will return to the museum in time for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.
“Joshua Reynolds’ Portrait of Mai and 18th-Century Portraiture” is on view at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles through March 14, 2027.

A fossil that sat in a museum collection for over a century is a previously unknown species of predatory dinosaur, researchers have found. The discovery could help scientists solve a longstanding mystery about how some of the Cretaceous period's most formidable hunters spread around the globe.

The dinosaur lived on what is now the Isle of Wight in southern England about 120 million years ago. It belonged to a group of two-legged carnivores called megaraptors, which are related to tyrannosaurs. But unlike tyrannousars, megaraptors are thought to have relied on their powerful arms and large curved claws to attack prey and defend themselves.

The newly identified species was described in an Oct. 14 study in the journal Royal Society Open Science. It is the first megaraptor identified in Europe, filling an important gap in the fossil record of a group whose evolutionary history remains poorly understood.

"It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years," study first author Cassius Morrison, a researcher in the Department of Earth Sciences at University College London (UCL) said in a statement. "Lots of bones are found on the Isle of Wight — who knows what else is waiting to be discovered."

The discovery of the megaraptor began in 1924, when an amateur fossil collector discovered a dinosaur skull fragment on the Isle of Wight. The specimen eventually entered the collections of London's Natural History Museum, but it was largely forgotten.

Recently, researchers revisited the fossil as part of a study on dinosaur braincases. To identify the animal, the researchers used micro-CT scanning to examine the fossil's internal structure and build detailed 3D digital models of the space that once held the dinosaur's brain.

The researchers then compared the animal's anatomy with that of other meat-eating dinosaurs, including tyrannosaurs, spinosaurs and other theropods (the group of two-legged, mostly meat-eating dinosaurs). Several features differentiated the unknown specimen, including an almost oval opening where the spinal cord entered the skull and an unusual, hourglass-shaped ridge at the back of the braincase.

Computer-based evolutionary analyses placed the fossils within the Megaraptora family tree, supporting the idea that the skull represented a never-before-seen species. The researchers named the dinosaur Invictibellatrix amberina, combining the Latin words "unconquered" and "female warrior" for the genus name, while amberina refers to amber found in the rocks associated with the fossil.

Megaraptors lived between roughly 125 million and 66 million years ago and varied considerably in size. While early members were relatively small, some later species became enormous predators. Maip macrothorax, discovered in Argentina, may have reached up to 33 feet (10 meters) long and weighed as much as an elephant. Based on comparisons with related dinosaurs, I. amberina was much smaller, likely around 10 to 13 feet (3 to 4 m) long and standing roughly 5 feet (1.5 m) tall. The researchers estimated it weighed around 440 to 660 pounds (200 to 300 kilograms), making it one of the smallest known megaraptors.

"It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex," Morrison said. "We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight. They definitely would have chased us."

Although the newly described fossil doesn't preserve the animal's arms or claws, its closest relative suggests that its claws may have measured around 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) long. The researchers also suggested I. amberina may have been feathered, though that feature can't be determined directly from the specimen.
A missing link in the dinosaurs' globetrotting

Scientists have long suspected that megaraptors originated in Asia before spreading to other parts of the world, eventually becoming the dominant predators across the southern supercontinent Gondwana, which included present-day Africa, South America and Antarctica. But a lack of European fossils left an important gap in verifying this migration route.

The new study's evolutionary models suggest that I. amberina descended from Asian megaraptors that dispersed into Europe around 130 million years ago. From there, members of the group may have moved through what is now Africa and further into Gondwana via temporary landbridges and temporary land connections across the shallow Tethys Ocean.

"This new species is the first proof we have that megaraptorans were also present in Europe and that they reached Gondwana this way rather than island-hopping further south," study co-author Charlie Scherer, a doctoral student at UCL Earth Sciences, said in the statement.

However, the specific route these animals took over millions of years is still unknown. The researchers also cannot yet explain why megaraptors disappeared from northern areas, but changes in climate or competition with other predatory dinosaurs may have contributed. More research on other megaraptor fossils like I. amberina could help uncover more clues.

"Work like this shows the exceptional value of working with historical museum collections where there are still many discoveries to be made," study co-author Paul Barrett, a researcher of dinosaur evolution at the Natural History Museum in London, said in the statement.

Stellar cores called white dwarfs come in an astonishing array of colors, including what scientists say is the first known green star and the reddest star ever found, new research reveals.

A white dwarf star is the dense, cooling core that remains after a low- to medium-mass star runs out of fuel. The new study, published Thursday (Oct. 15) in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments, shows that white dwarfs come in far more colors than their name suggests.

White dwarf stars got their moniker because the first known examples glowed in either white or pale blue. The new study, however, suggests that "white" dwarfs also emit visible-light colors like pink, green, cyan, purple and yellow.

"Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their colour is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," Mark Hollands, an astronomer at the University of Warwick in the U.K. and first author of the study, said in a statement. "It turns out these incredibly dense stars can produce colours nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me."

The variety of colors is possible due to white dwarfs' densities compared with main-sequence stars, the study suggests. Cooler white dwarfs have a density of about 1 gram per cubic centimeter, much like flowing water on Earth. The density of these white dwarfs is also millions of times denser than the sun's visible surface, or photosphere, leading to unusual conditions.

"Any trace elements that may be present, such as carbon, calcium and sodium, interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colours than they would at lower densities," the researchers said in a statement. "This shifts a star's colour away from the orange, white and blue [typical] of a perfect radiator."

White dwarfs are far away and small, making it difficult to verify their color. So, in the new study, astronomers inferred the colors using spectra, the distinctive chemical fingerprints produced by stars' light. The team analyzed the spectra within a model of color vision that the human eye can see, making the color pop out.

Scientists found that carbon-rich white dwarfs tend to be purple or pink, while those that contain debris from asteroids or comets are usually yellower. Cyan or pale-blue white dwarfs occur when hydrogen and helium molecules strike each other in very dense atmospheres.

The team also discovered WD J1330+6435 — a green star that contains rocky material. The green comes from the additional elements of calcium, lithium and sodium in the star's atmosphere, creating a unique "chartreuse green appearance" that would be visible to the human eye, if we could see it up close.

"The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow," Hollands explained, adding that the one-of-a-kind green star "feels like something out of science fiction." The team also discovered what is likely the reddest star ever found. This white dwarf, called WD J1011+2845, is located roughly 48 light-years from our planet. It has carbon closer to its surface — because the element is being lifted from the interior, due to strong convection currents — that is bending the star's light. This process is making a "deep salmon-pink glow" because the carbon molecules are obstructing the star's other wavelengths.

Overall, in the sample of stars studied — 151 white dwarfs within 65 light-years of Earth — about 1 in 30 white dwarfs glowed in a color other than white. This could mean there are far more colorful stellar remnants littering the universe than anyone anticipated.

The aftermarket has lived through major technological shifts before. The internet connected us. Mobile technology put that information in everyone’s hands and reshaped communication between suppliers, distributors and customers.
Artificial intelligence feels different.

AI can work through volumes of information no person could reasonably process, finding patterns across customers, products, vehicles and markets in seconds. New capabilities emerge more quickly than businesses can figure out how to use them. The technology reaches across departments, workflows and decisions, creating opportunities that can be difficult to fully understand before the next one arrives.

At times, it’s hard to tell if AI development is a rush of excitement or the pull of a riptide. Yet, in this moment of frenetic change, NexaMotion Group’s Neil Sethi sees the technology as an agent that can bring people together.

“I’m as data hungry as anyone maybe on the planet … but technology actually should push you toward more interaction with people,” NMG’s CEO said. “We live in a changing world and it could be scary. Now, more than ever, it’s important to acknowledge and be thankful for your team members and partners.”

That idea is echoed across the organization’s values in commitment, humility, optimism, integrity and respect, and its mission statement: “Simplifying complex vehicle repair to keep the world moving.” They provide a foundation as its transmission expertise, general repair business, supply chain, customer relationships and technology become increasingly connected.

And it’s seen in the executive team that Sethi has assembled around the table to dig into how the company is investing in AI, modernizing Transend, connecting customer behavior to inventory decisions and using data to identify emerging repair needs. Bringing those capabilities together starts with creating a consistent experience across businesses with their own histories, markets served and specialties.

Scott Weinstein, president of NexaMotion Group, wants customers to recognize a common experience throughout the organization. Transtar and NexaMotion’s general repair businesses carry established identities and customer relationships. Weinstein sees communication, service, reliable distribution, urgency and accountability as the qualities connecting them.

“Whether you’re dealing with Transtar, whether you’re dealing with Arch and all of our other brands, it should have the same consistent feel,” Weinstein said. “Communication is the key. It’s important for us to be able to very accurately tell a customer why they should do business with us. Internally, communication is important so that our teams hear the same message across the organization.”

That experience becomes increasingly important as NexaMotion expands the range of business it can support for a customer. A transmission specialist may know Transtar through decades of sourcing highly specific components and technical information. General repair creates a broader purchasing relationship built around everyday availability, delivery speed and service.

Tim Cox, executive vice president of supply chain, reiterated the distinction: General repair customers place a premium on availability and speed. Transmission shops place a heavy emphasis on accuracy and technical support.

The company’s Platinum Program extends that customer strategy on the general repair side. Weinstein described the program as a commitment to customers that place more of their business with NexaMotion. Those customers can receive additional attention through sales and delivery operations.

“When they commit to us, we want to commit to them,” Weinstein said. “For example, I fly a lot. So with a certain airline, I go to the front of the line. But I spend a lot of money with them. Same is true in our business. Where we distinguish ourselves is going to be on communication, service and making business easier by simplifying the complex vehicle repair. We want to be the best partner. If they partner with us, we want to partner with them and reward them.”

The groundwork in general repair for that program has been laid. Billy Gwinn, executive vice president, NexaMotion Group operations and general repair sales, joined the company with much of its expansion into general repair already underway. The work ahead was building an operating structure capable of supporting that growth.

Five business units brought different systems and different ways of operating. Gwinn’s first months included work to bring operating procedures together, standardize expectations for outside sales representatives and branch managers, and move the businesses toward a common ERP platform.
“If I’m a manager in Arch, I should be able to walk into a branch at 4M in Texas and be able to run it,” Gwinn said. “And that’s the scalability we’re talking about.”

Getting the businesses onto the same ERP system gives NexaMotion a common source of operational information for purchasing and analytics. Gwinn said the company is nearly finished with that work, with one business unit remaining to convert. The next layer is execution.
His early visits to branches reinforced that point. Gwinn said the employees interacting directly with customers stood out quickly.

“The people we have are phenomenal,” he said. “The boots on the ground, the ones that interacted with the customers—they wanted to win every day. That says a lot about our culture. They want to take care of customers. They want to make sure that they’re getting the right parts to the customers in a timely manner via delivery.”

That requires visibility into what customers need across a growing assortment of products and applications. NexaMotion is increasingly finding those signals within the digital activity generated before, during and after a sale.

If you were working in an alignment pit before the 1980s, obtaining the initial angles was a relatively easy process because most vehicles had steel wheels. Mounting the alignment “sensor” with rim clamps provided a very accurate representation of the front wheels’ planes of rotation for measuring camber, caster and toe. However, because the tools used to measure these angles were contained inside the sensor head, they were very fragile and frequently fell out of calibration.

By the 1980s, more vehicles were being equipped with cast-alloy wheels that did not have a suitable lip for mounting the sensor head. Getting a secure grip on the rim became more difficult. It was not uncommon for a rim clamp to come off during an alignment and damage the expensive head.

In the 1990s, alignment technology began to change with improvements in digital cameras. Engineers started mounting cameras to fixtures positioned in front of the vehicle. The expensive sensors at the wheels were replaced with simple targets that the cameras could scan to determine the alignment angles.
However, cameras added a new wrinkle to the alignment process: the rolling-compensation procedure. This procedure also helped resolve problems caused by attaching alignment targets to alloy wheels.

Nearly every modern chassis alignment system uses this step to obtain accurate alignment measurements. First, the vehicle is positioned 12 to 20 inches behind the front turntables. Most systems require the targets to be attached so that a specified part of each target is level with the center of the wheel. The vehicle is then rolled forward onto the turntables. This process is called rolling compensation.
Modern camera-based aligners attach a target to each wheel, and the vehicle is rolled backward or forward a short distance while the cameras track each target through part of a wheel revolution.

As the wheel rotates, the aligner observes the path traveled by the target. The system detects changes in the target’s orientation or the center of the wheel’s rotation caused by clamp runout, wheel damage or an off-center target. From these observations, the software calculates the relationship between the target and the wheel’s actual plane of rotation. This prevents a slightly crooked clamp or target from being interpreted as camber or toe.

The primary purpose of rolling compensation is to establish the true rotational plane and centerline of each wheel while compensating for target or clamp mounting errors. Camber and toe can then be calculated directly. Caster and steering-axis inclination require a separate steering sweep.

Some systems do not require rolling compensation. These systems typically use lasers, mirrors or other devices mounted near the center of the lift to calculate the alignment angles. On some heavy-duty alignment systems, the target or sensor is mounted directly to the spindle.
With today’s electronic parking brakes and advanced driver-assistance systems, including collision-mitigation systems, the alignment process is becoming more challenging.

Even pulling a vehicle onto an alignment rack can be a struggle. We recently had a 2024 Audi Q4 come into our training center. As the technician began driving the vehicle onto the ramps of the drive-on lift, the car applied the brakes, stopped and displayed a collision warning on the instrument panel. The technician applied the accelerator, and the vehicle eventually began moving again.

Even after reviewing the service information, it was unclear what caused this behavior. Was the alignment equipment interfering with the vehicle’s sensors, or was the system reacting to the proximity of the wall and toolbox in front of the vehicle? Were the lasers on the cameras causing the issue?

We had a similar incident with a 2023 Ford F-150 that bucked like a bronco (not a Ford Bronco) while we were positioning it on a drive-on lift. Once again, neither the service information nor the owner’s manual clearly explained the behavior.

Most other late-model vehicles with collision-mitigation systems that we have driven onto the same lift issue audible and visual warnings when they detect what they interpret as a possible threat in the bay. However, they rarely intervene and stop the vehicle.

Even more challenging are the procedures for preparing a vehicle for an alignment when it must be moved during rolling compensation. The primary difficulties involve keeping the parking brake released and the transmission in neutral.

Many modern vehicles use electronic parking brakes that engage automatically when the vehicle is parked. Some systems do this for safety, while others use the parking brake to prevent slight vehicle movement before the transmission’s parking pawl fully engages.
Even if the transmission is placed in neutral and the ignition is switched off using a push button or physical key, the parking brake may engage automatically without any action from the driver.

On many vehicles, the driver’s gear selection does not have final authority. Even after neutral is selected, a control module may shift the transmission into park when it detects certain conditions, such as an open driver’s door or an unbuckled seat belt.

Modern transmissions use electronic driver interfaces and communicate with numerous other vehicle systems. This integration has made selecting neutral—and keeping the transmission in neutral—more challenging.

Working around systems designed to protect the driver requires awareness, accurate information and, in some cases, a scan tool. Many vehicles have built-in procedures or operating modes that allow them to remain in neutral and roll freely. The challenge is finding the correct procedure.

Many late-model Ford vehicles have a Stay in Neutral or Temporary Neutral mode that remains active for a limited period. Depending on the vehicle, the mode may be engaged by holding the brake pedal, selecting neutral and pressing the manual-mode or low-range button when prompted.

Some Tesla alignment procedures require the technician to buckle the front seat belts and manually close the front door latches before placing the vehicle in neutral. This prevents the vehicle from determining that the occupants have exited and automatically applying park or the electronic parking brake.

Other vehicles allow technicians to activate these modes through the infotainment system. Some require a particular sequence of button presses to keep the transmission in neutral and the electronic parking brake released. Instructions for these procedures may be found in the service information or owner’s manual.

In other cases, a scan tool with bidirectional controls or dedicated service functions may be needed to select neutral, place the braking system in a service mode or release the electronic parking brake. Regardless of the method, technicians must follow the manufacturer’s instructions and use wheel chocks whenever the vehicle is not being moved for the rolling-compensation procedure.

It is easy to see that alignment and ADAS calibration are beginning to merge into a single service as chassis alignment and ADAS sensor positioning become increasingly dependent on each other. One area that is currently growing is the integration of vehicle communication capabilities into the alignment and calibration bay. As more late-model vehicles come out of warranty, alignment service will require an even more increased use of scan tools to initiate adjustments and calibrations.

The subject vehicle today is a 2014 Mini Cooper Countryman AWD, with a six-speed manual transmission. Mini is one of the only makes that the large local dealership it originally came to does not sell; being in good standing with this dealership, they brought it to us to perform the repairs needed and get their customer back on the road. With very little information available on the internet for removal and installation, we did think about purchasing a short-term subscription to BMW/Mini service information, but hey, it’s a clutch job so how hard could it be?

The vehicle needed a clutch replacement, which seemed fairly straight forward, so we jumped right in to get this back to the customer as quickly as we possibly could. We ended up needing to call the local Mini dealer and order OE parts since there was limited availability of aftermarket clutch parts. This vehicle was equipped with a Dual Mass Flywheel set up, so with this knowledge we started the removal process. Remove the air box, get the battery out of the way, removed the bell housing bolts, etc., all from the engine compartment, then raise the vehicle up to start taking off the front two wheels. Also, a good trick we found was taking the driver’s side head light out, and removing the front bumper cover as this gave us better access to the transmission and it was removed fairly easily and quickly, we felt that this added step saved us a lot of time not trying to fight getting access in such a tight area. After this, things started to get interesting.

Figure 1 shows the rear driveshaft where it attaches to the Power Transfer Unit. We discovered a TSB that referred to this attachment. It told us we needed a special tool to get it apart and it is a large wrench end that attaches to a long half-inch extension to get it apart (Figure 2). We obviously did not have anything even remotely close to this tool, nor did any of our other shops in the area. Calling the local dealer, we could buy the special tool, but it was a little over a week out to get one. Upon further investigation we decided the PTU possibly could come out with the driveshaft still attached.

After unbolting the PTU and separating it from the transmission we found the next road block: the intermediate shaft in the PTU is too long to get the PTU removed without it hitting the back of the engine. We started looking over how everything is put together, to see if we could still make this work. While looking, we found a snap ring around the passenger side axle (Figure 3). With that snap ring removed (and with the help of a sharp, new pry bar, and hammer) the axle popped out of the PTU, allowing us to remove that PTU with the driveshafts still attached. This might not be the easiest method, but it worked, and we transmission technicians always seem to find a way to get ’er done!

Figure 4 shows the PTU on the floor with the attached pieces mentioned. After getting these parts out of the way, we could then remove the transmission. As a side note, if you do need to service the driveshaft for any reason, you will need that special tool I mentioned previously to get the driveshaft separated from the PTU. Back on track, everything else went very smoothly and we finished replacing the clutch, flywheel and all associated parts. We put the vehicle back together, and then went for that final test drive.

Some additional notes: Make sure the correct parts are ordered for these vehicles and the labor charge is sufficient. This was a very big clutch job, and very expensive as the total bill came out to be around $2,700 retail. Make sure if it is supposed to have a Dual Mass Flywheel (DMF) it gets replaced, trying to cut corners on a job like this does not do you or your customer any good. Not pricing this job out correctly up front can mean one of those phone calls that you do not want to make after the vehicle is disassembled. It can mean a very large pricing difference, as well as correct fitments.

This is where the LUK clutch catalog or online catalog can come in handy with this catalog you can check to see if they offer the DMF set up for your application. LUK offers a much more affordable option for your customers versus the OE parts (for many applications, LUK or Valeo are the OE supplier), so you will save your customer quite a bit of money if your application is available from them. In their catalog, you can also find the “flywheel options” if you are sending out the flywheel to be surfaced, as the information in the catalog will tell you if it is a flat, step, DMF (cannot be turned), or cupped style. It will give you dimensions and measurements so you can make sure the flywheel will still be in spec after having it surfaced.

In closing, I just want to say if you get one of these all-wheel drive Mini Coopers in your shop, do not turn it away for fear of being too complicated. The job ended up being fairly easy, the shop made good money, and the R&R technician made good time on it. Next time he will be able to do it even faster, and have an even better turnaround time.
