On the surface, sleeving an engine may sound simple: machine the block, install the sleeves and finish hone the cylinders. In reality, success comes down to getting the details right.

Today’s sleeves benefit from advanced metallurgy and high-grade materials, while modern machining offers remarkable precision and repeatability. Even so, experienced builders still see sleeved-engine failures pretty regularly.

More often than not, those problems are the result of machining or installation errors. Some issues are obvious, while others, like poor ring seal or reduced heat transfer, can quietly affect performance and durability over time.
For Joe Irwin of Fast Forward Race Engines, preventing those problems starts with taking extra time on the sleeve itself.

“We probably have four or five hours more in each Coyote sleeving process than most guys do, and it’s simply deburr work on the sleeve,” Irwin says. “The entry of the sleeve needs to be radiused, and the surface finish of both the sleeve and the receiver bore matters.

“The better you finish those areas, the better off the end product will be. The sleeve will stay more dimensionally stable and is less likely to lose position or distort. Anytime you can make that geometry more stable, your crankcase pressure goes down and your bores seal up better. It’s all about doing your best work when you sleeve a block, and I think guys sometimes get away from that.”
Irwin’s approach reinforces a common theme among top builders: defective parts usually aren’t the real problem.

“Most failures come back to improper application, incorrect installation, or poor machining practices,” says Larry Goldbeck of Track Tamer Engines. “Modern sleeves themselves are usually extremely accurate.”
With that in mind, let’s take a closer look at some of the most common mistakes that continue to undermine sleeved engines, and the best ways to avoid them.

Ask engine builders what keeps a sleeve in place, and most will point to dimensions – counterbore depth, diameter, interference fit, and so on. Those factors are critical, but Jay Meagher of RS Garage believes one of the most overlooked variables is the quality of the receiver surface itself.

“Let’s give the builder the benefit of the doubt that his critical measurements are fine,” Meagher says. “Both the step where the sleeve is going to stop and the diameter in which the sleeve is to be received – let’s say all that stuff is right. I think the honing finish on the block that’s to receive the sleeve may matter more than people think.”

The reason comes down to contact area. A rough or inconsistent receiver surface creates microscopic high and low spots between the sleeve and parent material. The sleeve may still press in correctly, but uneven contact can weaken support, create stress concentrations and reduce heat transfer.

“You want as homogeneous a bond as possible between the sleeve and the block,” Meagher says. “Whether it’s a dry sleeve or a wet sleeve, some honing after boring goes a long way toward creating a better home for the sleeve.”

Irwin’s process includes honing the receiver bore after machining. “We’ll actually bore that block and then we’ll hone that block to get the actual press that we’re looking for and the actual surface finish as smooth as we possibly can,” he says.

The extra step adds time, but Irwin says it’s worth the effort. “We try to have as much contact area from the outside of the sleeve to the surface of that block, the parent material,” he explains. “That way you can dissipate the heat from the piston through the rings into the sleeve, from the sleeve into the block and then into the cooling system like it’s supposed to.”

That’s a key point, because the sleeve does more than contain cylinder pressure; it also helps carry heat away from the combustion chamber. When that path is compromised, problems can show up during teardown.

“A lot of times when we take those engines apart and we see that the cylinder’s cracked and we pull the sleeve out, you’ll see oil that’s migrated up the backside of that cylinder,” Irwin notes. “Hot oil gets thin and starts to run. There’s clearance there.”
That often suggests the sleeve and block never made full contact to begin with.

While interference fit determines how securely the sleeve sits in a block, getting it there depends on temperature management. Every sleeving job is an exercise in thermal expansion and contraction, using heat and cold to create enough clearance for assembly before components return to their normal dimensions.

“The parts have to be right,” Irwin says. “They’ve got to be the right size, and you need to have the right temperature differential between the two parts in order to have the clearance you’re looking for so you can slide them in without beating on them or pressing them in.
“Those blocks are able to hold a lot of horsepower, but they’re delicate. The last thing you want to do is go beat on them any more than you have to.”

Irwin explains that every sleeving job requires its own temperature strategy. A Coyote block behaves differently than an Alusil BMW casting or a cast-iron diesel block. Rather than using a fixed formula, builders should measure how the block material expands to determine exactly how much clearance is needed for installation.

“You can figure that out pretty easily – set a bore gauge, heat the block, check your clearancing, and then you just need to know how much larger that bore needs to be for you time-wise to get in however many sleeves it might be,” he says. “If you’re putting in one at a time, you need more of a temperature differential than if you do half the sleeves at once.”
The greater the interference fit, the more important temperature control becomes also.

“When we do the Brad Anderson blocks, I’m going to have a .008” press fit,” Goldbeck says. “You can’t just force a sleeve in with a press, so we carefully heat the block up, keeping it below the annealing temperature of aluminum so we don’t soften the casting. Once it reaches the right temperature, we literally just slide the sleeves in with no pressure at all. Then, when the block cools, you’ve got your full .008” interference fit back.”

Meagher also says the installation process shouldn’t necessarily end once the sleeves are in place. He remembers working alongside a veteran machinist who regularly heat-cycled sleeved blocks, alternating oven cycles with a vibratory stress-relief table before the final deck and bore hone.
“I never had a dropped sleeve with him,” Meagher says. “My sleeving jobs were always successful, which was pretty great because he was doing it with manual machines.”

Meagher suspects some sleeve movement, particularly on newer platforms like the B58, S58, and S55, may happen during the engine’s initial heat cycles, after the car has already been put together and run a few times.

“The head gasket leaks because the sleeve has moved in the block,” he says. “They’ll take the block out, deck it a second time, put it back in and they won’t have problems. But they do get initial movement through the first few heat cycles. I think that could be eliminated by heat cycling the block while it’s still in the workshop.”

Even when a sleeve is installed correctly, the job isn’t done until the engine has made it through repeated heat cycles under load. If the sleeve isn’t secure, it can move or “walk” inside the block. That often shows up as coolant leaks, head gasket failures, or sealing issues that are hard to pin down.

One way to help prevent sleeve movement is with a step at the receiver bore. Many builders machine a register into the block to physically support the sleeve and keep it from sliding down once the engine is running.

“On retrofit repair sleeves, I typically leave a step at the bottom of the block, so the sleeve has a positive stop,” Goldbeck says. “A lot of machinists don’t leave that bottom step and the sleeve can move during operation because cylinder temperatures get extremely high. Once the sleeve moves, you lose your press fit, the sleeve drops and you end up with coolant leakage.”

Some shops skip the step because it’s more difficult to machine. “You have to bore to a specific depth, then come back with a counterbore tool and flatten the step at the bottom,” Goldbeck notes. “You also need to make sure the sleeve is touching that step. I put sealant down there as well to help prevent leaks.”

Leaving out that feature can be costly. Goldbeck recently inspected a 390 block that had been sleeved without a bottom step. The sleeve moved and it started leaking coolant at the top because the head gasket wasn’t sealing properly anymore.

Meagher has observed similar failures. “I’ve seen where the bottom register isn’t in the right place and the sleeve drops,” he says. “That’s probably one of the worst things because then you have to take the engine completely back apart.”

Both agree that sleeve movement usually isn’t caused by just one factor. It can result from not enough interference fit, a poorly designed register, lack of support at the bottom of the bore, or repeated heat cycles. High-horsepower engines are especially vulnerable, since extreme cylinder pressure and temperature make it harder for the sleeve to stay put.

Securing the sleeve is one thing. But if the cylinder bore isn’t machined correctly, it can still lead to poor ring seal, excessive blow-by, oil consumption, and uneven wear – any of which may show up long before the sleeve itself becomes an issue.

According to Goldbeck, builders may not always account for bore distortion once the heads are bolted in place. Often, he says, that comes down to not having the right torque plate during honing. It is why Goldbeck has a wall full of them in his shop.

Tightening the head changes bore shape. A torque plate simulates those stresses during machining, allowing the cylinder to be honed under assembled conditions. But distortion isn’t just limited to head-bolt loading.

“The other thing that sometimes isn’t done is setting up the over and under stroke on the hone correctly,” Goldbeck says. “And that would depend on your manufacturer. If that process isn’t right, it can give you several different shapes on the cylinder you really don’t want. It could end up V-shaped, hourglass-shaped, barrel-shaped, or otherwise distorted.”

Goldbeck also points to surface finish and the crosshatch pattern in the sleeve itself. While some machinists still like reading cylinder walls by sight and touch, today’s ring packages require a more dialed-in approach.

“You can’t just feel it by hand or look at it and say it has an Ra of this or an Rp of that,” he notes. “You really need to check it with a profilometer. They’re not cheap, but for higher-end work you’re probably going to need one.”

Honing remains one of the most important steps in the sleeving process. “We finish ours up with a plateau honing technique like the OEMs use,” Goldbeck states. “A cylinder can look great, but then you start checking the ovality of it, the taper in it, or whether it’s barrel shaped.

“The hone job is just critical. It’s the last thing the block gets before you put the rings in it. Years ago, rings were big and forgiving. Maybe you’d have a 5/64 and a 3/64. But now we’re running 1.1mm- and 1.2mm ring packages with almost no tension. They’re a lot less tolerant of mistakes, which makes honing hugely important.”

If there’s a common thread connecting most successful sleeving jobs, it’s that no single measurement can guarantee a great outcome. Even with the right parts and equipment, trouble can still show up if critical dimensions, material expansion and surface finish aren’t working together. Those elements affect nearly every aspect of sleeve performance and durability.
That’s why achieving consistent results still depends on understanding each platform’s unique requirements, as well as the skill and experience of the person doing the work.

Tim Eichhorn has been building engines since the mid-1990s. But he’s been putting things together for a lot longer than that. “When I was younger, I was a big LEGO guy,” Eichhorn says, “so I think that’s where it came from. I can’t get away from it – I love building stuff.”

That passion eventually led Eichhorn to open MPR Racing Engines in Boynton Beach, FL in 2005. The shop initially focused on Mustang and modular work, but has since expanded into precision machining, Coyote and Hemi builds, and a growing number of exotic and import platforms like McLaren, Lamborghini, BMW, and Nissan GT-R. Its portfolio spans countless class- and championship-winning engines, along with plenty of serious street and performance combinations.

Recently, Eichhorn opened up about what he’s learned from three decades in the industry. Whether it’s running a shop, managing people or staying excited about the day-to-day, his raw, honest insights go far beyond the technical side of engine building.
Engine Builder: MPR became well-known for its Ford work, but over the years you’ve really diversified. Was that deliberate?

Tim Eichhorn: We obviously do our fair share of Coyote stuff, but a lot of other guys are doing it now too, and they do a great job. The Coyote market has become a lot like the LS market in that sense. We diversified by getting into more of the machine work side of it. A lot of guys want to build their own engines nowadays and there are also a lot of shops around town that want to do their own assembly but need the machining work done. We do so many different kinds of work now that we’re not depending on just one thing. We don’t have all our eggs in one basket.

Eichhorn: I do turn people away, usually because we either don’t have the manpower to do it or it just takes too much time. Or, sometimes it’s not worth the effort. There’s stuff that fits, there’s stuff that doesn’t fit, but then there’s stuff that we really get into because it’s new. When a guy comes to us and says, “Hey, I’ve got this McLaren, and nobody makes any parts for it. You’ve got to make everything,” that’s intriguing to us. We like taking on the new stuff and developing solutions for applications where something doesn’t already exist.
EB: Taking a step back, then, what does good growth for MPR look like to you?

Eichhorn: Good growth to me is getting stuff out in a timely manner and continuing to build on the machining side of the business. I’m leaning toward more machine work than I am engine assembly nowadays, only because we can get the machine work done a lot faster than we can engine assembly right now. A lot of guys are giving up assembly altogether. But I don’t want to do that, mostly because I still enjoy putting engines together.
EB: You’ve talked about automation as a practical necessity for the shop. Why is that?

Eichhorn: Obviously, we’ve spent a lot of time trying to find good employees and additional help and that’s really hard nowadays. As a business, the only way we can continue to grow is by investing in more CNC and automated equipment – more things that don’t require as many employees to operate. I hate to say it, but today’s workforce just isn’t the same as it was 10 years ago, or even five years ago. We’ve been dealing with that for a long time and I feel like we’re in a good place right now with the team I have. This is the team I want to keep for a long time. I’m really not looking to add anybody else. Maybe a couple of new machines though.
EB: Speaking of machinery, there’s a myth that having top-of-the-line CNC equipment means you don’t need experienced machinists anymore. True or not?

Eichhorn: Absolutely not true. No. You still have to have a guy who knows what to do, who understands what’s not going right with the process and everything else. I mean, obviously the advent of the CNC machine has made it a lot easier for basically one person to run a machine, but that person has to know what’s going on. When you have multiple steps in a machining process, like sleeving for example, you have different tools, different cutters and so on… so you always have to have an experienced eye on that machine at all times.
EB: Fair enough. What would you say is the most important measuring tool in the shop?

Eichhorn: Oh, the human eye, for sure. Obviously, we have all the top-of-the-line measuring equipment from Sunnen, Mitutoyo and all that kind of stuff, but it comes down to how you read it. You can have the best equipment in the world, but if the person using it doesn’t know how to read a micrometer or a dial bore gauge, that’s what causes problems.

The human eye is definitely the most important tool when you’re measuring something, especially when you’re dealing with tenths of thousandths of an inch. You have to be able to read the instrument correctly and understand exactly where the measuring point needs to be, rather than putting it somewhere it shouldn’t be.
EB: You touched on a few of these earlier, but what’s the most challenging part of running a top-flight engine building and machine shop in 2026?

Eichhorn: You really have to be a business owner who knows how to do everything. I can go into the shop and do cylinder heads, block work, honing, assembly, and I can degree cams. I’m the type of guy who, I won’t say I micromanage, but I know how to do everything that everybody else does. I think that’s important.

With my son Tyler, he started with me when he was five years old, basically coming to the shop with me on weekends and whatever. He has grown into, I think, one of the top machinists I’ve seen in a long time. That makes me proud, even though he’s my son. It makes me proud knowing that he’ll be able to continue the legacy. That gives me hope that at least it’s going to go on for one more generation and that’s good.

That said, the biggest challenge for us right now is parts. Parts that are supposed to be on the shelf are on back order – we’re talking up to 10 or 12 weeks just for something basic. Then you speak to the manufacturers and they just aren’t able to get the material. It’s a slippery slope of everything coming down on us. Something that would take us six weeks to build five or six years ago can take up to 16 weeks to build now just because we’re waiting on parts. That gets to be aggravating.
EB: Do you find customers are pretty understanding of this “new normal” or is there still some frustration on their end?

Eichhorn: Most of the time they’re pretty understanding, because I give them a pretty good lead time. I give myself a few weeks of cushion, so if I know something’s going to take a while, I let them know. I’d say eight out of 10 customers are good with it, and two are like, “Eh, it’s taking a long time. What’s going on?” But if I told somebody 12 weeks and we’re at 14 weeks and I didn’t give them an update, then yeah, they can yell at me.

Customer communication is key, especially when you’re dealing with delays. If I forgot to tell you we’re still waiting on a part, or something didn’t fit and we’re waiting on a replacement, that’s on me. You can yell at me. I’ll take the beating and then I’ll go home and have a whiskey.
EB: After all these years, you’ve obviously learned a lot about building engines. Is there one or two things, in your opinion, that should never be overlooked or taken for granted?

Eichhorn: Don’t ever get complacent building engines, because not every engine is the same. You’re going to have 10 that take the same bearing, the same this, the same that, but there’s going to be that one that needs something a little bit different. When you’re complacent, you’re going to miss it.

Complacency doesn’t belong in an engine shop, an assembly room or a machine shop. You never want to cut corners or let something go out the door without getting your eyes on it. You always want to be hands-on and make sure every product leaving the door is 100 percent what the customer is paying for.
EB: What still keeps you motivated to stay that hands-on?

Eichhorn: I love what I do. I really do. There are times when I don’t love what I do. You’re having issues with parts, you’re having an issue with a customer, you’re having an issue with a machine, it’s not working right, and it just piles up. It stresses you out and you get aggravated.

But then you need to step back and think, “Hey, you know what? This is what I was born to do. I’m not born to sit behind a desk. I’m not born to drive a truck. I wasn’t born to do anything else. I was born to do this.”
EB: Is that how you deal with those occasional aggravations?

Eichhorn: Absolutely. You have good days and bad days and the good days usually outweigh the bad days. If I have a bad day, I go out to the assembly room, clear my head and put a couple engines together. I put some parts together and that’s what it’s all about. That’s what keeps me motivated – the actual thrill of getting it done.
More of this full interview will be featured in Tim Eichhorn’s Intellectual Horsepower episode airing soon on enginebuildermag.com and on the Engine Builder YouTube channel.

Choosing between static and dynamic ADAS calibration depends on the procedure specified by the vehicle manufacturer. Regardless of the method, the vehicle and its surroundings must meet the manufacturer’s requirements.
ADAS systems affected by a repair may need to be calibrated, relearned or re-zeroed. Terminology may vary, but the purpose is to establish an accurate reference point for the system.
A static calibration is performed while the vehicle remains stationary.
Technicians position targets at exact distances and heights. The targets must also be square to the vehicle’s centerline.
The vehicle must meet specified requirements for weight, ride height, tire pressure, fluid levels, lighting and background conditions.
Dynamic calibration takes place while driving. The technician places the system into calibration mode and drives the vehicle under specified conditions.
During the drive, the sensors verify that they can identify the roadway, recognize objects and align correctly with the vehicle’s centerline.
Extra weight, improper tire pressure, incorrect ride height or environmental interference can cause calibration to fail. These conditions can also establish an inaccurate reference.

Whether the procedure is static or dynamic, technicians must follow the manufacturer’s instructions exactly. ADAS calibration depends on precision, and even small inconsistencies can affect system performance.
Verra Mobility Corp.’s latest survey of 2,000 U.S. adults shows that 72% expect their next vehicle to function like a smartphone, with built-in apps and services.

Active connected services usage has crossed the majority threshold for the first time, with 54% of drivers using at least one manufacturer-provided connected service, up from 49% in Verra Mobility’s 2024 survey. Familiarity with the term “connected vehicle” rose to 69%, compared with 60% two years ago.

Fifty-one percent said connected features would influence their decision to buy a different make, model, or higher trim level. All survey respondents own or lease a 2019 or newer vehicle and were at least 18 years old in May at the time of the survey.

The survey defined connected vehicle services as those that use a vehicle’s embedded communications rather than a mobile phone connection. That definition didn’t include services accessed through smartphones, such as Apple CarPlay or Android Auto.

“The story of this year’s survey is that consumers have arrived at the connected vehicle category, and they’re bringing real expectations with them,” said Cathi Chinn, Verra Mobility’s innovation vice president, in a press release. “Drivers now expect their vehicles to behave like the connected devices they use everywhere else in their lives, which puts pressure on the automotive industry to deliver experiences that justify it, especially around the embedded payments, mobility services and safety features consumers say they want most.”

Survey respondents also said they want their vehicles to do more of the work for them, with safety leading the list of services they value most. Accident and theft protection ranked first (31%) when respondents were asked which service category is most appealing if cost is not a factor, followed by maintenance and payments. Fifty-nine percent said they believe connected vehicles make driving safer.

Seventy-two percent said they would value proactive trip suggestions from their vehicles such as parking, fuel, or charging station locations, and handling toll transactions. Forty-three percent said they’ve already signed up for an app or service through their vehicle’s infotainment system regarding parking, EV charging, or tolling.
Sixty-six percent said it would be a valued convenience not having to connect a smartphone every time they get in the car.
The survey results also show that younger drivers led adoption across nearly every measure of the survey:
- Sixty-seven percent of those ages 18–24 actively use at least one connected service, compared to 44% of those ages 55–64.
- Sixty-nine percent of 18–24-year-olds said connected features would influence their vehicle purchase, versus 40% of those ages 55–64.
- Sixty-three percent of 18–24-year-olds and 61% of 25–34-year-olds find the in-vehicle digital wallet concept appealing compared to 44% overall.

As for data privacy, willingness to trade data for tangible benefits has held steady since 2024, but understanding and trust haven’t kept pace with adoption, according to the survey results. Sixty-six percent said they would share driving and location data for insurance discounts, automatic toll payments, and emergency services — mirroring the 2024 findings.
Only 14% said they fully understand what data their vehicle collects, down from 22% in 2024. Fifty-four percent expressed at least some concern about vehicle data collection practices.

Based on a recent large-scale study of the connected vehicle ecosystem, Northeastern University researchers conclude that improved transparency is necessary to identify and address existing harm to passengers caused by the data that “smartphones on wheels” collect.

Researchers found that vehicles and companion apps contact numerous third-party domains, including advertisers and trackers. They also found that vehicle-specific information is being tied to individual consumers. Companion apps expose VINs and a secondary type of personally identifiable information, such as email addresses, to three companies.

Last year, 54% of Americans believed new cars have too much technology, while 72% worried about repair costs if something breaks, according to the second annual Enterprise Mobility’s “On the Move” survey released in October 2025. Nearly 7 in 10 (68%) drivers said they would willingly give up the latest tech for a more affordable vehicle.
More than half of the “On the Move” survey respondents said they would prefer a mix of touch screens and physical buttons.

CCC Intelligent Solutions Holdings announced Thursday that a consortium of private investment firms, led by GTCR and including Elliott Investment Management, will acquire it in an all-cash transaction with an enterprise value of $6.1 billion.
Until the transaction closes, CCC will remain publicly traded and continue operating as an independent company, according to a CCC press release.

“The transaction is not subject to a financing condition,” the release states. “Upon completion of the transaction, CCC will become a privately held company, and its common stock will no longer be listed on the Nasdaq.”
Githesh Ramamurthy, CCC’s chairman and CEO, says Thursday’s announcement “follows a thorough review of strategic options with assistance from our financial and legal advisors.”

The release states that CCC’s Board of Directors approved the transaction, which is expected to close in Q1 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, including the receipt of required regulatory approvals and CCC stockholder approval.

“Our Board of Directors is confident this transaction recognizes the strength of the business our team has built while delivering immediate and premium cash value to our stockholders,” said Ramamurthy.

Under the terms of a definitive agreement, CCC stockholders will receive $7.75 in cash for each share of CCC common stock, representing a premium of 44% to CCC’s unaffected closing stock price on July 9, 2026, and a premium of 59% to the 30-day average price as of July 9, 2026.

A press release announcing the acquisition notes that July 9 was the last trading day before media speculation of CCC’s potential sale. At the time, Reuters reported that CCC was “exploring a sale of the company, according to three people familiar with the matter.”
The article stated: “The Chicago-based company has hired Morgan Stanley to advise on a sale process and has reached out to prospective buyers, including private equity firms, the sources said.”
In August, Seeking Alpha, Bloomberg News, and Reuters reported that private equity firms and Copart were reportedly interested in buying CCC.
At the time Repairer Driven News reached out to CCC for comment on the reported interest. A company spokesperson responded, “CCC doesn’t comment on rumors and speculation.”
Now, Ramamurthy says that with the experience and resources GTCR and Elliot provide, CCC will continue to build on its momentum and extend its leadership.

“Throughout CCC’s history, we have helped customers navigate growing complexity and achieve better outcomes through technology and innovation,” he said. “Together, we will accelerate the AI and agentic capabilities our customers want from us, expand the network at the center of our platform, and continue to develop and build our world-class team. I am deeply grateful to our employees for their dedication and commitment to our customers, and I am excited for all that we will accomplish together in this next chapter.”
He shared similar commentary to a Facebook post by CCC announcing the sale.

A Reuters article published after the CCC announcement noted that “earlier this year, the company faced investor concerns over slowing growth, softer claims volumes and a slower-than-expected rollout of some newer software products, which had weighed on its share price.” Meanwhile, the acquiring firms have expressed confidence in CCC’s underlying business and its opportunities for future growth, particularly through artificial intelligence.

When Repairer Driven News asked CCC for comment on its reasoning for the acquisition, CCC reiterated that its Board of Directors approved the transaction and said it “delivers immediate and certain value to shareholders at a significant premium to the unaffected share price.”

“CCC remains a strong business,” a CCC spokesperson said. “Our Board of Directors is confident this transaction recognizes the strength of the business our team has built while delivering immediate and premium cash value to our stockholders. Beyond today’s announcement and related SEC filings, we do not have additional information to share at this time.”
CCC went public in 2021 after announcing its owners at the time, and a Dragoneer Investment Group spinoff had agreed to a merger and subsequent listing of shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Private equity firm Advent, which owned the majority of CCC at the time, would continue to hold most of the shares once CCC went public. Reuters previously reported that Advent “fully exited its investment in 2025 through a series of secondary share offerings, including the sale of its remaining stake in November.”

On Thursday, Mark Anderson, GTCR media and telecommunications managing director and head of technology, said the PE firm has followed CCC for years and believes it’s “uniquely positioned to support their customers as they increasingly adopt AI solutions to improve decision-making and efficiency across the claims and repair lifecycle.”

“We look forward to partnering with Githesh and the talented CCC team to support continued investment in product innovation and AI capabilities, expand the company’s offerings and build long-term value,” he said. “Our focus will be on helping CCC deliver better outcomes for its customers while supporting CCC’s next phase of growth.”

David Kerko, Elliott’s head of global private equity, added: “We have [a] strong belief in CCC’s position as the trusted third party at the center of the automotive insurance and repair industry. CCC’s role within the large ecosystem of insurers, repair facilities, automakers and parts suppliers creates strong data advantages and network benefits for their more than 35,000 customers. We believe these advantages make CCC a highly durable franchise in vertical software – which AI will only make more valuable as CCC delivers the next generation of capabilities to its customers.”
CCC will report its Q3 earnings on Oct. 29 without a conference call and webcast “in light of the pending transaction,” according to the release.

Morgan Stanley & Co. is serving as financial advisor in the transaction. Kirkland & Ellis is serving as legal counsel, and Joele Frank, with Wilkinson Brimmer Katcher, is serving as strategic communications advisor to CCC.

J.P. Morgan is serving as lead financial advisor to GTCR and lead arranger of committed financing for the transaction. Citi is also serving as financial advisor and participating in the committed financing. Simpson, Thacher & Bartlett is serving as GTCR’s legal counsel. Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher and Debevoise & Plimpton are serving as Elliott’s legal counsel.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) says it “cannot confirm the status” of the remaining 9% of more than 67 million recalled Takata airbags, or whether they remain on U.S. roads.
NHTSA told Repairer Driven News that according to its latest 2024 completion-rate estimates, 91% of the affected airbags had been replaced or were otherwise accounted for.

The Takata airbag inflator recall is the largest safety recall in automotive history and spans worldwide. Issues first came to light in 2008. Vehicles across more than 30 brands are equipped with the airbags, according to NHTSA.
NHTSA says the airbags have killed 28 people and caused at least 400 injuries in the U.S. It linked the 28th death to an incident that occurred in Alabama involving a Honda vehicle.

“NHTSA cannot confirm the status of the remaining 9% or if they remain on U.S. roads,” a NHTSA spokesperson told Repairer Driven News. “NHTSA encourages everyone to check for open recalls at nhtsa.gov or by downloading our SaferCar app. Anyone with an open Takata recall should follow any manufacturer warnings and call their vehicle’s dealership immediately to schedule a free repair.”

The chart below shows the net percentage of airbags remaining for replacement for priority groups 1–12. “Net” refers to the percent remaining from the total airbags count, according to NHTSA. NHTSA includes these groups because vehicle manufacturers have submitted verifiable underlying data.

The chart above specifies the percentage of dispositioned airbags, as approved by NHTSA, including stolen and scrapped vehicles and those exported from the U.S. jurisdiction, according to NHTSA. It also includes vehicles with aftermarket modifications, degraded to the point that the recall remedy cannot be completed, and those to which owners have been nonresponsive to or have affirmatively refused the recall remedy outreach.

The data in this chart begins in 2022 when NHTSA added several reporting categories: nonresponsive, affirmative refusal, aftermarket modification, and vehicle degradation. NHTSA must receive a request before a vehicle manufacturer can submit to these categories. NHTSA notes that not all vehicle manufacturers have been approved for or have requested inclusion in the categories.

Takata, a bankrupt parts supplier, was responsible for manufacturing airbag canisters in defective airbag inflators that can explode and spray sharp metal fragments toward the driver and passengers, comparable to shrapnel from an exploding grenade, which has caused severe injuries and deaths.

According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), propellant in the inflators breaks down after long-term exposure to high temperature fluctuations and humidity. This can cause the propellant to burn too quickly, creating too much pressure and leading to explosions.

As of Aug. 21, Honda says it has voluntarily removed over 535,000 inflators from salvage yards, and the effort continues. The OEM says it has also asked major online auction sites to prohibit and stop any sales of the affected airbags.
A separate group of defective Takata airbags was recalled in late 2019. According to NHTSA, unlike the airbag inflators in the larger Takata recalls, this recall involves non-azide driver inflators.
According to the latest Carfax data, 4.7 million vehicles equipped with recalled Takata airbags remain in the U.S.
Carfax says the number of vehicles on the road with the Takata airbags has dropped 20% from 6 million in 2024.

“Many automakers are working to find owners of vehicles that still have Takata airbags and finally get those airbags replaced,” Carfax states in its September recall tracker report. “Some are even sending teams out across the country to locate affected owners and provide help.

“Despite the drop in affected vehicles, nearly 5 million still need those Takata airbags replaced, and as they get older, they’re more likely to continue to change hands, which makes tracking down the owners more difficult. And some of those vehicles even have ‘do not drive’ orders.”

INDASA announced it has partnered with Save the Rhino International, a UK-registered charity working to safeguard rhino species and their landscapes. The partnership brings together two organizations connected by a shared symbol: the rhino.

For INDASA, the Rhyno has represented strength, resilience and performance for decades. For Save the Rhino International, the vision is a future where all five rhino species thrive in the wild. The idea is straightforward: the symbol that has represented INDASA for decades should also help protect the species behind it.

At the center of the initiative are INDASA’s Rhynogrip and Rhynostick White Line, both in 150mm and in 125mm. Throughout the campaign, these products will feature bespoke packaging designed to reflect INDASA’s commitment to the partnership with Save the Rhino International and to carry the conservation message to markets around the world.

The special-edition packaging becomes a visible platform for the conservation cause, placing it in the hands of the professionals who use these products every day. Every package sold also contributes directly to rhino conservation, creating a clear connection between a professional-use product and a global environmental cause.

Through its products, packaging, digital communication and international network, INDASA aims to raise awareness of rhino conservation beyond traditional environmental audiences, reaching the body shops and distributors where the cause has never been addressed before.

Save the Rhino International works in partnership with conservation organizations, governments and local communities to conserve rhinos and their landscapes. These collaborations bring together knowledge, expertise and resources to support evidence-based conservation, address the challenges facing rhino populations and secure their long-term recovery.

Through this partnership, INDASA is contributing to those ongoing projects and giving the conservation message a route into an industry outside the organization’s usual reach. The campaign gives industry professionals a way into the cause: by acquiring the products they already use in their surface preparation activities, they contribute to conservation efforts, creating a direct connection between product, people and purpose.

Running for one year, the campaign connects every package sold with a direct contribution to Save the Rhino International’s conservation work. For every campaign box sold, INDASA will donate €0.03 directly to the organization.

The campaign identity captures the connection at the heart of the partnership. “By The Rhyno” represents the means: the strength and reach of INDASA’s own symbol, put behind the cause. “For the Rhino” represents the purpose: raising awareness and supporting the conservation of rhinos and their natural habitats.

The donation matters. So does the attention it brings: rhinos placed in front of professionals who would otherwise never come across the cause, and the reminder that a routine purchase can be part of protecting a species.
